fields.title: Portraits of Courage – Mary Slessor
fields.subtitle: A Dundee Weaver, the Twin-Mothers of Calabar, and a Life Laid on the Altar
fields.description: A Christian biography of Mary Slessor (1848–1915), the Dundee factory girl who spent almost forty years in south-eastern Nigeria — learning Efik, living alone in Okoyong, sheltering twin babies and their mothers, sitting as a magistrate, and opening the Enyong Creek to the gospel. Built on her own letters and checked against the civil records and modern historians, it tells the real woman behind the legend: frightened and brave, loving and sometimes harsh, tied to empire and devoted to Africa. All Scripture from the public-domain ASV (1901).

qa.question: What is this biography of Mary Slessor about?
qa.answer: It is a Christian biography of Mary Slessor (1848–1915), the Scottish missionary who went from the jute and linen mills of Dundee to Calabar in 1876 and spent the rest of her life in what is now south-eastern Nigeria. It follows her from her poor childhood and conversion, through Okoyong, the Enyong Creek and Ikpe, to her death at Use in January 1915, drawing mainly on her own letters as printed by W. P. Livingstone in 1916.

qa.question: Who was Mary Slessor?
qa.answer: Mary Slessor was a Scottish weaver who became a missionary of the United Presbyterian Church in Calabar. She learned Efik fluently, lived alone among the Okoyong people from 1888, protected twin babies and their mothers, presided over local courts, and opened new mission work along the Enyong Creek. The people called her Ma, and remembered her as Eka kpukpru owo, ‘Everybody’s Mother.’

qa.question: Did Mary Slessor end the killing of twins?
qa.answer: No, and she never claimed to. The Efik rulers of Calabar, with British consuls, had banned the killing of twins from 1849, and missionaries had been rescuing twins since 1852. What she did was to carry that protection into the interior, take twins and their mothers into her own household for decades, and over time help families keep their children. Many of the babies she rescued died.

qa.question: Why did Mary Slessor never marry?
qa.answer: She was engaged in 1890 to Charles Morrison, a young teacher on the mission staff, on condition that he join her at Okoyong. The Church would not transfer him, she would not leave the people she had promised to serve, and his health then broke down. She wrote that her life had been ‘laid on His altar for that people long ago.’

qa.question: How does the book handle her connection with British colonial rule?
qa.answer: Honestly. Her work coincided with the British conquest of southern Nigeria. She relied on consuls and officials, sat in a colonial court, and entered Aro country with the commander of the 1901–02 expedition. She also refused a government house, said that Europeans were ‘foreigners, and they own the country,’ and defended local people against officials. The book quotes historians who see her as both imperialist and liberator.

qa.question: Which famous quotations are really hers?
qa.answer: The book quotes her letters as Livingstone printed them — for example ‘Heaven is now nearer to me than Britain’ and ‘I am a poor exponent of faith.’ It notes that ‘Why should I fear? I am on a Royal Mission’ cannot be traced before the 2000s, that ‘God and one are always a majority’ was an older proverb she wrote in her Bible, and that the ‘Failed, failed’ quotation came from a newspaper article her friends thought was a leg-pull.

qa.question: How is Scripture used in the book?
qa.answer: Each chapter opens with a passage from the American Standard Version (1901) that carries its theme — from ‘God chose the weak things of the world’ to ‘not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls’ — and further passages are woven through the story, including verses she marked and annotated in her own Bibles. Every quotation was checked against the ASV text.

qa.question: Where should a reader begin?
qa.answer: At the beginning. The preface and introduction explain the sources and how the legend differs from the record; the chapters then follow her life in order, from Aberdeen and Dundee to Calabar, Okoyong, the Creek, and Ikpe. Appendix A gathers lessons from her life, Appendix B is a study guide for groups, Appendix C a chronology, and Appendix D a note on sources.

fields.title: Preface
fields.body_html:
“but God chose the foolish things of the world, that he might put to shame them that are wise; and God chose the weak things of the world, that he might put to shame the things that are strong”

— 1 Corinthians 1:27, ASV

The first volume of this series told the story of Watchman Nee, who spent his last twenty years in a Chinese prison. The second told the story of John Hyde, whose courage was spent on his knees in the Punjab. The third told the story of Corrie ten Boom, whose family hid Jews behind a false wall in Haarlem. This fourth volume goes back further in time, and further from the places where most of its readers live. It tells the story of a Scottish factory girl who spent almost forty years in the forests of south-eastern Nigeria, and who died there, in a mud-walled room, in January 1915.

Mary Slessor was born in Aberdeen in 1848 and grew up in the slums of Dundee. From the age of eleven she worked at a loom in a textile factory. She had almost no schooling. She was small, shy of public speaking, and so timid about ordinary things that she would not cross a busy city street alone. At twenty-seven she sailed for Calabar, on the coast of what is now Nigeria, as a teacher for the mission of the United Presbyterian Church of Scotland. She learned the Efik language so well that people who heard her said she spoke it better than they did. She walked, barefoot and usually alone, into districts where no missionary had lived. She took in twin babies whom their families had been taught to throw away, and she sheltered their mothers. She sat as a magistrate in a British colonial court. She raised a household of adopted African children. Long before she died, the people of the Cross River were calling her “Everybody’s Mother.”

Why Courage?

Her courage is the easiest part of her story to see, and it is real. She stood between armed men who were about to fight. She sat for nights beside prisoners who were to be made to drink poison. She walked through the forest in the dark to reach a dying chief whose people were ready to kill his household if he died. None of it came naturally. She wrote to friends that her courage often threatened to “take wings and fly away,” and that nobody guessed it.

But this book will suggest that there was a harder courage in her life than facing armed men. There was the courage to go on for years with almost nothing to show for it. Her first district saw no baptisms for fifteen years. The African friend who did most to protect her never became a Christian. Many of the babies she rescued died in her arms. She quarrelled with the Church that sent her, and more than once she was tempted to cut herself loose from it. She was often ill, often lonely, and sometimes deeply depressed. She kept going, not because she was sure of success, but because she believed that she had been sent, and that the results belonged to God.

How This Book Is Written

Like the earlier volumes, this book tries to be honest about its sources, and the reader deserves to know what they are.

The main source is the biography by W. P. Livingstone, Mary Slessor of Calabar: Pioneer Missionary, published in 1916, the year after her death. Livingstone worked chiefly from her own letters, and he printed long passages from them. His book is now in the public domain, and so, unlike the Corrie ten Boom volume, this book is able to let Mary Slessor speak in her own words. Her letters are vivid, funny, sometimes sharp, and often moving, and they are quoted throughout.

Livingstone was an admirer, and he wrote in the manner and language of his time. His book is also more honest than many later retellings. He kept her doubts, her illnesses, her temper, and her failures. This book draws on him gratefully, and also checks him. It uses the Scottish civil records of her family, the census returns, and the work of modern historians in Scotland and Nigeria. Where the popular story says more than the evidence, this book will say so.

Two things in particular need care. The first is that Mary Slessor lived and worked at the time when Britain was taking control of southern Nigeria. She depended on British officials, and she sometimes welcomed their power. She also defended African people against them, and against her own Church. A Christian biography should neither hide that story nor pretend that she stood outside it. The second is that the language used about Africans in her day, including sometimes her own, was often contemptuous. This book quotes that language only where it is needed to understand her, and it does not adopt it.

Scripture in This Book

As in the earlier volumes, all Scripture quotations are from the American Standard Version of 1901, which is in the public domain. Each chapter opens with a passage that carries its theme, and further passages are woven through the story. Mary Slessor read her Bible every day from before dawn, with a pen in her hand, and she filled its margins with comments. Some of them appear in these pages.

The verse at the head of this preface is Paul’s: “God chose the weak things of the world, that he might put to shame the things that are strong.” It is not a flattering verse. Paul was not saying that God likes weak people for their own sake. He was saying that when God does great things through unlikely people, nobody can mistake where the power came from. Mary Slessor would have agreed. Near the end of her life, when she was given a royal honour, she wrote that she was nothing more than “the unworthy, unprofitable, but most willing, servant of the King of Kings.” She knew what she was, a factory girl from Dundee. She knew, too, that “we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the exceeding greatness of the power may be of God, and not from ourselves” (2 Corinthians 4:7, ASV). This book is the story of that treasure, and of the earthen vessel that carried it.

fields.title: Introduction: The Legend and the Letters
fields.body_html:
“He that pleadeth his cause first seemeth just; But his neighbor cometh and searcheth him out.”

— Proverbs 18:17, ASV

A Woman Who Became a Legend

Within a year of her death, Mary Slessor had become a legend. Her first biography was widely read in Scotland and beyond. A version for children appeared the same year under the title The White Queen of Okoyong. Popular lives followed in almost every decade of the twentieth century, some for adults, many for Sunday school prizes. From 1997 until a redesign in 2009, her portrait appeared on the Clydesdale Bank’s ten-pound note, with a map of Calabar and a picture of her with African children. In Calabar a roundabout bears her name, with a statue of her carrying twin babies. Schools, a hospital, a road, and even a small asteroid are named after her.

A legend is a kind of compliment, but it is also a kind of distortion. Popular retellings of her life made her taller than she was, and sometimes less interesting. They invented dialogue for her, and gave names to people who were never named in any record. One popular book has a panther carry a baby out of her tent, a scene with no source at all. Others credit her with ending the killing of twins in Nigeria single-handed, or with being the first woman magistrate in the British Empire. Some put words into her mouth that she never wrote. A saying often quoted as hers, “Why should I fear? I am on a Royal Mission,” is not in Livingstone or any source from her lifetime; the earliest printings found are devotional books published nearly a century after her death.

This book is written in the conviction that the real woman is better than the legend. The verse at the head of this chapter is a proverb about lawsuits: the first person to tell a story always sounds right, until the next person comes and asks questions. This introduction explains which stories this book trusts, and why.

Livingstone’s Biography

The foundation of everything written about Mary Slessor is W. P. Livingstone’s Mary Slessor of Calabar, published in 1916. Livingstone was given access to a great mass of her letters, and he built his book out of them. He also gathered the memories of fellow missionaries, government officials, and friends in Scotland. He tells us in his prefatory note that late in life she was urged to write her own story, and was surprised that anyone thought she had done enough to deserve a book.

Livingstone was an admirer, and in places he writes as one. He calls her “one of the most heroic figures of the age.” He sometimes hints that she was more than human, and he defends both her Church and the colonial government whenever they are criticised. His descriptions of Africans are full of the racial theories of his time, and some of them are painful to read today.

Yet he was also, in important ways, an honest biographer. He admitted that she could be “stern and exacting,” that she was “often depressed and worried,” and that many people “could not see her greatness for what they called her eccentricities.” He printed letters in which she confessed her fears and her failures. He recorded that her first district had no baptisms for fifteen years, that her closest African friend never became a Christian, and that some of her rescues ended in death. He told stories of her temper that a more careful admirer would have left out. The result is a book that often contains the evidence against its own enthusiasm, and that makes it useful.

Letters Burned and Letters Kept

Mary Slessor did not leave a large personal archive. She was a tireless letter-writer, but in her last months she destroyed many of the letters she had received, “in case anything should happen.” A colleague is said to have found her burning her personal papers. What survives is scattered: letters in Dundee, in the National Library of Scotland, and in Edinburgh; two small diaries; her Bibles with their crowded margins; and letters to a colonial official who became her friend. Most of what we know of her inner life comes from the letters her friends in Scotland kept and gave to Livingstone.

That means her own voice reaches us through a selection made by an admirer. It is still her voice, and it is quoted freely in this book. But the reader should remember that we hear what Livingstone chose to print.

The Records and the Historians

Some facts can be checked against records made at the time, and where they can, this book checks them. The Scottish parish and civil registers correct several details of the traditional story. Her father was baptised in Aberdeen, not in Buchan as Livingstone says. Her mother bore eleven children, not seven. The deaths of her brothers were from tuberculosis and croup, not pneumonia, as is often repeated. The census of 1891 finds her on furlough in Devon, described as a teacher of the Church in West Africa, with her adopted daughter Janie in the house.

Modern historians have also examined her life. The fullest scholarly study is Jeanette Hardage’s Mary Slessor, Everybody’s Mother, published in 2008. Asked whether Slessor was an agent of empire or a liberator of the oppressed, Hardage answers, “Both, to some degree.” Esther Breitenbach, a Scottish historian, has studied how her fame was built after her death. She argues that much of it was deliberate invention, and that there was little in Slessor’s actual practice as a missionary that was unique. Nigerian historians have their own views. The church historian Ogbu Kalu praised her vision as “much broader and more activist” than that of her fellow missionaries. Other Nigerian writers have pushed back against the idea that a single Scottish woman saved the twins of Calabar, and have restored the Efik rulers, consuls, and earlier missionaries who acted before her.

This book has learned from all of them. It does not accept every criticism, and it does not repeat every tribute. It tries to put her back into her own world, alongside the African men and women who sheltered her, argued with her, worked beside her, and sometimes resisted her.

Her World and Ours

Mary Slessor went to Calabar in 1876, when no European power ruled the region. She died in 1915, when it was part of the British colony of Nigeria. Her whole working life coincided with the British conquest of the country, and she was caught up in it. She asked British consuls for help, sat in British courts, travelled in government cars, and told African children that the government was, at bottom, Christian. She also refused a house the government offered to build for her, so as not to be too closely identified with it. She said plainly that Europeans were “foreigners, and they own the country.”

This book will not pretend that those tensions are easy to resolve. It will tell the story as it happened. The reader will meet a woman who loved African people deeply, lived among them as few Europeans did, learned their language and laws, and spent her life defending the weakest of them. The reader will also meet a woman who shared many assumptions of her time and race, who could be imperious, and who was sometimes wrong.

What This Book Is For

The purpose of telling her story truthfully is not to diminish her. It is the same reason she herself gave for reading the Bible with a pen in her hand. She wanted to know what was really there. Jesus said, “ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (John 8:32, ASV). A legend can inspire for a while, but it cannot bear much weight. A real life, told with its failures and its unanswered questions, can teach us how God works through ordinary, flawed people. Mary Slessor would have preferred that. She spent her last years insisting that she was “not goody-goody at all,” and that her life was a record of what God had done, not of what she had done.

fields.title: A Wild Lassie
fields.body_html:
“Like as a father pitieth his children, So Jehovah pitieth them that fear him.”

— Psalm 103:13, ASV

Aberdeen, 1848

Mary Mitchell Slessor was born on 2 December 1848 in Gilcomston, a district on the edge of Aberdeen. Her birth was entered in the register of the parish of Old Machar. She was named after her mother.

Her father, Robert Slessor, had been baptised in Aberdeen in 1815. Livingstone says he “belonged to Buchan,” the farming country to the north, and perhaps his family did, but the parish register records his baptism in the city. He is usually remembered as a shoemaker, and the records confirm it, but they also show a man who moved from trade to trade. In 1841 he was a handloom linen weaver. At Mary’s birth he was a shoemaker. A few years later he appears as a fireman, a stoker of furnaces. Later still he was a labourer. It is the record of a working man in a hard time, when the old hand trades were dying and the new factories wanted cheap labour, not skill.

Her mother, also Mary, had been born in 1821 at Old Meldrum, a small town in the Aberdeenshire countryside, the only child of William Mitchell and Ann Wilson. She married Robert Slessor in 1840. Those who remembered her described her as sweet-faced, patient, gentle, and retiring, with a deep and quiet faith. She was a member of Belmont Street United Presbyterian Church in Aberdeen, and she followed with intense interest the mission that her Church had begun on the far side of the world, at a place called Calabar.

That mission was only two years old when Mary was born. It had been founded in 1846, and its reports appeared every month in the Church’s Missionary Record. In the Slessor house they were read aloud and talked over. “I had my missionary enthusiasm for Calabar in particular from her,” Mary said long afterwards of her mother. “She knew from its inception all that was to be known of its history.”

Eleven Children

Livingstone says that Mary was the second of seven children. The registers tell a sadder story. Her mother bore eleven children, and at least four of them died as infants, too young even to be baptised. The eldest, Robert, born in 1844, was dead by the time of the 1851 census. After Mary came William in 1850, a second Robert about 1852, Susan in 1855, John in 1857, and Janie, the youngest, in 1862.

Family memory preserved a story about Robert, the elder brother. He announced that he would be a missionary when he grew up. A girl could not hope for such a career, but he consoled Mary by promising to take her into the pulpit with him. Livingstone also tells us that when Mary played at keeping school, the imaginary pupils she scolded and taught were always Africans. Drink

“Dark days came,” Livingstone writes. Robert Slessor drank. He lost his work, and in 1859, hoping that her husband might make a fresh start where nobody knew him, his wife agreed to move the family south to Dundee. The furniture was sold to pay for the move, and the money soon ran out. By the census of 1861 the family was living in Dura Street, in the east of the city, near the textile mills.

The move did not cure him. Livingstone’s account of these years is restrained, but it is enough. Every penny Robert Slessor could lay his hands on went on drink. His wife, who was not strong, went out to work in a factory. Mary, still a child, was sent with parcels to the pawnbroker. She ran by the quietest back streets so that her friends from church would not see her. Then she came home with enough money for the week, and her mother kissed her and sent her out to pay the most pressing bills.

There was one night of terror in every week. On Saturdays, after the younger children were in bed, mother and daughter sat sewing or knitting in silence, waiting for the sound of uncertain footsteps on the stair. Now and then they prayed to quiet their hearts. When he came, he would sometimes throw into the fire the supper they had gone without in order to provide for him. Mother and daughter tried to hide the family’s shame. The younger children, Livingstone says, knew nothing of the Saturday vigils, and the neighbours and church friends were kept from the secret. The family was never publicly disgraced, and they believed that was an answer to prayer. Few families, Livingstone adds, looked brighter or more hopeful in church on Sunday. That was their faith, and it was also their pride.

Mary Slessor rarely spoke of her father. Livingstone tells us that she once wrote and published, under her own name, a story that her friends knew to be an account of these years, but he chose not to reproduce it. He says the memory was the only one that could “send a shaft of bitterness across the sweetness of her nature.” It made her shy, and it made her dread speaking in public. It also, he suggests, made her the fierce defender of children and of the weak, and prepared her for a lifelong fight against the trade in cheap spirits on the West African coast. A Prayer That Was Not Answered

Much later, writing to a friend about prayer, Mary Slessor said something she seldom said about her own life. She was trying to explain that God does not always answer prayer in the way we expect. “I know what it is to pray long years and never get the answer,” she wrote. “I had to pray for my father. That sentence carries the weight of a childhood. She had prayed for her father for years, and he had not changed. She did not pretend otherwise. But she had found another Father, one who did not fail, and she had learned to trust him with the question she could not answer. The psalm at the head of this chapter says, “Like as a father pitieth his children, So Jehovah pitieth them that fear him.” The next verse gives the reason: “For he knoweth our frame; He remembereth that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14, ASV). Mary Slessor knew what a weak and failing father looked like. She came to know a Father who understood weakness because he had made us, and who pitied it instead of despising it. It may be that some of the tenderness she later showed to drunken chiefs and frightened slaves was learned in Dura Street.

A Wild Lassie

In spite of it all, she was not a gloomy child. She remembered herself as “a wild lassie,” and in later life she would describe her childhood escapades with a mixture of amusement and shame. Her mother took the children to Wishart Church, a plain building above a row of shops in the Cowgate, near the old Port Gate, from whose walls the Reformer George Wishart had preached during the plague of 1544. The children went to church with a drop of perfume on their handkerchiefs and a peppermint in their pockets for the sermon.

Her conversion came through an old widow who lived in a room in the back lands of the tenements. The old woman used to watch the children playing in the street, and worried about their souls. One winter afternoon she gathered some of the girls in from the cold and dark to sit by her fire, and talked to them about the danger of neglecting salvation. Then she pointed to the fire. If they put their hands into it, she said, it would burn them. But if they did not repent and believe on the Lord Jesus Christ, their souls would burn forever in a fire far worse.

The words went, Livingstone says, like arrows to Mary’s heart. She could not get the picture out of her mind, and it kept her awake at night. She decided that she had better make her peace with God, and in the words that she herself used, she “repented and believed.” Years later she would sometimes say that it was hell-fire that drove her into the Kingdom.

That is not the kind of conversion story Christians usually like to tell today, and she did not recommend it either. But it is honest, and it is worth noticing what she did with it. The old widow was saying what the apostles said to the jailer at Philippi: “Believe on the Lord Jesus, and thou shalt be saved” (Acts 16:31, ASV). Fear brought Mary to the door. But once inside, she found, as Livingstone puts it, that it was a Kingdom of love and tenderness and mercy. In all her later work she never tried to frighten anyone into it. Livingstone says that she never sought to bring anyone into the Kingdom, as she had come, “by the process of shock and fear.” The girl who had been frightened into faith grew into a woman who drew others by kindness.

So the story of Mary Slessor begins not with courage but with fear, and not with a strong father but with a broken one. It begins in a poor and anxious home, where a mother prayed through Saturday nights and a daughter ran to the pawnbroker by back streets. God had not given her an easy start. fields.title: Fourteen Years at the Loom
fields.body_html:
“It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.”

— Lamentations 3:27, ASV

The Half-Timer

Dundee in the 1860s was a city of chimneys. Its mills and weaving-sheds spun and wove flax and jute into sailcloth, sacking, and canvas for half the world, and they ran on the labour of women and children. Men’s wages were low and men’s work was uncertain, and in many families it was the mother and daughters who kept the house going. The Slessors were one of those families.

At the age of eleven, Mary went to work at Baxter Brothers, one of the largest textile firms in the city. She became what was called a half-timer. The law then allowed children to work in the factories only if they spent part of each day at school, so she worked half the day and went to the school attached to the works for the other half. When she was put on full time she went to school at night instead. For a while she moved to the Rashiewell factory to learn weaving under her mother, who was also working there, and she tried two other works. By the age of about fourteen she was back at Baxter’s, where she became a skilled and well-paid weaver.

Livingstone was careful about the word. In Dundee a “mill-girl” was a spinner, and Mary Slessor was not a spinner. She was a weaver, a “factory girl,” and she would have wanted the distinction kept. She worked at the loom, eventually in charge of two wide looms at once, for about fourteen years.

When she brought home her first wages, her mother wept over them and put them away, saying they were too sacred to spend. But they could not stay unspent for long. The family needed every shilling, and before many years had passed Mary’s wages were the main support of the home.

Six Till Six

The working day ran from six in the morning to six at night, with an hour for breakfast and an hour for dinner. Mary rose at five to do her share of the housework before she left, and there was more of it waiting when she came home. In the weaving-shed the belts whirred overhead, the shuttles flew, and the noise was so constant and so loud that talking was almost impossible. It was, as Livingstone says, hard and monotonous work, and she was one small figure among thousands.

It would be easy to make this sound picturesque, and it was not. It was the life of the Scottish industrial poor, with its long hours and its tiredness, its crowded rooms and its early deaths. Of Mary’s own brothers, the younger Robert died of croup in December 1860, when he was about eight. William, who had become an apprentice blacksmith, died of tuberculosis in April 1870, not yet twenty. Five months later their father died. Mary was twenty-one, and she was now, in all but name, the head of the household.

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from the book of Lamentations, written in the ruins of Jerusalem. It is not a cheerful book, and the verse is not a cheerful sentiment. “It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.” The poet does not pretend the yoke is light. He says that it is good, because of what it teaches: to sit alone and keep silence, to wait quietly, to hope in God when there is nothing else to hope in. Mary Slessor did not choose her yoke. It was put on her by her father’s drinking and her family’s poverty. But when she later found herself alone in an African forest, with fever in her bones and no one to help her, she had already learned to work while exhausted, to make do, and to keep going. The loom had made her hard and patient.

A Book on the Loom

She came out of the factory schools with little more than reading and simple arithmetic, and almost no knowledge of the world. The only books she had read were from the Sunday school library. But her mind was waking up, and she was hungry to learn. She began to take time from her sleep to read. She carried a book to the factory and laid it open on the loom, glancing at it when the work allowed. She read on her way to work and on her way home, walking through the grey streets with her head down over a page. Livingstone compares her to David Livingstone, the explorer, who as a boy in the cotton mill at Blantyre had propped a book on his spinning-jenny. The comparison is his, but it would not have displeased her.

She read above all the Bible. Once a girl asked her for something to read, and Mary handed her own Bible, saying, “Take that; it has made me a changed lassie.” She read it, Livingstone says, not as a duty but as a letter addressed to herself, full of news about the God who had loved her. The psalmist’s words were true for her in a literal way: “Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, And light unto my path” (Psalm 119:105, ASV). She walked a dark road every morning, and she walked it reading.

Her Mother’s Sayings

Her real school was the Church. From the Sunday school she went on to the Bible class, and she brought home the questions that puzzled her and put them to her mother. Mrs. Slessor did not always find them easy to answer. “Is baptism necessary for salvation, mother?” Mary asked once. Her mother thought, and said that the Bible says he that repents and is baptised shall be saved, but it does not say that he that repents and is not baptised shall be damned.

Some of her mother’s sayings stayed with Mary all her life. “When one duty jostles another, one is not a duty,” she was told. It is a piece of hard-won wisdom from a woman who had more duties than strength, and her daughter would one day need it badly, when the claims of her family at home and her work in Africa pulled against each other. Another saying was a kind of prayer: “Thank God for what you receive: thank God for what you do not receive: thank God for the sins you are delivered from; and thank God for the sins that you know nothing at all about, and are never tempted to commit.” It is not hard to hear in the last phrase the voice of a wife who knew exactly what temptation had done to her husband.

Mary’s friends noticed something in her even then. A younger girl in the Bible class, the daughter of an elder, remembered going early to meet her so as to walk with her to the class, drawn by her goodness and her kind ways.

Work as unto the Lord

Paul wrote to the slaves at Colossae, men and women whose work belonged to someone else, “whatsoever ye do, work heartily, as unto the Lord, and not unto men” (Colossians 3:23, ASV). He was not telling them that their condition was good. He was telling them that even labour they had not chosen could be offered to God. The weavers of Dundee were not slaves. But many of them had as little choice about their work as Mary had, and the Church that taught them this verse was teaching them that their lives were not wasted.

She was not wasted. The fourteen years at the loom gave her a body that could endure, a will that did not give up, and a working woman’s understanding of the poor that never left her. It gave her, too, the habit of supporting her family, which would shape her decisions for the next twenty years. She would send most of her missionary salary home to her mother and sisters, and would live on African food because she could not afford anything else. And it gave her a way of looking at people. When she stood years later in an African village, surrounded by women carrying loads on their heads and babies on their backs, she did not look down on them as a lady looks at labourers. She had been a labourer herself.

fields.title: Taming the Roughs
fields.body_html:
“And the common people heard him gladly.”

— Mark 12:37, ASV

Wishart Church

Outside the factory, Mary Slessor’s life was the Church. She went to the Sabbath morning fellowship meeting and the week-night prayer meetings. She taught a Sunday school class of what she called “lovable lassies,” and she added, looking back on it, “I had the impudence of ignorance then in special degree surely.” She took a monthly tract paper, the Monthly Visitor, round the homes of the district. However tired she was after ten hours at the loom, she was not absent from any meeting. “We would as soon have thought of going to the moon as of being absent from a service,” she wrote shortly before she died. “And we throve very well on it too.”

Wishart Church stood in the middle of a slum. Narrow arched passages, called pends, led off the Cowgate into tall tenements with stone stairs climbing outside the buildings to landings and crowded rooms. Out of these dark courts poured crowds of boys and girls who ran the streets day and night with no one to govern them. Mary loved them, Livingstone says, in spite of their roughness. When the church decided to open a mission for them, and took a room at 6 Queen Street, nearly opposite one of the worst of the pends, she volunteered to teach.

The Roughs

It was dangerous work. The older boys came to the meetings to wreck them. “That little room,” she wrote later, “was full of romantic experiences,” and she remembered how some of the older men on the mission staff would surround the “smaller individuals,” herself among them, when they left at night and faced the crowd outside. Before the Sunday meetings she would go through the dark passages of the tenements, knocking on doors, waking the lads, and pleading with them to come. They adored her, Livingstone says, with a shy loyalty, and many of them changed. She visited their homes, and she went “not as one who was superior to the inmates, but as one of themselves.” She would sit down by the fire and nurse a baby, or take a cup of tea at the table. Paul wrote of his own ministry, “To the weak I became weak, that I might gain the weak: I am become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22, ASV). Mary Slessor did not have to become poor to reach the poor of Dundee. She was one of them already, and she never forgot it.

She was criticised for being unconventional. On Saturday afternoons she would take her class of rough boys out of the city into the countryside, which respectable church workers did not do. She loved the green fields, and she thought the boys should see them. It is a small thing, but it is the first sign of a pattern that would run through her whole life. When she thought something was right and useful, she did it, and she let other people worry about whether it was proper.

Learning to Think

She read everything she could borrow. Not all of it suited her. One book much admired in Scottish homes was Philip Doddridge’s The Rise and Progress of Religion in the Soul, which urged its readers to practise meditation. A friend found her looking gloomy and asked what was the matter. “I canna meditate,” she said, “and Doddridge says it is necessary for the soul. If I try to meditate my mind just goes a’ roads.” Her friend told her not to worry about meditation, but to go and work, “for that’s what God means us to do.” She took the advice. It was a lesson in knowing herself. Some Christians are made for quiet contemplation, and she was not. Her prayer would always be the prayer of a busy woman, spoken in the middle of the work.

Another friend, wanting to test her, lent her Thomas Carlyle’s Sartor Resartus, a difficult book. When he asked her about it, she said it was grand. She had sat up reading it and had not noticed the time until she heard the factory bells calling her to work in the morning. From then on her reading grew wider and deeper. She learned to argue with the freethinkers she met on her visits, and she learned to write. Papers she read at the church’s fellowship association were remembered for their good sense and their fervour. Her style, Livingstone says, was formed by the Bible.

The Common People

She was often asked to speak at meetings in other parts of the city, and she dreaded it. Once a friend went with her to such a meeting, but she could not be persuaded to go up onto the platform. Instead she sat in the middle of the hall among the people and gave a quiet talk on the words of the verse at the head of this chapter: “And the common people heard him gladly.” Her friend wrote that the common people heard her gladly too, and crowded round her afterwards to ask her to come back.

It is fitting that this is the first Bible text we know she spoke on. Mark says that when Jesus taught in the temple, the religious experts argued with him, but the ordinary crowd listened with delight. He spoke their language. He told stories about sheep and coins and bread. He did not stand above them. Mary Slessor would spend her life among people whom the respectable world despised, and she would find, again and again, that they heard the gospel more gladly than the respectable did.

fields.title: “Pray for Me!”
fields.body_html:
“And I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then I said, Here am I; send me.”

— Isaiah 6:8, ASV

A Mission Born in Jamaica

The mission to which Mary Slessor gave her life did not begin in Scotland. It began in Jamaica, among people who had been slaves.

Many of the enslaved Africans brought to the Caribbean had been shipped from the Bight of Biafra, and a great number of them passed through Calabar. When slavery ended in the British colonies in the 1830s, the freed people of Jamaica had not forgotten the land their parents had come from. Many had become Christians through Scottish and other missionaries, and they began to ask whether the gospel that had come to them in their captivity might be taken back to Africa. The Scottish missionaries in Jamaica took up the idea, and a small number of them offered to go.

A link with Calabar came through a ship’s surgeon named Ferguson, who had once been wrecked on a slaving ship near the coast and had been kindly treated by the people there. Later, as a Christian living in Liverpool, he used the captains of trading vessels to ask whether the rulers of Calabar would receive missionaries. An invitation came back in 1843, from the king and chiefs of the Efik towns, offering land and a welcome. In 1846 the Rev. Hope Masterton Waddell, an Irish-born minister who had served in Jamaica, led a small party to Calabar. It included men and women from Jamaica of African descent. The mission they founded in Duke Town and Creek Town was taken over the next year by the new United Presbyterian Church of Scotland, and it was this Church that Mary’s mother followed so eagerly in the pages of the Missionary Record.

It is worth remembering that beginning. Later histories of the mission often made it sound as if Scotland brought light to a dark land on its own initiative. In fact the mission was first imagined by freed African Jamaicans, invited by African rulers, and carried out with the help of both. Mary Slessor inherited that story, and in her own way she carried it on.

The Death of a Brother

Mary’s mother once heard the Rev. William Anderson, a veteran of the Calabar mission, speak in Dundee about the needs of Old Calabar, and she was so moved that she longed to give her son John to the work. John was a gentle boy, much loved by Mary. But his health failed. He was advised to seek a warmer climate, and he emigrated to New Zealand, where he died soon after landing. His mother, Livingstone says, felt the loss of her hope for him even more than his death.

For Mary, John’s death was a bitter grief, and it turned her thoughts towards the mission field. Could she take her brother’s place? She told no one. For some time the thought floated in her mind, unspoken, until it slowly became a purpose. She sometimes considered the Church’s mission in South Africa, but her heart always came back to Calabar.

She knew what people said about the place. West Africa was called the white man’s grave. Fever killed Europeans there with frightening speed, and the graveyards of the coastal missions were full of young men and women who had not lasted a year. One of her fellow students later remembered her answer when people asked her why she wanted to go. Calabar, she said, was the post of danger, and therefore the post of honour. Few would volunteer for it, and so she wanted to go, because the Master needed someone there.

1874

Early in 1874 the news reached Britain that David Livingstone had died in the heart of Africa. His body was carried to the coast by his African companions and brought home to be buried in Westminster Abbey. The whole country was moved, and a wave of missionary enthusiasm followed. For Mary Slessor it was the moment to act.

She thought through her situation carefully. Her sisters were now working and could contribute to the home. If she became a missionary, she believed she could still send money back to support her mother. She did not realise how much that decision would cost her in the years to come, but she made it with her eyes open. She would go to Africa, and she would go on helping her family. For the rest of her mother’s life she did both.

When she finally spoke to her mother, Mrs. Slessor gave a glad consent. Some of her church friends were lukewarm. James Logie and J. H. Smith encouraged her. Logie, who soon joined the Church’s Foreign Mission Committee, promised to look after her affairs while she was away. To save money for the change, she took on two sixty-inch looms at the factory, hard work for anyone.

In May 1875 she offered herself to the Foreign Mission Board of the United Presbyterian Church. Her heart was set on Calabar, but she was so anxious to be accepted that she said she would go anywhere. Women had been part of the Calabar mission since its early years, and the Board had found them, in its own rather chilly phrase, “economical and effective.” More were needed. She was accepted as a teacher for Calabar and told to go on with her studies in Dundee. In December the Board decided to bring her to Edinburgh for three months of special preparation.

On the night before she left Dundee, in March 1876, a friend found her standing at the mouth of the close where she lived, in tears. “Good-bye,” she said. And then, with passion, “Pray for me!”

Edinburgh

She arrived in Edinburgh lonely and shy, and found her way first to Darling’s Temperance Hotel, where a small service of worship was held every evening. She lodged with a city missionary, Robert Martin, and became friends with his daughter Mary, and through her with another young woman, Mary Doig. She went to live with the Doig family, who treated her as one of their own. A married daughter, Mrs. M’Crindle, became a friend for life. In later years it was to Mrs. M’Crindle’s house that the tired missionary came first when she returned on furlough.

She attended the Normal School, where teachers were trained, though she was never formally enrolled and her name does not appear in its registers. She was never, in the modern sense, a trained teacher. What she had was a working woman’s intelligence, a wide if irregular reading, and a gift for people.

In the evenings she worked in the city missions with her two friends. At one of them, in the High Street, she gave her first address to a meeting of women. A friend remembered it long afterwards. It was on the question Pilate asked the crowd: “What then shall I do unto Jesus who is called Christ?” (Matthew 27:22, ASV). Christ, she told the women, was standing before them as surely as he had stood before Pilate. “Dear women,” she said, “you must do something with Him: you must reject Him or you must accept Him. What are you going to do?” She said nothing about hell-fire. She put the question to their reason and left it with them.

Her two friends came under her influence. Both offered themselves to the Church for missionary work and were accepted for China. The three Marys, as people called them, spoke at meetings together before they sailed for their different fields. In July the Committee declared itself satisfied with her preparation. Her salary was fixed at sixty pounds a year.

Here Am I

The verse at the head of this chapter comes from Isaiah’s vision in the temple. He saw the Lord high and lifted up, and heard the seraphim crying, “Holy, holy, holy.” His first response was not courage but dread: “Woe is me! for I am undone.” Only after his lips had been touched with a coal from the altar did he hear the question, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” And then he answered, “Here am I; send me.”

That is the right order. The call to go does not begin with a person’s gifts or courage, but with God’s holiness and mercy. Mary Slessor was not a heroine when she offered herself for Calabar. She was a factory worker of twenty-six, poorly educated, frightened of public speaking, carrying the weight of a family she could not abandon. What she had was a sense that God had loved her, and that she owed him everything. Jesus told his disciples, “The harvest indeed is plenteous, but the laborers are few. Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he send forth laborers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:37-38, ASV). She had prayed that prayer in Dundee. Now she was the answer to it.

Scores of Casks

She sailed from Liverpool on 5 August 1876 on the steamer Ethiopia. Two friends from Dundee went with her to the docks. As they stood on the quay they watched cargo being loaded into the ship, and much of it was casks of spirits for the West African trade.

“Scores of casks!” she said ruefully. “And only one missionary!”

It was a joke, but it was also a judgement, and it named something she would fight for the rest of her life. The same ships that carried missionaries to Africa carried gin and rum by the ton, and much of it came from Christian countries. The daughter of Robert Slessor knew what drink did to a home. She was about to discover what it did to a whole people.

fields.title: Learning Calabar
fields.body_html:
“therefore thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner-stone of sure foundation: he that believeth shall not be in haste.”

— Isaiah 28:16, ASV

Arrival

The voyage was a delight to her in most ways. She had spent her whole life inside the walls of a factory and a tenement, and now there was sunshine, sea, and space. Her one grievance was that no service was held on board on Sundays. “My very heart and flesh cried out for the courts of God’s house,” she wrote. Some of the crew told her not to worry: there was always a Sabbath in Calabar.

In September 1876 the Ethiopia entered the wide, muddy estuary of the Cross and Calabar rivers. Mangrove swamps lined the banks. On the islands she could see the ruins of the barracoons, the pens where enslaved people had once been held to wait for the ships. Some fifty miles from the sea the steamer turned into the Calabar River, and at last anchored off Duke Town. On the hill above the town stood the buildings of the mission. Canoes swarmed out to meet the ship, and she stepped down into the mission boat and went ashore.

The World of the Efik

Calabar in 1876 was not part of any European empire. Britain had a consul on the coast and regarded the region as within its sphere of influence, but it governed nothing. The towns along the river were ruled by their own people, the Efik, who had grown rich for two centuries as middlemen in trade with Europe, first in slaves and then, after the slave trade ended, in palm oil. Duke Town, Creek Town, Old Town, and Henshaw Town were in effect small trading states, each with its ruling families and its great Houses.

Mary quickly learned that these were not lawless people. Their society was ordered by laws and customs as powerful as any in Europe. The basic unit was the House, a large household under a master or chief, with his wives, children, and slaves. Slaves could rise to positions of wealth and trust, but they could also be sold or killed at their master’s will. Anyone outside the protection of a House was at the mercy of Ekpe, called Egbo by Europeans, a powerful men’s society that made and enforced law. Its masked messengers could come out suddenly with whips, and women found in the streets could be flogged and stripped. Livingstone admits that Egbo “had a certain power for good” as well, and was often used to keep order.

She also learned that the people had a religion of their own, far more complex than she had expected. They believed in a high God, but lived in fear of spirits, witchcraft, and the dead. Sickness and death were not thought to be natural. When someone died, someone else was to blame, and the blame was settled by ordeal, especially by making the accused drink a poison made from the Calabar bean. When a great man died, slaves and wives might be killed to go with him into the spirit world.

She saw early what this meant for Christian converts. If a man with several wives became a Christian, what was to happen to the wives? If a slave-owner was converted, what was to happen to the slaves? The missionaries were not simply preaching to individuals. They were asking people to step out of a whole social system that held their lives together. Mary concluded, Livingstone says, that the missionary must help to create “a new set of conditions” in which converts could actually live. It was a thought that shaped the rest of her life.

A Church After Thirty Years

The mission had been at work for thirty years, and the results were modest. There were 174 communicant members in all the congregations, though more than a thousand people attended Sunday services. The staff was small: a handful of Scottish ministers and teachers, one African ordained minister, and eighteen African agents. They worked in five stations along the rivers.

But Mary was impressed. She heard African Christians sing the hymns of her childhood in their own language, and heard one of them preach with eloquence and power. At Creek Town she heard King Eyo Honesty VII speak at a congregational meeting. He was a Christian, who led worship in his own town, and she liked him at once. When she told him that her mother in Dundee followed the mission’s affairs with great interest, he was so pleased that he wrote to Mrs. Slessor, and the two corresponded: an African king and a poor widow in a Scottish tenement, brought together by the gospel.

Her first address in Africa was given under a tree, beside a small spirit-house built for a dead man and stocked with food for his ghost. An African agent of the mission, John Baillie, spoke first in Efik, then turned to her and asked whether she had anything to say. She could hardly speak. She asked him to read the fifth chapter of John, the story of the man who had lain by the pool for thirty-eight years, and as he read, her thoughts cleared. She spoke through him as interpreter about the people’s need of healing, and asked them the question Jesus asked the sick man, which she knew in the words of her King James Bible: “Wilt thou be made whole?” The version used in this book renders it, “Wouldest thou be made whole?” (John 5:6, ASV). It was the question she would put, in one form or another, to everyone she met for the next forty years.

Not in Haste

She was impatient. She wanted to see results. “It is difficult to wait,” she said. But she wrote in those early months some words that could stand over her whole life:

Christ never was in a hurry. There was no rushing forward, no anticipating, no fretting over what might be. Every day’s duties were done as every day brought them, and the rest was left with God.

She added a verse, and it is the verse at the head of this chapter: “He that believeth shall not make haste,” in the words she knew. In Isaiah it is God’s promise of a foundation stone laid in Zion, a stone that has been tested and will not give way. Those who trust in it do not need to run. The first Christians saw in that stone a picture of Christ. For Mary Slessor, a woman who by nature wanted everything done at once, it became a discipline. She would spend almost forty years in Calabar, and she would see very little of the harvest. She needed to learn early that the work was built on a foundation she had not laid, and that it did not depend on her speed.

Learning Efik

She was determined to learn the language properly. She had already seen how untrustworthy interpretation could be. She was told of an interpreter who, translating a sermon on the rich man and Lazarus, remarked to the audience that for his own part he would rather be the rich man. She learned Efik by ear, from the people, more than from books, and she learned it so well that visitors in later years said she spoke it better than many Efik did. The inspectors who visited the mission in 1881 and 1882 put her influence down largely to “the singular ease with which she spoke the language.”

She lived at first with the senior missionaries on Mission Hill, the Rev. William Anderson and his wife, whom everyone called Daddy and Mammy Anderson. Mammy Anderson was a formidable woman who, as Livingstone puts it, ruled the town from the mission house. One of Mary’s duties was to ring the bell for morning prayers before dawn. Once or twice she overslept and was scolded. Once she woke in a panic to a room flooded with light, rushed out and rang the bell, and discovered it was the moon. She claimed to have climbed every tree worth climbing between Duke Town and Old Town, and she was often late for meals. When she was sent to bed without food, Daddy Anderson smuggled her biscuits and bananas.

Another friend of those days was Mammy Fuller, a Black Jamaican woman who had come to Calabar in 1858 as a nurse with a missionary family and stayed. She could remember the day slavery ended in the West Indies. Someone once said to her, “Mammy, I believe you would say a good word about the devil himself.” “Well,” she replied, “at any rate he minds his own business.” She would outlive Mary and stand at her grave.

The Man Selling Rum

Livingstone reconstructs, in the present tense, a Sunday she spent visiting in Duke Town. She talked with a father whose only child had died, and who was more troubled by the thought that an enemy had bewitched the child than by the death itself. She sat with women in crowded yards, some listening, some mocking, and she met a girl being fattened in seclusion for her marriage. She concluded that the women were “the greatest problem in the Mission Field.”

In the poorest part of the town she came on a group of men selling rum. When she spoke against the drink, one of them answered her in the pidgin of the coast: “What for white man bring them rum suppose them rum no be good? He be god-man bring the rum, then what for god-man talk so?” Why did the white men bring the rum, if it was bad? It was God’s people who brought it. So why did God’s people speak against it?

Livingstone says simply, “She cannot answer the man.” She could not. The trade spirit that poured into West Africa came from Europe, much of it from countries that called themselves Christian, and it did terrible harm. The man had seen straight through the contradiction. It was a lesson she never forgot, and it gave her an anger against the liquor trade that lasted all her life.

An old woman in one of the poorest huts told her, “I have prayed and prayed till there is no breath left in me. God does not answer. He does not care.” Mary asked her whom she prayed to. “I don’t know,” she said, “but I call Him God.” Mary sat with her and spoke to her of the God who did care.

Old Town

The climate soon broke her early confidence. She had fever again and again, and once she came close to death. In one illness, half-conscious, she thought she had lost her faith in God; when she came to herself she realised that she had given herself into his keeping and need not fear. She grew homesick. “I want my home and my mother,” she wrote. In June 1879, after less than three years, she went home on her first furlough. Before she returned she asked the Committee to send her anywhere but Duke Town. In October 1880 she came back to Calabar, and found to her joy that she was to be in charge of Old Town. She was, she felt, a real missionary at last.

At the entrance to Old Town a human skull hung on a pole. She lived in a house of wattle and mud with a mat roof, with a young woman and several boys and girls in her household. On Sundays she walked a circuit of the villages of Qua, Akim, and Ikot Ansa, holding services under trees and in chiefs’ yards, and came back for Sunday school and an evening service in the chief’s yard at Old Town, where a white cloth was spread on a table with a lamp and a Bible.

It was at Old Town that she began to live on local food, and her colleagues thought it was because she preferred to live like the people. Livingstone tells us the real reason. Boarding with the other missionaries was expensive, and she was sending a large part of her salary home to her mother and sisters. She could not afford to live as the other women did, so she ate what the people ate. She was, Livingstone says, “too loyal to her home and too proud of spirit to reveal the reason.” The simple way of life that later became part of her legend began as poverty, kept secret out of pride.

Twins

At Old Town she came face to face with the custom that would become the great cause of her life. Among the Efik, as among many peoples of the region, the birth of twins was a disaster. It was believed that one of the children must have been fathered by an evil spirit, and that the mother had committed some terrible sin. The babies were killed, often by being crushed into a pot and carried out through a hole broken in the back wall of the house, and left in the bush. The mother was driven out to live alone.

It is important to be accurate about what Mary Slessor found. She was not the first to oppose the custom. The Efik rulers of Calabar, working with the British consul, had agreed to ban the killing of twins as early as 1849 and 1851, and the agreements had been renewed since. The missionaries had been rescuing twins since 1852, and some mission houses, Livingstone says, “were alive with babies.” But laws do not change beliefs. The killing went on secretly in the towns and openly in the countryside. Livingstone adds that Mary “could even see how, from the native point of view, it was essential for the safety of the House, but her heart was hot against it.”

She understood, too, why the babies of slave mothers who died were thrown away. No slave woman could afford to raise another woman’s child, who would belong to the master once grown. She wrote to the Committee asking that one woman missionary be set aside just to care for rescued children. “If such a crowd of twins should come to her as I have to manage,” she said, “she would require to devote her whole time to them.” An old chief, watching the women missionaries at work, gave his verdict: “them women be the best man for the Mission.”

A Storm and a Flogging

She began to travel. A chief named Okon, living in exile across the estuary, begged her to visit his people, and she went in a state canoe with thirty-three paddlers, who sang songs in her honour through the night. She spent two weeks in his compound, sleeping in a room that opened onto the women’s yard, treating the sick and holding services morning and evening.

While she was there, two young wives of a chief were caught having gone at night into a yard where a young man was sleeping, and two other girls who had known and said nothing were accused with them. The men decided that each should receive a hundred lashes. Mary went to Okon, who said that if she forbade it they would listen to her, but people would say that God’s word destroyed the power of the law. So she did something characteristic. At a public meeting she first told the girls that they had done wrong and that she could not shelter them from punishment. Then she turned on the men. “It is your system of polygamy,” she said, “which is a disgrace to you and a cruel injustice to these helpless women. Girls like these, sixteen years old, are not beyond the age of fun and frolic.” After long argument, the punishment was reduced to ten strokes each, with none of the salt and mutilation that normally followed. Mary nursed the girls afterwards and gave them an opiate for the pain.

It is not a comfortable story. She did not stop the flogging; she bargained it down. She had gone, Livingstone says, “as far as she dared.” But it shows the way she would work for the rest of her life: respecting the people’s sense of law, confronting its injustice to the weak, and settling for the best that could actually be won.

On the way home a storm struck the canoe. The crew panicked and the chief was helpless, and she took command, got the canoe into the shelter of the bush, and sat with water up to her knees and the children tied to her under a waterproof sheet. She reached Old Town shaking with fever.

Towards the end of 1882 a tornado wrecked her house at Old Town. She was brought to Duke Town so ill that she was sent home, and in the spring of 1883 she was carried on board the ship, too weak to walk. With her she took a baby girl, one of a pair of twins. She had rescued both, but while she was out of the house the relatives had come, taken the boy by a trick, and killed him. She was determined that the girl would live. The child’s name was Atim Eso. In Scotland she would be baptised Janie.

fields.title: Bereft
fields.body_html:
“Whom have I in heaven but thee? And there is none upon earth that I desire besides thee. My flesh and my heart faileth; But God is the strength of my heart and my portion for ever.”

— Psalm 73:25-26, ASV

Janie

Mary spent most of her second time at home with her mother and sisters at Downfield, a village on the edge of Dundee to which she had moved them on her first furlough. She saw few people, and gave most of her time to nursing the baby she had brought from Calabar. The little girl was baptised in the Sunday school of Wishart Church and given the name Janie, after Mary’s youngest sister. In later records she appears as Janie Annan Slessor. She was the first of Mary’s African children, and she would be with her, with one short interval, until the end of her life.

It is worth pausing on what it meant to bring a rescued twin to Scotland in 1883. In Calabar the child was believed to be accursed, and the woman who carried her was taking on a share of that curse. In Dundee she was a curiosity, a “living illustration,” as Livingstone puts it, of the work of the mission. Mary took Janie with her to the meetings where she spoke, and audiences were deeply moved. It is easy to be uneasy about that today. But the child was loved, and she was alive. Her brother was not.

A Recruit

On a visit to her old friends the Doigs in Edinburgh, Mary met a young woman named Jessie Hogg, who worked in the same city mission where Mary had helped before she sailed. Jessie had heard a great deal about her and was eager to meet her. Within five minutes Mary turned to her and asked, “And what are you doing at home? What is hindering you from going to the mission field?” “There is nothing to hinder me,” Jessie said. “Then come,” said Mary; “there is a good work waiting for you to do.” Jessie Hogg applied, was accepted, and reached Calabar before Mary did. She served there for thirteen years and became one of the women the Africans called the mothers of the mission.

A letter Mary wrote at this time to a friend in Dundee shows how she thought about working among the poor. It is one of the clearest statements of her convictions that survives:

Nothing, I believe, will ever touch or raise fallen ones except sympathy. They shrink from self-righteousness which would stoop to them, and they hate patronage and pity. Of sympathy and patience they stand in need.

She went on to say that the poor also needed teaching, real knowledge of the Bible as a whole, not only the favourite passages used at evangelistic meetings. “I am pained often at home,” she wrote, “that there is so little of depth, and of God’s word, in the speeches and addresses I hear.” The factory girl who had been scolded for her lack of education had become a woman who thought the Church often underestimated what ordinary people could understand.

No Men in the Room

In January 1884 she told the Committee that she was well and ready to go back. The women of Glasgow, however, asked that she be kept at home for a while to speak to women’s meetings around the country, and for some months she travelled and spoke. She found it an ordeal. She was so shy that it was often simply impossible for her to open her mouth if men were present, and she would make it a condition that there be none in the audience. In December the Committee gave her permission to return, and decided to send her, for the time being, to Creek Town.

Cut Adrift

Then her youngest sister, Janie, fell seriously ill. The doctors said that only a milder climate would save her. Mary was torn between her sister and her work, and she came up with a plan she would never have proposed for herself. She wrote to the Committee early in 1885 that she could not go to Creek Town unless she was allowed to take her sister with her, and to build a small mud house where the two of them could live apart from the other missionaries. By living on local food, she explained, she could go on supporting her family.

The Committee, as Livingstone puts it, received the proposal “with a certain mild astonishment,” and refused it. It is not hard to see why. A sick young woman from Dundee would hardly have recovered her health in Calabar. Mary then took the advice of a lady from Exeter and moved her sister to the south of England. The Committee replied kindly. It regretted her troubles, said it would welcome her offer of service again, and continued her home allowance until the end of April. Mary thanked them, and accepted the allowance only until the end of February. She would not take money for work she was not doing. For a time she had cut herself adrift from the service of the Church.

She settled her sister at Topsham, a small town on the estuary of the Exe in Devon, in a house found for her by a deacon of the Congregational church. The records of that church show the family living at 48 The Strand in 1885. Her mother came south to join them. Janie began to improve. Mary joined in the life of the Congregational church and spoke at its meetings about Calabar.

Then another blow fell. Her sister Susan, a dressmaker in Scotland, died suddenly in Edinburgh in April 1885. Livingstone says she collapsed as she entered the house of Mary’s friend Mrs. M’Crindle. It was Mary who registered the death. She was now earning nothing, and she alone had to provide for her mother, her invalid sister, and the African child.

“I Have Given You Back to Him”

She needed to go back to work. Before she applied, she told her mother that she wanted to go up-country, into the unreached interior, if the opportunity ever came, and asked whether her mother would let her. Mrs. Slessor’s answer stayed with her all her life. “You are my child, given to me by God, and I have given you back to Him. When He needs you and where He sends you, there I would have you be.”

The Committee reinstated her gladly. There was talk of a new advance into the interior, and in the meantime she was to go to Creek Town. Friends in Topsham promised to look after her mother and sister. Then, a month before she was due to sail, her mother suddenly failed and took to her bed. All Mary’s arrangements collapsed. She was, says Livingstone, “like a wild creature at bay.” She prayed, and the next day she wrote to an old friend from the factory in Dundee, asking her to come and keep house. The friend came. Mary wrote her long, careful letters of instructions for the journey, forgetting no detail that might make it easier.

Livingstone records one small scene from those last days. On Guy Fawkes’ night, when bonfires and fireworks filled the streets, Mary wanted to take her friend to a church meeting, and did not dare to go out among the crowds of rough young men. She was a woman who would soon walk alone into the most feared district of Calabar, and she was afraid of a Devon street on bonfire night. The contradiction is not a flaw in the story. It is the story. Courage, for her, was never the absence of fear.

The Turn of the Year

She sailed in November 1885 and was back in Calabar early in December. On New Year’s Day, 1886, she began a long letter to her mother and sister, full of love and cheer and news. She finished it two days later, when the mail from home arrived. “I was hardly able to wait for mine,” she wrote, “and then I rushed to my room and behaved like a silly body, as if it had been bad news. It brought you all so clearly before me. At church I sat beside the King and cried quietly into my wrap all the evening.” The letter ended, “Tell me all your troubles, and be sure you take care of yourselves.”

She never had an answer. Her mother had died at Topsham, peacefully, in December, within weeks of Mary’s sailing. Three months later, on 5 March 1886, her sister Janie died too, and was buried beside their mother in Topsham cemetery.

Mary was inconsolable. “I, who all my life have been caring and planning and living for them,” she wrote, “am left, as it were, stranded and alone.” And again: “There is no one to write and tell all my stories and troubles and nonsense to.” She asked hungrily for every detail of the last days, and for keepsakes. “I would like something to look at,” she wrote again and again. Even in her grief she remembered to repay the factory friend for the sixpences she had spent on stamps for her letters to Calabar.

On the night she heard of her mother’s death, she led her usual prayer meeting. She told no one what had happened. She thought her mother would have wanted her to go on.

Nearer Than Britain

Then she wrote a sentence that tells us more about the next thirty years of her life than any other:

Heaven is now nearer to me than Britain, and no one will be anxious about me if I go up-country.

It is a sentence of grief, and of something harder to name. For twenty years her life had been bound up with the needs of her mother and sisters. She had worked at the loom for them, shaped her missionary life around them, and lived on local food to send money home. Now there was no one to send it to. The ties that had held her to the coast, and to Scotland, were cut. She was free, with the terrible freedom of the bereaved.

The psalm at the head of this chapter was written by a man who had almost lost his faith. He had watched the wicked prosper while the righteous suffered, and it nearly broke him, until he went into the sanctuary of God and saw things differently. Then he wrote, “Whom have I in heaven but thee? And there is none upon earth that I desire besides thee. My flesh and my heart faileth; But God is the strength of my heart and my portion for ever.” Mary Slessor was not a psalmist, but she came to the same place by the same road. Her flesh and heart had failed. Everything she had lived for on earth had been taken. What remained was God, and a people who did not yet know him.

Creek Town

She was placed in charge of the women’s work at Creek Town, where she lived in part of the house of the veteran missionary Hugh Goldie. It was a season of famine and sickness. She lived on rice and sauce so that she could feed the hungry, and she had more fever than ever before.

Her household was small but lively. Janie, now about four, was “as wild as a boy,” and shared Mary’s bed, meals, and thoughts. Mary talked to her about the family in Scotland who had died, and the child never stopped praying for “all in Scotland who remember us.” One day a man appeared at the mission house, and Mary learned that he was Janie’s father. She had been told that both parents were dead. She asked him to come and see his child. He shrugged. “Let me look from a distance,” he said. Mary took him by the arm and drew him to the child, who was trembling with fear, and told her in Efik to put her arms round his neck. She did, and hid her face on his chest, and his face softened. After that he walked a long way every other day, with his new wife and a gift of food, to visit her.

There were others in the house: Okin, the son of a slave woman whose mistress wanted him brought up as a Christian; Ekim, the son of the king of Old Town, whose mother had given him to Mary years before; and Inyang, a big, steady girl of thirteen who did the cooking and washing and was kind to the little ones. There were rescued twins, and a baby whose mother had died after a charm was thrown at her door. When Mary asked the child’s owner, a daughter of an old king of Creek Town, to lend a slave woman to nurse it, the answer came back, “Let it die.” Livingstone’s comment is four words long: “She let it live.”

She found comfort in unexpected people. One was an old blind woman in Creek Town, who had nothing in the world except what the mission gave her, and whose hut was open to the rain. “Blind Mary is our one living, bright, clear light,” Mary wrote. “She knows the deep things of God. That old hut is like a heaven here to more than me.” Another was the king himself. King Eyo became her friend and confidant, and she often sat in his state room advising him on the affairs of his small kingdom and his dealings with the British.

In every letter home she asked for one thing. “Pray for us here,” she wrote. “Pray in a business-like fashion, earnestly, definitely, statedly.”

Forward

There was talk of sending her to one of the stations on the Cross River. But her mind was fixed elsewhere, on the people inland whom no missionary had reached. She was, says Livingstone, of the same order of spirits as David Livingstone, and she borrowed the explorer’s own words: “I am ready to go anywhere, provided it be forward.” In October 1886 the mission council in Calabar decided to send her to Okoyong, and informed the Church at home, adding carefully that this was in line with her own desire. The Church agreed.

It would take nearly two more years before she could go. But she had found the comfort Paul describes, the God “who comforteth us in all our affliction, that we may be able to comfort them that are in any affliction, through the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God” (2 Corinthians 1:4, ASV). She had lost her mother. She was about to become a mother to a great many people.
