fields.title: “Father!”
fields.body_html:
“Have not I commanded thee? Be strong and of good courage; be not affrighted, neither be thou dismayed: for Jehovah thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.”

— Joshua 1:9, ASV

Okoyong

Okoyong was a stretch of forest country lying between the Cross River and the Calabar River, a day’s journey inland from Creek Town. Its people had come down generations before from the hills to the east and taken the land by force. They were farmers and hunters, living in scattered clearings under their own chiefs, and they were feared by everyone around them. With the Efik of Calabar they were in a state of more or less permanent feud. Raids, kidnappings, and killings went back and forth, and heads and captured slaves were counted as trophies. British consuls had sent messages to the Okoyong chiefs, and the messages had been ignored.

Livingstone describes Okoyong in the darkest colours his vocabulary allowed, and some of what he says is plainly the race theory of his day. But the practices that troubled Mary were real, and she described them herself. Sickness and death were not believed to be natural, and when a free man fell ill or died, the witch-doctor would name those responsible. They were chained and made to take the ordeal of the poison bean, or of boiling oil poured over the hands. When a chief died, slaves and wives were killed to accompany him. A few months before she arrived, Livingstone says, a chief of middling rank was buried with eight slave men, eight slave women, ten girls, ten boys, and four of his free wives. After she had lived there some time, she made her own inquiries and estimated that at least a hundred and fifty lives a year were being taken at funerals within twenty miles of her house, and as many again by the ordeal. We cannot check her figures. They were what she believed after careful questioning, and they explain why she went.

There was drink everywhere. Gin, guns, and chains, Livingstone says, were almost the only goods that came into Okoyong. Babies were given gin. Work was paid for in gin. Fines and debts were settled in gin. Quarrels followed the drinking, and then the guns came out, and after the guns the chains.

The mission had tried before. One missionary exploring the district had been seized and held for a ransom of rum, and escaped with difficulty. An African teacher from Calabar had settled there, and had been driven out after a shooting. When the Okoyong heard about the new laws in Calabar, Livingstone says, they were amazed. Killing for witchcraft forbidden? Then what was being done to stop witchcraft from killing? Twins and their mothers taken to Duke Town? Had no disaster followed? To them the reforms of the coast looked like madness.

Three Visits

It took a year of negotiation before Mary could go. Three times she went up with parties from the mission, and each time the people, men, women, and children, came out armed and sullen and promised nothing. She wrote afterwards, “I had often a lump in my throat, and my courage repeatedly threatened to take wings and fly away, though nobody guessed it!”

In June 1888 she went up once more to settle the arrangements. King Eyo lent her the royal canoe, a hollowed tree-trunk twenty feet long with a shelter of palm leaves, a piece of Brussels carpet, and six pillows. The paddlers were Efik, sworn enemies of the people she was going to meet. As they paddled up the river she thought, “Man can do nothing with such a people,” and left the matter with God.

From the landing beach a forest track led four miles inland to a village of mud huts called Ekenge. The people crowded round her and called her “Mother.” The chief, Edem, was sober and welcoming. That night she gathered the paddlers for family worship, and the villagers stood watching in wonder as they heard the Efik boys repeat together the words, “God so loved the world.” The women kept her talking until late. One of them, the chief’s sister, drew her attention. “I think,” Mary said, “she will be my friend, and be an attentive hearer of the Gospel.” The first half of that hope came true. Her name was Eme Ete, and everyone called her Ma Eme.

At Ifako, a neighbouring village, the chiefs promised her ground for a school. She asked whether the school would be a place of refuge, as the mission buildings in Calabar were, for people accused of witchcraft or marked for death at a funeral. They agreed. She asked whether her own house would be a refuge too. They agreed again. She chose two sites at once, one at Ekenge and one at Ifako, so that the promise would cover as many people as possible.

When her friends in Creek Town saw her packing, they looked at her with pity. They said that nothing on earth would subdue Okoyong except a consul and a gunboat. She smiled and went on packing.

4 August 1888

By the evening of Friday 3 August 1888 everything was ready. She lay down, but did not sleep.

The next morning was grey and pouring with rain. The carriers grumbled and quarrelled. She was tired and low, and was glad to see King Eyo, who had come down himself to see the canoe loaded. Few people wished her well. One young man said to her, with a sob in his voice, “I will constantly pray for you, but you are courting death.” Livingstone remarks that it was not great faith for a Christian, but that Mary’s own faith that morning was not strong enough for her to criticise him. At the last moment the senior missionary decided that someone should go with her, and the mission printer, Mr. Bishop, stepped into the canoe. With five children from her household, Mary settled into a corner, and the canoe pushed off into the rain.

It was nearly dark when they reached the landing beach, and there were four miles of forest still to walk. She went ahead with the children, to get them fed and asleep, leaving Mr. Bishop and the carriers to follow with the loads. As she faced the forest, dark and loud with the noises of the night, a feeling of helplessness and fear came over her. What would she find at the end? Would the people be fighting, or drinking, or dancing? Livingstone says that her heart “played the coward,” and she wanted to turn and run. She tried to pray and could not even move her lips. She could only look up and say, inwardly, one word: “Father!”

It was enough. Paul wrote to the Romans, “ye received not the spirit of bondage again unto fear; but ye received the spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15, ASV). The cry of a frightened child to its father is the most basic prayer there is, and it is the one the Spirit teaches. Mary Slessor had learned to pray for an earthly father who did not change. Now, alone in the forest at the start of the great work of her life, the only prayer she had was to her heavenly one.

The Procession

Livingstone describes the little procession that walked into Okoyong that night. First came a boy of about eleven with a box of tea, sugar, and bread on his head, his wet clothes clinging to him, his feet slipping in the mud. Behind him was a boy of eight, crying, carrying a kettle and pots. Then a little boy of three, crying loudly, trying to keep up, and a girl of five, sobbing. Last came Mary, with a bundle on one arm and a baby girl riding on her shoulders, pulling herself along by the branches. She was singing nonsense songs to cheer the children, with tears close to her own eyes.

It is hard to imagine a less impressive invasion. Livingstone could not resist the obvious comment, and it is the verse at the head of the preface of this book: God often chooses the weak things of the world to confound the strong.

When they reached Ekenge, the village was silent. Two slaves came out and explained that the chief’s mother had died that morning at Ifako, and everyone had gone to the funeral. Mary knew what that might mean: a death in a chief’s family was exactly the occasion for killing. She undressed the children, got them to sleep, and sat in her wet clothes to wait.

When Mr. Bishop arrived, it was with bad news. The carriers were exhausted and refused to bring anything up that night. There was no food. The children had nothing dry to wear, and the next day was Sunday. So she sent a boy with a lantern to the beach, asked Mr. Bishop to gather some slaves from the farms as carriers, and went back into the forest herself, without boots or hat. One of the other boys ran after her so that she would not be alone. It was so dark that she kept losing sight of his white clothes, and she fell again and again. When she reached the river she waded out to the canoe, pulled back the cover under which the paddlers were sleeping, and roused them. By midnight the loads were at Ekenge. Her feet were so badly cut that for six weeks she could not wear boots.

The Saddest Sunday

Her first Sunday in Okoyong, she told friends later, was one of the saddest days she ever spent. She ached all over. It rained without stopping. The village was squalid, the people were at a funeral that might end in killing, and she was more than once close to tears. Livingstone wonders whether her faith had weakened. Perhaps it had. What is certain is that she did not go home. A few women came back from Ifako with fretful babies or to fetch food, and she gathered them together and told them, as simply as she could, about Jesus. Livingstone calls it “the first faint gleam of a better day for Okoyong.”

The verse at the head of this chapter was spoken to Joshua at the edge of a land he had to enter. “Be strong and of good courage; be not affrighted, neither be thou dismayed.” It is often read as if it describes a brave man. It does not. God does not tell people not to be afraid unless they are afraid. The command came with a reason: “for Jehovah thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.” Joshua’s courage was not a feeling. It was trust in a presence. Mary Slessor walked into Okoyong afraid, and she stayed there afraid, on and off, for fifteen years. What kept her there was not that the fear went away, but that she was not alone.

A Room in the Women’s Yard

She was given a room in the women’s yard of Chief Edem’s compound, which had belonged to one of his wives. With her own hands she fitted a door and a window frame, and filled the gaps in the walls with mud. For many weeks this was her home, shared with the three boys and two girls of her household, next to the rooms of the chief and his wives, with two cows on the other side of the partition.

Her work began with a child. In a fight between Okoyong and Calabar, a man from Ekenge had been killed and beheaded. His wife died of the shock, and their baby girl was brought to Mary, starved and weak. People laughed to see the white woman carrying the child about. But the grandmother came and blessed her. For a few days the baby seemed to rally, and then she died. It was the custom to bury infants anywhere near the huts. Mary dressed the little body in white, laid it in a wooden box, covered it with flowers, and buried it in her own ground with prayer, while the grandmother knelt sobbing at her feet. People from Ifako came to watch the white woman’s “witchcraft,” and said, in effect, “Why this waste?” The words are the ones the disciples used when a woman poured her precious ointment over Jesus. A First Victory, and Its Price

When the people came back from the funeral, they turned on a young man who had stayed behind in the village and been attentive to Mary. They accused him of deserting their customs, and made him take the ordeal of boiling oil. She saw what was happening too late to stop it, and watched the oil poured over his hands.

Soon afterwards a young slave woman, newly bought as a wife by a local master, went into the hut of a male slave at one of the farms and refused to leave, and then walked into the forest and hanged herself. The male slave was brought in chained. The master and his family decided that he must die, since he must have used sorcery to put the thought into her mind, and the witch-doctor had said so. Mary argued that he had done nothing wrong. The crowd grew angry, and people shouted that a stranger who was there only on sufferance had no right to interfere with the dignity of the free-born. Guns and swords were waved in her face. She stood her ground, quiet and patient, and in the end they agreed to spare his life. It was, says Livingstone, her first victory.

But Livingstone, to his credit, does not stop there. The man’s life was spared, but he was loaded with chains, starved, flogged, and his body was cut to drive out the sorcery they believed was in him. When Mary went to find him, he was lying unconscious, a bleeding heap, tied to a post, while the women of the yard sat by and took no notice.

That was what victory looked like in Okoyong in 1888. It was real, and it was partial. A life had been saved that would otherwise have been taken, and the price of saving it had been paid in the man’s own body. Mary Slessor would win many such victories over the next fifteen years, and very few of them would be clean. She had not come to a place where one brave act would change everything. She had come to a place where the old customs were woven into every part of life, and where the people themselves, as she would later discover, were often as weary of them as she was, and as unable to break free.

Its people had come down generations before from the hills to the east and taken the land by force. They were farmers and hunters, living in scattered clearings under their own chiefs, and they were feared by everyone around them. With the Efik of Calabar they were in a state of more or less permanent feud. Raids, kidnappings, and killings went back and forth, and heads and captured slaves were counted as trophies. British consuls had sent messages to the Okoyong chiefs, and the messages had been ignored. Livingstone describes Okoyong in the darkest colours his vocabulary allowed, and some of what he says is plainly the race theory of his day. But the practices that troubled Mary were real, and she described them herself. Sickness and death were not believed to be natural, and when a free man fell ill or died, the witch-doctor would name those responsible. They were chained and made to take the ordeal of the poison bean, or of boiling oil poured over the hands. When a chief died, slaves and wives were killed to accompany him. A few months before she arrived, Livingstone says, a chief of middling rank was buried with eight slave men, eight slave women, ten girls, ten boys, and four of his free wives. After she had lived there some time, she made her own inquiries and estimated that at least a hundred and fifty lives a year were being taken at funerals within twenty miles of her house, and as many again by the ordeal. We cannot check her figures. They were what she believed after careful questioning, and they explain why she went. There was drink everywhere. Gin, guns, and chains, Livingstone says, were almost the only goods that came into Okoyong. Babies were given gin. Work was paid for in gin. Fines and debts were settled in gin. Quarrels followed the drinking, and then the guns came out, and after the guns the chains. The mission had tried before. One missionary exploring the district had been seized and held for a ransom of rum, and escaped with difficulty. An African teacher from Calabar had settled there, and had been driven out after a shooting. When the Okoyong heard about the new laws in Calabar, Livingstone says, they were amazed. Killing for witchcraft forbidden? Then what was being done to stop witchcraft from killing? Twins and their mothers taken to Duke Town? Had no disaster followed? To them the reforms of the coast looked like madness. Three Visits It took a year of negotiation before Mary could go. Three times she went up with parties from the mission, and each time the people, men, women, and children, came out armed and sullen and promised nothing. She wrote afterwards, “I had often a lump in my throat, and my courage repeatedly threatened to take wings and fly away, though nobody guessed it!” In June 1888 she went up once more to settle the arrangements. King Eyo lent her the royal canoe, a hollowed tree-trunk twenty feet long with a shelter of palm leaves, a piece of Brussels carpet, and six pillows. The paddlers were Efik, sworn enemies of the people she was going to meet. As they paddled up the river she thought, “Man can do nothing with such a people,” and left the matter with God. From the landing beach a forest track led four miles inland to a village of mud huts called Ekenge. The people crowded round her and called her “Mother.” The chief, Edem, was sober and welcoming. That night she gathered the paddlers for family worship, and the villagers stood watching in wonder as they heard the Efik boys repeat together the words, “God so loved the world.” The women kept her talking until late. One of them, the chief’s sister, drew her attention. “I think,” Mary said, “she will be my friend, and be an attentive hearer of the Gospel.” The first half of that hope came true. Her name was Eme Ete, and everyone called her Ma Eme. At Ifako, a neighbouring village, the chiefs promised her ground for a school. She asked whether her own house would be a refuge too. They agreed again. She chose two sites at once, one at Ekenge and one at Ifako, so that the promise would cover as many people as possible. When her friends in Creek Town saw her packing, they looked at her with pity. They said that nothing on earth would subdue Okoyong except a consul and a gunboat. She smiled and went on packing. 4 August 1888 By the evening of Friday 3 August 1888 everything was ready. She lay down, but did not sleep. The next morning was grey and pouring with rain. The carriers grumbled and quarrelled. She was tired and low, and was glad to see King Eyo, who had come down himself to see the canoe loaded. Few people wished her well. One young man said to her, with a sob in his voice, “I will constantly pray for you, but you are courting death.” Livingstone remarks that it was not great faith for a Christian, but that Mary’s own faith that morning was not strong enough for her to criticise him. At the last moment the senior missionary decided that someone should go with her, and the mission printer, Mr. Bishop, stepped into the canoe. With five children from her household, Mary settled into a corner, and the canoe pushed off into the rain. It was nearly dark when they reached the landing beach, and there were four miles of forest still to walk. She went ahead with the children, to get them fed and asleep, leaving Mr. Bishop and the carriers to follow with the loads. As she faced the forest, dark and loud with the noises of the night, a feeling of helplessness and fear came over her. What would she find at the end? Would the people be fighting, or drinking, or dancing? Livingstone says that her heart “played the coward,” and she wanted to turn and run. She tried to pray and could not even move her lips. She could only look up and say, inwardly, one word: “Father!” It was enough. Paul wrote to the Romans, “ye received not the spirit of bondage again unto fear; but ye received the spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father” (Romans 8:15, ASV). The cry of a frightened child to its father is the most basic prayer there is, and it is the one the Spirit teaches. Mary Slessor had learned to pray for an earthly father who did not change. Now, alone in the forest at the start of the great work of her life, the only prayer she had was to her heavenly one. The Procession Livingstone describes the little procession that walked into Okoyong that night. First came a boy of about eleven with a box of tea, sugar, and bread on his head, his wet clothes clinging to him, his feet slipping in the mud. Last came Mary, with a bundle on one arm and a baby girl riding on her shoulders, pulling herself along by the branches. She was singing nonsense songs to cheer the children, with tears close to her own eyes. It is hard to imagine a less impressive invasion. When they reached Ekenge, the village was silent. Two slaves came out and explained that the chief’s mother had died that morning at Ifako, and everyone had gone to the funeral. fields.title: Ma Eme
fields.body_html:
“A friend loveth at all times; And a brother is born for adversity.”

— Proverbs 17:17, ASV

Life in the Harem

For many weeks after she arrived, Mary Slessor lived in the women’s yard of Chief Edem’s compound at Ekenge. Her room was next to that of the chief and his head wife. Five lesser wives lived close by, and other wives, slaves, visitors, and children came and went all day. Goats, fowls, rats, cockroaches, and centipedes were everywhere. At night the three boys of her household slept behind a barrier of boxes, and the two girls shared her side of the room. Every evening her belongings had to be carried outside to make space for everyone to lie down, and since it was the rainy season they had to be dried in the sun each morning.

There was no privacy at all. The wives and their visitors thought it their duty to keep her company, because in Okoyong, as Livingstone puts it, the idea of being alone was terrible, and good manners required that a guest never be left by herself. Mary longed for silence. She wanted a place where she could pray aloud. When she escaped to the patch of ground set apart for her, the women followed her. So she took a machete and hacked at the bush, praying as she worked, so that the noise of the blade covered her voice.

It is one of the most human pictures in the whole of her story: a small, exhausted Scotswoman chopping at the undergrowth in a forest clearing, talking to God at the top of her voice so that nobody would hear.

Eme Ete

The woman who made those months bearable was the chief’s sister, Eme Ete, whom Mary had noticed on her first visit. Ma Eme was the widow of a powerful chief. She had just come back from the ceremonies after her husband’s death, where all his wives had been under suspicion of having caused it. Each wife had brought a white fowl to the place of trial, and the witch-doctor had cut off its head and judged her guilt or innocence by the way the body fluttered. When Ma Eme was declared innocent, she fainted with the strain.

One day Mary noticed marks on Ma Eme’s arms and, showing her own vaccination scar, said that white people had marks like that too. Ma Eme answered simply, “These are the marks of the teeth of my husband.” In Okoyong a man could do almost what he liked with his wife.

She was a big woman, fattened in the way that was admired in her society, and with the other women she spoke in the rough manner of the yard. But when she spoke to Mary or the children, Livingstone says, her voice softened. She was a mother to everyone in the compound. She scolded, encouraged, and advised, and when her brother was drunk or in a temper she stood between him and his wives. She brought Mary food and looked after her comfort, and did it, Livingstone says, “with the delicacy and reserve of a well-bred lady.” Mary called her “a noble woman, according to her lights and knowledge.”

A Secret Ally

What nobody else knew was that Ma Eme had made herself Mary’s ally. At the risk of her life she kept Mary informed of everything that was planned in secret: who had been accused, who was chained in a farm hut, when an ordeal was to be held, when a war was about to begin. She became, in Livingstone’s phrase, a sort of secret intelligence department.

In later years the two women worked out a signal. If Ma Eme learned that some killing was being planned, she would send a certain bottle to the mission house with a request for medicine. It was a warning that Mary should be ready to act at a moment’s notice. On one occasion, Livingstone says, Mary lay down every night for a month without undressing, ready to go out the moment she was called. The first night she allowed herself to undress and sleep properly, the call came, and she went as she was.

The chiefs came to believe that the white woman could read their minds. Much of what looked like second sight was Ma Eme.

It is worth being clear about what this meant. Ma Eme was the sister of the chief. She belonged to one of the leading families of Okoyong, and she had herself been through the ordeals and the fear. She was not a Christian, and she did not become one. She sacrificed to the spirits every day of her life. And yet, again and again, she risked her own safety to warn a foreign woman about plans to kill people accused of witchcraft. We do not know all her reasons. Perhaps she loved Mary. Perhaps she, too, was weary of the killing. Perhaps she knew what it was to stand before the witch-doctor waiting for the verdict. Whatever her reasons, much of the life-saving for which Mary Slessor became famous would have been impossible without her.

The Women of the Yard

Mary saw terrible things in those months. A young wife gave a hired slave a piece of yam as part of his wages while her husband was away, breaking the law of the harem, and was condemned to the ordeal of boiling oil. As the drinking went on, the cords that bound her were tightened for sport until she screamed. Mary went out, faced the crowd, and carried her off, and kept her chained to her own verandah until the dancing ended at dawn, which was the only way to keep her safe.

She also saw the women of the yard at their best. Once a large number of prisoners lay chained in the heat all day, waiting for the poison ordeal. Among them were mothers with babies. At dusk, when the guards left for a while, some of the older women crept up to them with water for the children and the mothers. Mary had had rice cooked in readiness, and the women smuggled that to the prisoners too. If they had been caught, Livingstone says, their lives would have been forfeit.

She did not idealise Okoyong. Some of the things she saw in the harem, she said, she could never describe, and years later the memory of them would still make her flush. “Had I not felt my Saviour close beside me,” she said, “I would have lost my reason.” She had no patience with people at home who talked about the innocence of those who lived outside civilisation. She told them to go and live for a month in a West African harem. It may have owed as much to a Calvinist’s conviction that sin runs through every human society as to the prejudices of her time. She had, after all, grown up with a drunken father in a Dundee slum.

School by Lamplight

She began teaching almost at once, before she had any buildings. At Ifako the school was held on the verandah of a house by the roadside, with lengths of firewood for seats and an alphabet card hung on a post. At Ekenge it was held in the evening, in the chief’s outer yard, when the wives and slaves had finished their work. Men and women, old and young, slave and free, crowded in to learn the alphabet and the multiplication table. Then she held worship, standing bareheaded and barefoot beside a small table with a lamp and a Bible on it, while the people sat on the ground in the dark. She taught them to sing the gospel to their own tunes. One day, passing the school, she heard them singing to the melody of an Okoyong war-song:

Jesus the Son of God came down to earth,

He came to save us from our sins.

He was born poor that He might feel for us.

The Chief’s Abscess

Chief Edem had been kind to her from the beginning, and when he fell ill with an abscess on his back she nursed him. One morning she came in with his tea and found a live fowl impaled on a stick, charms hung all round him, and the chief holding out a parcel of shot, powder, teeth, bones, and eggshells that he said had been taken out of his back. Someone had bewitched him. Before her eyes, men and women were named, seized, and chained to posts in the yard.

She argued and pleaded, and the chief grew so irritated that he had himself carried off to one of his farms with the prisoners, and forbade her to follow. But she had her own ways of knowing what was happening, and she heard that more people were being chained. On New Year’s Eve, lying awake homesick with tears in her eyes, she was roused by a deputation from the farm. They had heard that an African minister in Calabar, the Rev. Esien Ukpabio, the first convert of the Calabar mission, knew how to treat such illnesses. Would she write to ask him to come? She wrote at once. Ukpabio refused, because he was told that the trouble was a soul troubling the chief, and he could do nothing about that. But his sister went, and under her care the abscess broke and the chief recovered.

All the prisoners were released except one woman, who was put to death. The chief sent his son to Mary to tell her, before anyone else could, that nobody had been hurt. Only one worthless slave woman, he said, had been sold away. Mary knew it was a lie. She knew the woman had been killed, and she thought of the faces of the three children the woman left behind. But she pretended to believe it. If she had shown that she knew the truth, the chief would have wanted to know how she knew, and scores of people might have been put to the poison ordeal to find her informant. Livingstone does not name the informant. It is hard not to think of Ma Eme.

That was the price of friendship in Okoyong. Mary’s knowledge saved lives, but only as long as it was secret. There were times when protecting the one who had told her meant keeping silent about a murder. She did not like it, and she did it.

A Foolish Choice?

The friendship lasted for twenty-five years. Ma Eme’s people built the boathouse at the river where Mary kept her canoe. Ma Eme stood beside her in the worst crisis of her early years, as the next chapter will tell. When the population of Okoyong moved inland in the 1890s, Ma Eme moved away to a distant farm, but they stayed in touch.

In July 1913, near the end of her life, Mary went back to Okoyong for a visit, and Ma Eme came to see her. She was still a devout follower of the old religion. She sacrificed daily to the spirits with food and blood, and she would not touch the twins who had grown up in Mary’s house, though she admitted it was a marvel that they had lived. The two old women sat together all day and talked about the past. “Do you remember this?” “Do you remember that?” They talked, Livingstone says, about “the killing time when they worked hand in hand in secret for the preservation of life.” Nothing Mary could say would move her friend. At the end of the day Ma Eme went away, as Livingstone puts it, “the same kind, high-bred, mysterious heathen woman that she had always been.” She died not long afterwards.

Mary said:

My dear old friend and almost sister, she made the saving of life so often possible in the early days. It is sad that she did not come out for Christ. She could have been the honoured leader of God’s work had she risen to it. I cannot fancy Okoyong without her. She made a foolish choice, and yet God cannot forget all she was to me, and all she helped me to do in those dark and bloody days.

Mary Slessor did not pretend that her friend was a Christian. She believed that Christ was the only way to God, and she grieved that Ma Eme had not come to him. She called her choice foolish. But she would not stop there. She knew what Ma Eme had done, and she trusted that God knew it too.

A lawyer once asked Jesus who his neighbour was, and Jesus answered with a story in which the one who stopped to help a wounded man was a Samaritan, a man the lawyer would have regarded as outside the true faith. Then Jesus asked, “Which of these three, thinkest thou, proved neighbor unto him that fell among the robbers? And he said, He that showed mercy on him. And Jesus said unto him, Go, and do thou likewise” (Luke 10:36-37, ASV). Jesus did not say that the Samaritan’s religion was right. He said that his mercy was real, and that it put the religious people to shame.

There is a proper humility for Christians in a friendship like this one. It does not mean pretending that all faiths are the same, which Mary would never have done. It means recognising mercy when we see it, being grateful for it, and leaving to God the things that only God can judge. When Abraham pleaded for the people of Sodom, he asked, “shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?” (Genesis 18:25, ASV). Mary Slessor left her dearest African friend in the hands of that Judge. That is where she belongs in this book too: honoured, grieved over, and left with God.

On one occasion, Livingstone says, Mary lay down every night for a month without undressing, ready to go out the moment she was called. The first night she allowed herself to undress and sleep properly, the call came, and she went as she was. The chiefs came to believe that the white woman could read their minds. Much of what looked like second sight was Ma Eme. It is worth being clear about what this meant. Ma Eme was the sister of the chief. She belonged to one of the leading families of Okoyong, and she had herself been through the ordeals and the fear. She was not a Christian, and she did not become one. She sacrificed to the spirits every day of her life. And yet, again and again, she risked her own safety to warn a foreign woman about plans to kill people accused of witchcraft. We do not know all her reasons. Perhaps she loved Mary. Perhaps she, too, was weary of the killing. Perhaps she knew what it was to stand before the witch-doctor waiting for the verdict. Whatever her reasons, much of the life-saving for which Mary Slessor became famous would have been impossible without her. The Women of the Yard Mary saw terrible things in those months. A young wife gave a hired slave a piece of yam as part of his wages while her husband was away, breaking the law of the harem, and was condemned to the ordeal of boiling oil. As the drinking went on, the cords that bound her were tightened for sport until she screamed. Mary went out, faced the crowd, and carried her off, and kept her chained to her own verandah until the dancing ended at dawn, which was the only way to keep her safe. She also saw the women of the yard at their best. Once a large number of prisoners lay chained in the heat all day, waiting for the poison ordeal. Among them were mothers with babies. At dusk, when the guards left for a while, some of the older women crept up to them with water for the children and the mothers. Mary had had rice cooked in readiness, and the women smuggled that to the prisoners too. If they had been caught, Livingstone says, their lives would have been forfeit. She did not idealise Okoyong. Some of the things she saw in the harem, she said, she could never describe, and years later the memory of them would still make her flush. “Had I not felt my Saviour close beside me,” she said, “I would have lost my reason.” She had no patience with people at home who talked about the innocence of those who lived outside civilisation. She told them to go and live for a month in a West African harem. It may have owed as much to a Calvinist’s conviction that sin runs through every human society as to the prejudices of her time. She had, after all, grown up with a drunken father in a Dundee slum. School by Lamplight She began teaching almost at once, before she had any buildings. At Ifako the school was held on the verandah of a house by the roadside, with lengths of firewood for seats and an alphabet card hung on a post. At Ekenge it was held in the evening, in the chief’s outer yard, when the wives and slaves had finished their work. Men and women, old and young, slave and free, crowded in to learn the alphabet and the multiplication table. Then she held worship, standing bareheaded and barefoot beside a small table with a lamp and a Bible on it, while the people sat on the ground in the dark. She taught them to sing the gospel to their own tunes. One day, passing the school, she heard them singing to the melody of an Okoyong war-song: Jesus the Son of God came down to earth, He came to save us from our sins. He was born poor that He might feel for us. The Chief’s Abscess Chief Edem had been kind to her from the beginning, and when he fell ill with an abscess on his back she nursed him. One morning she came in with his tea and found a live fowl impaled on a stick, charms hung all round him, and the chief holding out a parcel of shot, powder, teeth, bones, and eggshells that he said had been taken out of his back. Someone had bewitched him. Before her eyes, men and women were named, seized, and chained to posts in the yard. She argued and pleaded, and the chief grew so irritated that he had himself carried off to one of his farms with the prisoners, and forbade her to follow. But she had her own ways of knowing what was happening, and she heard that more people were being chained. On New Year’s Eve, lying awake homesick with tears in her eyes, she was roused by a deputation from the farm. They had heard that an African minister in Calabar, the Rev. Esien Ukpabio, the first convert of the Calabar mission, knew how to treat such illnesses. Would she write to ask him to come? She wrote at once. Ukpabio refused, because he was told that the trouble was a soul troubling the chief, and he could do nothing about that. But his sister went, and under her care the abscess broke and the chief recovered. All the prisoners were released except one woman, who was put to death. The chief sent his son to Mary to tell her, before anyone else could, that nobody had been hurt. Only one worthless slave woman, he said, had been sold away. Mary knew it was a lie. She knew the woman had been killed, and she thought of the faces of the three children the woman left behind. But she pretended to believe it. If she had shown that she knew the truth, the chief would have wanted to know how she knew, and scores of people might have been put to the poison ordeal to find her informant. Livingstone does not name the informant. It is hard not to think of Ma Eme. That was the price of friendship in Okoyong. Mary’s knowledge saved lives, but only as long as it was secret. There were times when protecting the one who had told her meant keeping silent about a murder. She did not like it, and she did it. A Foolish Choice? The friendship lasted for twenty-five years. Ma Eme’s people built the boathouse at the river where Mary kept her canoe. Ma Eme stood beside her in the worst crisis of her early years, as the next chapter will tell. When the population of Okoyong moved inland in the 1890s, Ma Eme moved away to a distant farm, but they stayed in touch. In July 1913, near the end of her life, Mary went back to Okoyong for a visit, and Ma Eme came to see her. She was still a devout follower of the old religion. She sacrificed daily to the spirits with food and blood, and she would not touch the twins who had grown up in Mary’s house, though she admitted it was a marvel that they had lived. The two old women sat together all day and talked about the past. “Do you remember this?” “Do you remember that?” They talked, Livingstone says, about “the killing time when they worked hand in hand in secret for the preservation of life.” Nothing Mary could say would move her friend. At the end of the day Ma Eme went away, as Livingstone puts it, “the same kind, high-bred, mysterious heathen woman that she had always been.” She died not long afterwards. Mary said: My dear old friend and almost sister, she made the saving of life so often possible in the early days. It is sad that she did not come out for Christ. She could have been the honoured leader of God’s work had she risen to it. I cannot fancy Okoyong without her. She made a foolish choice, and yet God cannot forget all she was to me, and all she helped me to do in those dark and bloody days. Mary Slessor did not pretend that her friend was a Christian. She believed that Christ was the only way to God, and she grieved that Ma Eme had not come to him. She called her choice foolish. But she would not stop there. She knew what Ma Eme had done, and she trusted that God knew it too. A lawyer once asked Jesus who his neighbour was, and Jesus answered with a story in which the one who stopped to help a wounded man was a Samaritan, a man the lawyer would have regarded as outside the true faith. Then Jesus asked, “Which of these three, thinkest thou, proved neighbor unto him that fell among the robbers? And he said, He that showed mercy on him. And Jesus said unto him, Go, and do thou likewise” (Luke 10:36-37, ASV). Jesus did not say that the Samaritan’s religion was right. He said that his mercy was real, and that it put the religious people to shame. There is a proper humility for Christians in a friendship like this one. It does not mean pretending that all faiths are the same, which Mary would never have done. It means recognising mercy when we see it, being grateful for it, and leaving to God the things that only God can judge. When Abraham pleaded for the people of Sodom, he asked, “shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?” (Genesis 18:25, ASV). Mary Slessor left her dearest African friend in the hands of that Judge. That is where she belongs in this book too: honoured, grieved over, and left with God.

fields.title: The Poison Bean
fields.body_html:
“Judge the poor and fatherless: Do justice to the afflicted and destitute. Rescue the poor and needy: Deliver them out of the hand of the wicked.”

— Psalm 82:3-4, ASV

A Carpenter from Edinburgh

In 1889, as far as can be told, a Scottish carpenter named Charles Ovens arrived at Ekenge. He had been working in Edinburgh and was about to go back to America when an elderly woman of the United Presbyterian Church asked him why he did not go to Calabar instead, where a missionary living alone in the bush wanted a man to put in her doors and windows. He changed the address on his luggage and went. He found Mary, he said, without hat or shoes, eating her dinner in the company of goats and hens. He was given a room eight feet by five, and he set to work building her a proper house.

Ovens was a cheerful man who sang Scottish songs in the evenings until she wept with homesickness, and he became one of the most valuable witnesses of her life at Ekenge. It was Ovens who was with her during the crisis that Livingstone calls her greatest battle.

Etim

One morning, as Ovens worked on the house and Mary sat on the verandah watching him, a strange cry came out of the forest. She stood up, listened, and said, “There is something wrong.” Then she went off into the trees. A little later a boy came back asking Ovens to come at once and bring something to revive an injured man.

He found her sitting beside a young man lying unconscious on the ground. “It is Etim, the eldest son of our chief, Edem,” she told him. Etim was about to be married, and had been building a house for his bride. A log he was carrying had slipped and struck him on the back of the neck, and he was paralysed. Ovens was surprised at how grave she looked. She told him why: “There’s going to be trouble; no death of a violent character comes apart from witchcraft.” Ovens made a stretcher, and they carried Etim to Ekenge.

For two weeks she nursed him in his mother’s house, hoping that he would recover and that the crisis she dreaded might be avoided. He did not. One Sunday morning, hearing the sound of wailing, she ran to the yard and found him dying. People were blowing smoke into his nostrils and rubbing pepper into his eyes, and his uncle Ekpenyong was shouting into his ears to call his spirit back. When he was dead, the chief dropped the body into Mary’s arms and cried, “Sorcerers have killed and they must die. Bring the witch-doctor.”

The Prisoners

The witch-doctor named a neighbouring village as guilty. The free men of Ekenge marched there at once with their guns, sacked the houses, and came back with more than a dozen men and women in chains, the rest having escaped into the forest. The prisoners were fastened to posts in a yard that had only one entrance.

Mary now did something that shows how well she understood the people. To calm the grief and anger of the dead man’s father and uncle, she offered to dress Etim for burial in the style his rank deserved. She wrapped the body in silk and put on it a suit she had made for his father. His head was shaved in patterns and painted yellow, and crowned with a silk turban and a tall black and scarlet hat with bright plumes. The body was seated in an armchair under an umbrella, with a whip and a silver-headed stick tied to the hands and a mirror placed in front so that he could admire himself. On a table beside him were the treasures of the house, including the skulls of enemies killed in war, and some candles Mary had given. When the people saw it they went wild with delight, and the drinking and dancing began.

Some readers may be uneasy at a missionary helping to stage a funeral display with war trophies on the table. Mary did not see it as a compromise of her faith. She saw it as honouring a dead young man and his grieving family in the way they understood, in the hope of turning their grief away from killing. She would do whatever she could within their customs, so long as no one died.

Then she told Ovens that he would have to stop all work. “This is going to be a serious business,” she said. “We can’t leave these prisoners for a moment. I’ll watch beside them all night and you’ll take the day.” For days and nights the two of them took turns sitting opposite the chained prisoners in the filthy yard, while armed men danced and drank around them and one barrel of rum followed another. At one point Ovens lost patience and said he would get a hammer and chisel and free the prisoners himself. “Na, na,” she said. “We’ll have a little more patience.”

The Beans on the Stone

One day she came to Ovens and said they wanted a coffin. When they went into the yard to take the measurements, she saw eséré beans lying on the pounding stone. She shivered. She went back to her hut and prayed, pleading with God for guidance in the struggle that was coming. When she stood up, Livingstone says, her fear had gone.

She went back and took the two chiefs, Edem and his brother Ekpenyong, aside, and told them that there must be no killing. They did not deny that the ordeal was about to take place. Only the guilty would die, they said. She did not argue. She went to the entrance of the yard and sat down, and made it plain that she would not move until the matter was settled.

The chiefs were furious. A white woman among them was a good thing, but she had no right to interfere with their laws. The dead man’s mother became violent. Even the slaves threatened her. The drunken crowd ran about waving guns and swords and shouting, “Raise our master from the dead, and you shall have the prisoners.”

That night Mary wrote a note to the mission in Duke Town and sent it secretly down the river with two African carpenters who were working with Ovens. Three of the women prisoners had babies who cried all night from hunger and fear. Another, a woman named Inyam, had a daughter of about fifteen, who clung to her mother and came again and again to clasp Mary’s feet, and offered herself as a slave for life if only her mother could go free. The girl was a cousin of the dead man, and she was betrothed to his father, the chief.

“Run”

Later that night, while Mary was keeping watch, several men came and unlocked the chains of one of the women, a mother, and led her out to the body to take the poison. Mary did not know whether it was a trick to lure her out of the yard, so that the others could be killed while she was gone. The prisoners begged her not to leave them. But she could not watch a woman walk to her death.

She followed. The woman was standing at a table covered with a white cloth, with a glass of water holding the poison in front of her, and was lifting the glass when Mary touched her on the shoulder and whispered, “Ifehe!” It means “Run.” The woman looked into her eyes, understood, and the two of them ran into the bush before anyone realised what had happened. They reached Mary’s hut, and she told Ovens to hide the woman, and he pulled her inside and locked the door. Mary went straight back to the yard. “Where is she?” the prisoners asked. “Safe in my house,” she said.

She wondered afterwards why no one had stopped her or harmed her. Perhaps the men were too drunk to react quickly. But she thought of her prayer.

One by One

Finding that she would not give way, the chiefs tried persuasion. “God will not let anybody die of the bean if they are not guilty,” they said. It was their own theology, and it is worth noticing that it was a theology of divine justice: the poison was believed to be God’s verdict. They released two prisoners, letting them swear the native oath instead of taking the ordeal. Later they released five more, and then two more. Then they stopped. “We have done more for you than we have ever done for any one,” they said, “and we will die before we go further.”

Three prisoners were left. One was a woman with a baby, whose chief, Akpo, had fled into the forest, which in their eyes proved his guilt. The other two, a free man and Inyam, the mother of the fifteen-year-old girl, were taken away. Mary had to choose whom to stay with, and she stayed with the woman and her baby.

The next day visitors warned her that Egbo was coming and that she should flee to Calabar. She said Egbo could come and play the fool as much as he liked, but she would not leave her post. The chief threatened to burn down her house. “You are welcome,” she said. “It is not mine.” He said the woman would die. The prisoner herself was so terrified and exhausted that she begged Mary to give in.

It was Ma Eme who broke the deadlock. She knelt before her brother, the chief, and begged him to let Mary keep the woman for the time being, chained to the verandah of her hut, where she could not possibly escape with such a weight of iron. To Mary’s astonishment, the chiefs agreed, on condition that if the woman were sent away to Calabar, Mary would pay a heavy fine and leave Okoyong for ever. The slaves pretended they could not find the keys. Mary waited, patiently and firmly, until the keys appeared. Then she and Ma Eme gathered up the long chain between them and hurried the woman and her baby through the scrub to Mary’s hut, where they hid them in a large packing-case behind a barricade.

Two missionaries arrived from Calabar that afternoon and gave a magic-lantern show to the crowd, which, Livingstone says, was meant to add dignity to the funeral and make up for the lack of human sacrifice. The next day the chief released the free man as a further act of mercy, but insisted that Inyam must take the poison. Mary followed him about all day, pleading. He looked at her at times, Livingstone says, as if he thought she were mad. That night she heard that the burial would take place in the chief’s house, and she was sick with dread.

Late in the evening she heard a faint voice at the barricade: “Ma, Ma, make haste, let me in.” She pulled the planks aside, and Inyam crawled in on her hands and knees, still heavily chained. She said she had rubbed through a link of the chain and escaped over a roof. Mary looked at the thick chain and guessed, Livingstone says, “whose were the kindly black hands that had given her aid,” but she kept the thought to herself. The funeral took place that night. In the coffin, instead of human companions for the dead man, was a cow.

What Followed

For the first time anyone could remember, a man of a chief’s family in Okoyong had been buried without human sacrifice. Livingstone calls it her greatest victory, and in one sense it was. But the story did not end cleanly, and Livingstone, to his credit, tells what followed.

On the way to the funeral, one party met another coming back drunk, remembered an old quarrel, killed a man and carried off his head. Fighting broke out. A few days later the village was seized by panic at the sound of an Egbo band approaching. Women and children and unarmed men poured into Mary’s yard, and she packed as many as she could into her room and sent the rest into the bush behind. The Egbo band stayed only a short time and no shot hit anyone there. But they burned every house in the village from which the prisoners had come, and burned the livestock alive. Then Edem’s village took its own revenge, and for more than a week armed men roamed the forest, shooting anyone they met.

The elder chief, Ekpenyong, was accused of having killed his nephew by witchcraft so that his own son could inherit, and in his fury he demanded to take the poison ordeal himself and to make his brother take it too. Mary scolded him, got his promise to give up the idea, and searched his house with the help of his wives, finding eleven beans at the bottom of a basket. That night he was found drunk, fighting with his women over a bag. She demanded it, and found palm-nuts and cartridges, and under them forty more beans. “I’ll take the liberty of keeping these,” she said, and walked out between the lines of armed men with her heart pounding. In the night he slipped away to take the ordeal anyway. Another chief held him by force until she arrived, and in the end he took the native oath instead and moved away to found a new settlement.

Blood for Blood

The hardest part of the aftermath was a case she refused to judge. The man who had killed and beheaded the mourner on the funeral road was the eldest son of a family known for violence, and he had killed before. War threatened between his family and the family of the dead man. Mary pressed for arbitration, and both sides asked her to preside. She knew that he was a triple murderer and that the penalty would be death, and she shrank from it. She asked them to take the case to a Calabar chief instead.

The verdict was blood for blood. Fines were offered and refused. Slaves were offered to die in his place and refused. His youngest son, a baby, was sent as an atonement and rejected. Then his second son, a young man of twenty, was sent, and it was agreed that his death would redeem his brother. Mary was in anguish, all the more because she had refused to act as judge. She was relieved to hear that the young man had escaped and was being hidden by a slave-trader across the river. But one morning she heard firing, and learned that he had been betrayed, brought back, filled with gin, and strangled and hanged in front of his mother and sister. Only those two mourned him.

Livingstone does not say that Mary blamed herself, but he says her distress was acute “especially as she had declined to act as judge.” It is not hard to see why. She had refused to sit in judgement because she could not bear to sentence a man to death, and the case had gone to a court where an innocent man died instead. Perhaps it taught her something. In later years, when the British asked her to preside over a court, she accepted.

Weary of the Old Customs

Some weeks later she went to find Akpo, the chief who had fled, and asked Edem whether he could come home safely. Edem said he could, and that all thought of vengeance was gone. Akpo did not believe it. Mary went to him three times before he would come back. When he stood again in his ruined village, with his house, farm, and animals all gone, he knelt and held her feet and vowed that he and his household would be under her yoke for ever.

Edem gave the returning men land and seed. That evening he came to Mary alone. He knelt, took her feet, and thanked her again and again for her love and courage, and for forbidding them to take life when his son died. Then he said something that changed how she understood the whole struggle:

We are all weary of the old customs, but no single person or House among us has power to break them off, because they are part of the Egbo system.

One by one, Livingstone says, secretly and without each other’s knowledge, free people came to her to thank her for the safety she was bringing, and urged her to keep going and do away with all the old customs, “the end of which was always death.”

That is perhaps the most important thing in this chapter. Mary Slessor has often been pictured as a lone Scotswoman imposing her will on a savage tribe. The truth Livingstone preserves is more interesting. The people of Okoyong were caught in a system that no single family could escape. If one chief refused to kill at a funeral, his dead would go unhonoured and his House would be shamed. Many of them wanted a way out, and could not find it alone. What Mary offered them was an outside authority strong enough to take the blame for breaking the custom. They could say that Ma would not let them.

The psalm at the head of this chapter is addressed to judges. God stands in their assembly and rebukes them for judging unjustly, and commands them: “Rescue the poor and needy: Deliver them out of the hand of the wicked.” The wise man of Proverbs puts it simply: “Open thy mouth for the dumb, In the cause of all such as are left desolate” (Proverbs 31:8, ASV). The prisoners chained in Edem’s yard had no voice. The girl clasping Mary’s feet had nothing to offer but herself. Mary Slessor spoke for them. She could not save everyone, and she knew it. One woman had died after the chief’s illness, and a young man of twenty had died for his brother’s crime. But on the night the cow was buried, a whole yard of prisoners walked free.

The chief threatened to burn down her house. “You are welcome,” she said. “It is not mine.” He said the woman would die. The prisoner herself was so terrified and exhausted that she begged Mary to give in. It was Ma Eme who broke the deadlock. She knelt before her brother, the chief, and begged him to let Mary keep the woman for the time being, chained to the verandah of her hut, where she could not possibly escape with such a weight of iron. To Mary’s astonishment, the chiefs agreed, on condition that if the woman were sent away to Calabar, Mary would pay a heavy fine and leave Okoyong for ever. The slaves pretended they could not find the keys. Mary waited, patiently and firmly, until the keys appeared. Then she and Ma Eme gathered up the long chain between them and hurried the woman and her baby through the scrub to Mary’s hut, where they hid them in a large packing-case behind a barricade. Two missionaries arrived from Calabar that afternoon and gave a magic-lantern show to the crowd, which, Livingstone says, was meant to add dignity to the funeral and make up for the lack of human sacrifice. The next day the chief released the free man as a further act of mercy, but insisted that Inyam must take the poison. Mary followed him about all day, pleading. He looked at her at times, Livingstone says, as if he thought she were mad. That night she heard that the burial would take place in the chief’s house, and she was sick with dread. Late in the evening she heard a faint voice at the barricade: “Ma, Ma, make haste, let me in.” She pulled the planks aside, and Inyam crawled in on her hands and knees, still heavily chained. She said she had rubbed through a link of the chain and escaped over a roof. Mary looked at the thick chain and guessed, Livingstone says, “whose were the kindly black hands that had given her aid,” but she kept the thought to herself. The funeral took place that night. In the coffin, instead of human companions for the dead man, was a cow. What Followed For the first time anyone could remember, a man of a chief’s family in Okoyong had been buried without human sacrifice. Livingstone calls it her greatest victory, and in one sense it was. But the story did not end cleanly, and Livingstone, to his credit, tells what followed. On the way to the funeral, one party met another coming back drunk, remembered an old quarrel, killed a man and carried off his head. Fighting broke out. A few days later the village was seized by panic at the sound of an Egbo band approaching. Women and children and unarmed men poured into Mary’s yard, and she packed as many as she could into her room and sent the rest into the bush behind. The Egbo band stayed only a short time and no shot hit anyone there. But they burned every house in the village from which the prisoners had come, and burned the livestock alive. Then Edem’s village took its own revenge, and for more than a week armed men roamed the forest, shooting anyone they met. The elder chief, Ekpenyong, was accused of having killed his nephew by witchcraft so that his own son could inherit, and in his fury he demanded to take the poison ordeal himself and to make his brother take it too. Mary scolded him, got his promise to give up the idea, and searched his house with the help of his wives, finding eleven beans at the bottom of a basket. That night he was found drunk, fighting with his women over a bag. She demanded it, and found palm-nuts and cartridges, and under them forty more beans. “I’ll take the liberty of keeping these,” she said, and walked out between the lines of armed men with her heart pounding. In the night he slipped away to take the ordeal anyway. Another chief held him by force until she arrived, and in the end he took the native oath instead and moved away to found a new settlement. Blood for Blood The hardest part of the aftermath was a case she refused to judge. The man who had killed and beheaded the mourner on the funeral road was the eldest son of a family known for violence, and he had killed before. War threatened between his family and the family of the dead man. Mary pressed for arbitration, and both sides asked her to preside. She knew that he was a triple murderer and that the penalty would be death, and she shrank from it. She asked them to take the case to a Calabar chief instead. The verdict was blood for blood. Fines were offered and refused. Slaves were offered to die in his place and refused. His youngest son, a baby, was sent as an atonement and rejected. Then his second son, a young man of twenty, was sent, and it was agreed that his death would redeem his brother. Mary was in anguish, all the more because she had refused to act as judge. She was relieved to hear that the young man had escaped and was being hidden by a slave-trader across the river. But one morning she heard firing, and learned that he had been betrayed, brought back, filled with gin, and strangled and hanged in front of his mother and sister. Only those two mourned him. Livingstone does not say that Mary blamed herself, but he says her distress was acute “especially as she had declined to act as judge.” It is not hard to see why. She had refused to sit in judgement because she could not bear to sentence a man to death, and the case had gone to a court where an innocent man died instead. Perhaps it taught her something. In later years, when the British asked her to preside over a court, she accepted. Weary of the Old Customs Some weeks later she went to find Akpo, the chief who had fled, and asked Edem whether he could come home safely. Edem said he could, and that all thought of vengeance was gone. Akpo did not believe it. Mary went to him three times before he would come back. When he stood again in his ruined village, with his house, farm, and animals all gone, he knelt and held her feet and vowed that he and his household would be under her yoke for ever. Edem gave the returning men land and seed. That evening he came to Mary alone. He knelt, took her feet, and thanked her again and again for her love and courage, and for forbidding them to take life when his son died. Then he said something that changed how she understood the whole struggle: We are all weary of the old customs, but no single person or House among us has power to break them off, because they are part of the Egbo system. One by one, Livingstone says, secretly and without each other’s knowledge, free people came to her to thank her for the safety she was bringing, and urged her to keep going and do away with all the old customs, “the end of which was always death.” That is perhaps the most important thing in this chapter. Mary Slessor has often been pictured as a lone Scotswoman imposing her will on a savage tribe. The truth Livingstone preserves is more interesting. The people of Okoyong were caught in a system that no single family could escape. If one chief refused to kill at a funeral, his dead would go unhonoured and his House would be shamed. Many of them wanted a way out, and could not find it alone. What Mary offered them was an outside authority strong enough to take the blame for breaking the custom. They could say that Ma would not let them. The psalm at the head of this chapter is addressed to judges. God stands in their assembly and rebukes them for judging unjustly, and commands them: “Rescue the poor and needy: Deliver them out of the hand of the wicked.” The wise man of Proverbs puts it simply: “Open thy mouth for the dumb, In the cause of all such as are left desolate” (Proverbs 31:8, ASV). The prisoners chained in Edem’s yard had no voice. The girl clasping Mary’s feet had nothing to offer but herself. Mary Slessor spoke for them. She could not save everyone, and she knew it. One woman had died after the chief’s illness, and a young man of twenty had died for his brother’s crime. But on the night the cow was buried, a whole yard of prisoners walked free.

fields.title: Twin-Mothers
fields.body_html:
“When my father and my mother forsake me, Then Jehovah will take me up.”

— Psalm 27:10, ASV

A House Full of Babies

Of all her work, Livingstone says, the sweetest and the saddest was the care of the babies of the bush. Her house became a refuge for small children: sick ones left with her to nurse and give back, unwanted ones brought to her, and abandoned ones she rescued from the forest. So many came and went, were named, written about in her letters, and then disappeared from them, that her friends in Scotland could not keep track.

Most came in the last stages of sickness or starvation. She washed them, fed them, and fought for their lives, sitting up night after night with a wasted little face in her lap, or walking up and down singing to a baby who could not sleep. She slung a hammock beside her bed and put the babies in it, so that when one woke in the night she could reach out a foot and rock it back to sleep without getting up. More than once, when the tinned milk ran out, she strapped her latest baby to her body and walked the long miles through the bush to Creek Town, and came back the next day with the child and the tins.

Many of them died. Those who died she dressed, laid among flowers in a box, held a service over, and buried in a small cemetery near her house, which in time, Livingstone says, “became full of tiny graves.” She mourned each of them as if it had been her own flesh and blood. The carpenter Ovens, who saw it, tried to comfort her in his own way: “Never mind, lassie, you’ll get plenty mair.” And there were always more.

It is important to hold both parts of this together. The story of Mary Slessor and the twins is often told as a story of rescue, and it was. But it was also a story of many small deaths, of babies who came to her too late or whom she could not save, and of a woman who kept opening her door knowing that much of the time she would end by digging another grave.

The Child of Wonder

Some did live. One baby girl, whose mother had died soon after her birth, was thrown into the bush beside the road to the market because of a quarrel between the families of her parents. She lay there for five days and six nights. Mary Kingsley, the English traveller, told the story in her book Travels in West Africa. Women from the village passed the spot on the next market day, heard a feeble cry, and mentioned it that evening in Mary’s yard as a curiosity. Mary was off at once, and brought the child home. Ants had eaten into her nose and upper lip. Leopards and snakes had somehow left her alone. She lived, and grew into a healthy girl, and the people who had thrown her away came to pet her and play with her, calling her “the child of wonder.” Mary named her after herself.

This Mary, together with Janie, the twin brought home from Old Town; Alice, another rescued twin; and Annie, a child whose mother had been accused in a case of a stolen dog, became the inner circle of her family. Later others would join them: Maggie, Dan, Whitie, Asuquo, and more. There was also Mana, a girl who had been kidnapped as she walked home from a spring, brought to Okoyong, and sold as a slave to Ma Eme. Mana became one of the most faithful members of the household, and, as we shall see, one of the first Christians of the Cross River.

We know less about most of these children than we would like. They appear in Livingstone’s pages chiefly as they related to Mary, and many of their later lives are hard to trace. But their names should be remembered. The story of “Everybody’s Mother” is also the story of the children who made her one.

Susie

Of all the babies who passed through her hands, none was loved more than Susie, her first Okoyong twin.

Susie’s mother, Iye, was a slave woman from Bende, owned by one of the leading women of the district, who treated her well. Then she gave birth to twins, a boy and a girl, and everything changed. Mary Kingsley happened to arrive at Ekenge that very day to meet Mary Slessor for the first time, and she described what she saw. The date was probably 1895; Livingstone says 1893, but Kingsley’s own account puts the visit later.

Iye was cursed and abused. Her clothes were torn and her treasured china basins smashed, and she was driven out of the village as an unclean thing. Kingsley believed she would have been killed with her children if the people had not feared Mary’s anger. The babies were crammed into an empty gin-case, which was put on Iye’s head, with her brass cooking-pot and her market calabashes on top. Mary heard the news and ran barefoot and bareheaded down the forest path, and four miles out she met Iye staggering towards her with the whole village yelling behind. Mary took the load from her head and carried it herself, since no one else would touch it.

Then she did something that Kingsley thought showed her understanding of the people. She did not take Iye down the village path to her house, because the path would then have been polluted, and the villagers would have had to cut a new one. Instead she stood in the blazing sun, at the height of the hot season, while the people cut a new track through the forest straight to her own grounds. Only then did she take the mother and babies home.

The boy was already dead. The people who had packed the twins into the box had crushed his head. Kingsley’s comment is brief: all the boy needed was burying. The girl lived. For days the villagers would not come near her. If Mary or Kingsley handed the baby to one of the household children, men and women fled off the verandah and over the fence. Iye herself would not hold her. She sat for hours singing a lament over her own fate, and Kingsley recorded the words:

Yesterday I was a woman, now I am a horror, a thing all people ran from. Yesterday they would eat with me, now they spit on me.

Kingsley noticed that Iye did not blame the villagers. She did not think they had done wrong. She only felt that some power beyond her had sent this curse of twins upon her.

“Mem, Mem”

The surviving baby was named Susie, after Mary’s own sister who had died in Edinburgh. She became the darling of the house. When she was fourteen months old, Mary left her for a few minutes with Mana, who put a jug of boiling water on the floor. The baby pulled it over on herself. For thirteen days and nights she was never out of Mary’s hands. A young woman missionary, Miss Murray, who had asked to be posted to Okoyong for a time, helped her; “She was like a sister to me,” Mary wrote. Thinking a doctor might do more, Mary carried Susie through the forest to Creek Town, arriving at midnight, and woke the doctor, who told her there was nothing more he could do. She went back to Ekenge and went on nursing her. In the dark, when everyone else was asleep, she would hear a faint voice saying, “Mem, Mem, Mem,” the child’s name for her, and a little hand would be held up for her to kiss.

Early one Sunday morning Susie died in her arms. They dressed her in a pinafore, with her beads and a sash and a flower in her hand, and Mary said she looked “like an angel child.”

The whole district was moved. While Susie was dying, none of the villagers went to their farms or to market, and when she died they came to mourn with Mary. Mary could not bring herself to lead the burial, and sat at the window while Miss Murray took the service. The villagers gathered round the grave of a twin, the very thing they had once fled from. One of the women, a leader in the old religion, stood up and praised the white mother’s God for the child, and prayed that they might all share her hope. “Surely,” Mary wrote afterwards, “they all felt the vast difference between their burials with all their drink and madness, and ours so full of quiet hope and expectant faith.”

Her own grief was terrible. “My heart aches for my darling,” she wrote. “Oh the empty place, and the silence and the vain longing for the sweet voice and the soft caress and the funny ways. Oh, Susie, Susie!”

Buying Iye

Iye had come to love the child she would not touch at first, and when Susie died she was broken. “Ma, don’t cry,” she said. “I have done this. God hates me. I shall go away and not bring any more evil on you.” And she went back to her hut in the bush.

Mary had always refused to buy slaves, even to set them free, because she thought the people would misunderstand it and think she was taking part in the trade. But she made an exception for Iye. She paid ten pounds for her freedom and brought her into the mission house. Iye stayed with her for years. In 1903, when the first baptisms took place in the district, Iye was among those baptised.

It is worth noticing the honesty of that detail. Mary Slessor did, at least once, buy a human being. She knew the arguments against it and had used them herself. She did it anyway, for one grieving woman whom everyone else regarded as cursed. It was not a policy. It was love, doing what it could.

Mary Kingsley

Mary Kingsley was one of the most remarkable travellers of her age, a clever, witty, independent Englishwoman who explored the rivers of West Africa alone and wrote brilliantly about what she saw. She was no friend of missions. She thought most missionaries misunderstood Africa and did more harm than good. But she and Mary Slessor became friends. They sat up late into the night arguing about religion and the immortality of the soul. “I would give anything to possess your beliefs,” Kingsley said, “but I can’t, I can’t; when God made me He must have left out the part that one believes with.”

Mary, for her part, said that Kingsley was one of the most truly Christian women she had ever met, whatever she believed or did not believe. She gave the traveller a great deal of what she knew about the religion and customs of the people, and much of it went into Kingsley’s books. When Kingsley died in South Africa in 1900, nursing prisoners of war, Mary grieved. “The world held not many so brave and so noble,” she wrote. “Life feels very cold and seems grey and sunless.” She sent a guinea towards a memorial.

Kingsley’s published verdict on Mary Slessor is one of the most valuable we have, because it came from someone who had no reason to flatter a missionary. She wrote that Slessor had been eighteen years in Calabar, that for the last six or seven she had lived alone in the forest at Okoyong, and that her knowledge of the people, their language, their thought, their diseases, and their difficulties was extraordinary. Okoyong, she wrote, had been given to killing at funerals, ordeal by poison, and constant warfare. “Many of these evil customs she has stamped out.”

What She Did and Did Not Do

It is often said that Mary Slessor ended the killing of twins in Nigeria. She did not, and she would not have claimed it. The practice had been banned in the Efik towns of Calabar decades before she arrived, and other missionaries had been rescuing twins since the 1850s. It persisted in the interior long after her death. When a news agency interviewed her in Liverpool in 1898, she said that she had saved fifty-one twins. Many more passed through her hands in the years that followed, and many of them died.

What she did was to carry the protection of twins and their mothers into places where the old agreements meant nothing, to take the babies and, increasingly, the mothers into her own household, and to wear down the fear by living with it year after year. Over time her approach began to change. For most of her life she took the twins into her own house, as the missionaries had always done; in 1895 the Okoyong chiefs still refused to let twins be kept in their homes. By 1901 some twins were being cared for by their own mothers in their villages, and late in life, at Ikpe, Livingstone says she “had come to realise that it was not good to take twins from their mother,” and insisted that a baby stay at home with its mother while she and Jean stood guard. That case ended in tragedy, as a later chapter tells. But the direction of her thinking, from rescuing children out of their families towards helping families keep them, was a sign of a deepening wisdom.

Taken Up

The verse at the head of this chapter is from David’s psalm of trust: “When my father and my mother forsake me, Then Jehovah will take me up.” It is an extraordinary thing for a psalmist to say. A parent’s love is the strongest human love there is, and David imagines a day when even that might fail, and declares that God’s love will not.

For the twin babies of Okoyong, that was not an imagined day. Their fathers and mothers did forsake them, not out of wickedness but out of fear, bound by a belief that told them their children were a curse. Mary Slessor went out into the bush and took them up. She could not save them all. She could not always save their mothers from their grief or their villages from their fear. But she showed, in her own tired arms, what the psalm says of God. The prophet wrote of the Lord as a shepherd who “will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and will gently lead those that have their young” (Isaiah 40:11, ASV). Mary Slessor carried a great many lambs, and led a great many mothers. She believed that she was only doing, poorly and partially, what God had first done for her.
