But the direction of her thinking, from rescuing children out of their families towards helping families keep them, was a sign of a deepening wisdom. Taken Up The verse at the head of this chapter is from David’s psalm of trust: “When my father and my mother forsake me, Then Jehovah will take me up.” It is an extraordinary thing for a psalmist to say. A parent’s love is the strongest human love there is, and David imagines a day when even that might fail, and declares that God’s love will not. For the twin babies of Okoyong, that was not an imagined day. Their fathers and mothers did forsake them, not out of wickedness but out of fear, bound by a belief that told them their children were a curse. Mary Slessor went out into the bush and took them up. She could not save them all. She could not always save their mothers from their grief or their villages from their fear. But she showed, in her own tired arms, what the psalm says of God. The prophet wrote of the Lord as a shepherd who “will gather the lambs in his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and will gently lead those that have their young” (Isaiah 40:11, ASV). Mary Slessor carried a great many lambs, and led a great many mothers. She believed that she was only doing, poorly and partially, what God had first done for her.

fields.title: Laid on the Altar
fields.body_html:
“I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.”

— Romans 12:1, ASV

A Surprise

In September 1891, while she was at home on furlough, the Foreign Mission Board of the United Presbyterian Church learned something that surprised almost everyone who knew her. Mary Slessor was engaged to be married.

Her friends had assumed that she had given herself entirely to Okoyong, and that there was no room in her life for anything else. They were half right. The story of her engagement is short, and Livingstone tells it with great reserve, but it is one of the most revealing episodes in her life. It shows what she wanted, and what she was prepared to give up.

Charles Morrison

The man was Charles W. Morrison, a teacher on the mission staff at Duke Town. He came from Kirkintilloch, near Glasgow, had been an active Christian worker at home, and had been accepted by the Board at once when he applied. Livingstone describes him as “a man of fine feeling, with a distinct literary gift.” He was, Livingstone adds, “in his twenty-fifth year.” Mary was about forty-two. Livingstone does not comment on the difference in their ages, and neither, apparently, did she.

They had met only a few times. Mary had been ill in Duke Town in 1890, and Morrison had been attentive and kind while she recovered. He was drawn, Livingstone says, to “the brilliant, unconventional little woman.” We can guess some of what drew her to him. He was a reader and a writer in a world where she had few people to talk to about books. Among the handful of possessions she kept to the end of her life were two battered novels, Bulwer-Lytton’s Eugene Aram and Dickens’s Sketches by Boz. On the flyleaf of one, in her handwriting, are the initials “C. W. M.” and “M. M. S.” In the other are their two signatures, one above the other. A photograph taken in 1891 shows her wearing an engagement ring.

They became engaged before she left for Scotland at the end of 1890. From the beginning there was one condition, and it was hers. She would not leave Okoyong. She had given her word to the people there, and she would not break it, even for her own happiness. If they married, Morrison would have to come and live at Okoyong. She thought he would make a good missionary, and that the two of them could share the work, one staying while the other went home on furlough.

On His Altar

While the Board considered the matter, friends wrote to congratulate her. Her reply to one of them is the heart of the story:

I lay it all in God’s hands, and will take from Him whatever He sees best for His work in Okoyong. My life was laid on His altar for that people long ago, and I would not take one jot or tittle of it back. If it be for His glory and the advantage of His cause there to let another join in it I will be grateful. If not I will still try to be grateful, as He knows best.

It is not a cold letter. It is the letter of a woman who wanted very much to be married, and who had decided beforehand what she would do if she could not have both. The phrase she used, “laid on His altar,” was the language of her Bible. It echoes the verse at the head of this chapter, where Paul urges Christians to present their bodies “a living sacrifice.” A sacrifice laid on the altar was not taken back. Mary Slessor believed that she had laid her life there years before, when she offered herself for Calabar, and later when she went into Okoyong. She did not think an engagement gave her the right to reclaim it.

Morrison, and perhaps Mary too, suspected what the Board would say. He asked her whether, if they refused to send him to Okoyong, she would come back to Duke Town to be with him. Her answer, written to a friend, was blunt:

It is out of the question. I would never take the idea into consideration. I could not leave my work for such a reason. To leave a field like Okoyong without a worker and go to one of ten or a dozen where the people have an open Bible and plenty of privilege! It is absurd. If God does not send him up here then he must do his work and I must do mine where we have been placed.

It is easy to read that as hard. It may be better to read it as honest. She did not pretend that the choice cost her nothing. She simply thought that one person’s happiness, even her own, could not weigh against the lives of the people of Okoyong, where she was the only missionary, when there were ten or a dozen stations on the coast with churches and Bibles already.

A Qualified Refusal

The Board’s answer was what Livingstone calls “a qualified refusal.” Morrison’s work at Duke Town was important, they said, and they could not approve his moving to Okoyong until full provision had been made for carrying it on. In effect, the answer was no.

When Mary was told, she said only, “What the Lord ordains is right.” Livingstone adds that she “apparently” dismissed the subject from her mind. The word “apparently” is his, and it is the only hint he gives that there may have been more to it than she showed.

What followed was sad. Morrison’s health broke down, and he had to return to Scotland. A specialist advised him not to go back to Calabar. He offered himself for the Church’s mission in South Africa, but there was no opening, and to the regret of the Committee, which thought highly of him, he resigned. Livingstone says he went later to America, and was living in a hut in the balsam woods of North Carolina when a fire destroyed the literary papers he treasured. The loss, Livingstone says, affected him deeply and hastened his death, which came soon afterwards. Livingstone gives no dates for any of this, and modern researchers have not been able to trace Morrison’s later life.

Popular books have often said that Mary Slessor never married because she was “married to Africa.” The truth is less poetic. She wanted to marry, and chose a man she thought would share her work. The Church would not let him join her, and she would not leave her people. His health failed. Whatever else they might have become to each other, those facts ended it. Livingstone closes the chapter with lines of verse about a solitary life lived “without cheer of sister or of daughter,” and says that she turned her face, alone, towards the future.

No Good Thing Withheld

It would be too easy to turn this story into a lesson that God rewards sacrifice with something better. Mary Slessor did not get something better. She did not marry. She went back to Okoyong and lived without a husband’s companionship for the rest of her life, often lonely, sometimes desperately so. Not long afterwards, overwhelmed by the work, she wrote, “I feel dreadfully lonely, and want a helper,” though the helper she meant was a fellow missionary, and in the end she did not ask for one because she knew how short-staffed the mission was.

And yet she did not think that God had cheated her. The psalmist says, “No good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly” (Psalm 84:11, ASV). She seems to have believed that literally, and to have concluded that if God withheld marriage from her, then for her, in her place, it was not the good thing. That is a hard kind of faith, and it is not one anyone should demand of another person. But it was hers. In the last years of her life she urged the young women at home: “Don’t grow up a nervous old maid! … I’m a witness to the perfect joy and satisfaction of a single life, with a tail of human tag-rag hanging on.” By then the tag-rag included eight or nine adopted children, a host of rescued babies, and a whole district that called her Mother.

A Letter to the Church

That furlough of 1891 produced one other thing that deserves a place in her story. Recovering from influenza and bronchitis, she read in the Church’s Missionary Record an appeal from a fellow missionary for more craftsmen to be sent to Calabar. He added, in passing, that Calabar was not yet ready for anyone to teach trades to its people. Mary disagreed. She wrote a long letter to the editor, so exhausting to write that she hardly knew whether the words were spelled right, and it was printed under the name “One of the Zenana Staff.”

She argued that the people of Calabar were entirely capable of learning trades, and that their weakness, a lack of persistence, was explained by their history, in which life had always been governed by “force of circumstance.” Training them was too big a task for individual missionaries. It was a matter for the whole Church. “Let the science of the evangelisation of the nations occupy the attention of our sermons, our congregations, our conferences, and our Church literature,” she wrote, “and we will soon have more workers, more wealth, more life, as well as new methods.”

According to Livingstone, the letter stirred the Mission Committee into action, and led in time to the founding of the Hope Waddell Training Institution at Calabar in 1895, which taught trades and gave a secondary education to generations of young men of the Cross River region. How much the Institution owed to her letter is hard to measure. Others were thinking along the same lines, and it had many parents. Livingstone says that she never took any credit for it and never mentioned it in her letters.

In February 1892 she sailed back to Calabar, with Janie. The Congregational church at Topsham held a farewell meeting in her honour. When illness upset her plans for that furlough, she said something that sums up the spirit in which she went back: “We alter things for the good of our children, and God does the same to us.”

fields.title: “The Woman’s God”
fields.body_html:
“Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called sons of God.”

— Matthew 5:9, ASV

A Walk in the Rain

In the first months at Ekenge, before the crisis over Etim’s death, a message came from a village near the Cross River, eight hours’ walk away. A chief there was dying. His people were waiting outside his house, armed and ready, because when a chief died, members of his household would be killed to go with him. One of the women of the village had told them about the white Ma at Ekenge, who had cured her grandchild. Send for her, she said, and the chief will not die. So they sent a message, with a bottle and four brass rods, worth about a shilling, as her fee.

Edem and Ma Eme told her she could not go. It was too far, the streams were too deep, the rains were too heavy. “I am going to get ready,” she said. She spent a sleepless night wondering whether she was right, and in the morning set out with an escort of women. The rain came down in torrents. First she abandoned her boots, then her stockings, then her broken umbrella, and then, one by one, most of her clothes, which the women carried on their heads in calabashes. She walked on in the lightest of garments through the dripping forest.

After three hours they came to a market-place where hundreds of people were gathering. Mary, soaked and half-dressed, felt humiliated, and hurried through the crowd, wondering whether she had lost their respect. She learned later that nothing she ever did won the hearts of the Okoyong more than that walk in the rain.

She reached the village, dressed herself in whatever odds and ends of clothing the women could find, and went straight to the sick man. Her medicine was not enough, and she persuaded a trader living in his canoe nearby to go across the river to the Scottish missionaries at Ikorofiong for more. He came back with what she needed, and with a letter and some tea from the missionary’s wife. She brewed the tea in a basin and thought it a feast. The chief recovered. No one was killed. The people began to talk about making peace with Calabar and learning to read. From then on, Livingstone says, Okoyong was open to her.

The Woman’s God

That chief did not forget her. At the end of 1890, as she was packing to leave for her furlough, messengers arrived from a distant township. A young freeman had accidentally shot himself in the hand while hunting, and they wanted medicine. She sent it. Then secret word came that the young man had died, that his brother had wounded a chief of a neighbouring town in revenge, and that the chief’s warriors were preparing to attack at dawn.

Everyone told her not to go. She was ill. She would miss the steamer. The men were savage, they said, the forest would be full of armed men firing at anything that moved, and in the dark no one would recognise her. She went anyway, with two armed attendants carrying lanterns, and stopped at the house of a chief eight miles away to ask for a free man to beat the Egbo drum before her, so that the warriors would know a protected person was coming.

The chief sent back a diplomatic answer. He had heard of no war, he said, and would inquire in the morning. And if there was a war, a woman who went into it only proved her ignorance of a people who had always loved fighting and were not likely to be helped by a woman. Mary sent him a reply that has been remembered ever since:

In measuring the woman’s power, you have evidently forgotten to take into account the woman’s God.

She went on without him. At the first village she was surrounded in the dark by armed men, who questioned her and then let her rest until cock-crow, when they would take her with them. At the second cock-crow they were gone before she was on her feet, running down the hillside like wild goats. The women stood at every door crying, “Run, Ma!” She ran as fast as her weakness allowed, lost sight of them, and fell back on prayer.

She found the war-party in the bush a hundred yards from the enemy village, and told them to behave like men and not like fools, as if they were schoolboys. Then she walked on to the village, where a wall of armed men stood silent. As she was about to push through them, an old man stepped out of the line and knelt at her feet. He asked her to help them make peace. It was the chief she had walked through the rain to heal.

What followed took all day. Two chiefs laid down their arms and knelt before the other side, begging them to accept a fine. Mary knelt too, and asked that arbitration might take the place of war. Bands of armed men kept arriving and demanding the old, manly way of settling things. In the end a fine was agreed, heavier than she thought fair, and part of it was paid on the spot in trade gin. As the boxes of gin were brought forward, she saw another fight about to start over the drink, so she took off as many of her outer garments as she decently could and threw them over the bottles, which put them under her protection by Egbo law. She then poured one glass for each of the senior men and kept the rest under her clothes. One band of young men begged to be allowed “a small scrap” on the way home, so as not to go back “like women” without having fought. She walked with them until they were past the danger. That night, too tired to hold a service, she spoke quietly to the people about Christ and walked home alone through the forest.

Knitting

After she came back from her furlough, the palavers grew larger. Ma Eme would send the signal bottle when trouble was brewing, and Mary would go. Sometimes, if she could not get there in time, she used a trick. She would scribble some words, any words, on a large sheet of paper, add a few blobs of red sealing-wax to make it look official, and send it by a fast runner to the chiefs. By the time they had finished puzzling over the mysterious document, which none of them could read, she had arrived.

At the palavers themselves she knitted. She said it kept her from being nervous and from showing fear, and that the sight of the needles going quietly on in the middle of the uproar calmed everyone down. An official told Livingstone that she once sat knitting and listening through a whole day and night, until both sides got hungry and went home without fighting.

Livingstone describes one of these meetings. Two sections of the Okoyong people had been quarrelling for some time, and she called them together in a forest clearing. Three years earlier, she said, such a meeting would have been impossible. She was frightened, and after a sleepless night she set out alone with her knitting and walked through the armed guards. Every chief was there under a great silk umbrella of blue, red, and yellow, with twenty to fifty armed men around him. A chair had been set for her in the middle, beside the oldest chief. She went round both groups first, joking, to ease the tension, then sat down, took out her knitting, and let them talk. She spoke only now and then, to draw out a fact or clear up a point. Night fell, torches were lit, voices rose, and when she sensed that things were getting out of hand she brought the matter to a head. An old chief summed up, she gave her verdict, and it was accepted with cheers.

Under Protest

Then came the oath to seal the agreement. A razor, corn, salt, pepper, and rum were brought. A free man from each side knelt at her feet and clasped the other’s fingers. Cuts were made on the backs of their hands, and when the blood flowed, salt, pepper, and corn were laid on the wounds. The two men then sucked up the blood-soaked mixture and swallowed it, and the covenant was made.

Out of courtesy, the chiefs asked her to pray. She refused. Livingstone says that she always witnessed such oaths “under protest, recognising that they knew no better way.” She did not object when one of the chiefs prayed instead.

It is a telling moment. She was willing to sit through the oath, because it was the only way the people knew of making an agreement binding, and because the agreement meant peace. But she would not lend her prayers to a rite she believed belonged to another religion. She drew a line, and she drew it gently. Then, after a ten-hour sitting, she walked four miles home in the dark, tired and hungry and happy.

Run, Ma, Run

Her letters from these years are full of interruptions. A letter will begin with household news, break off, and start again with “It is many days since I had to leave off here,” followed by the account of some sudden journey. The cry that sent her out of the house was always the same: “Run, Ma! Run!” She called this her “commonplace” work. “So, you see,” she wrote, “life here, as at home, is just a record of small duties which occupy the time, and task the strength without much to show for it.”

Livingstone collected some of the episodes. A chief had died, and the people had moved the poison ordeal to a hidden place deep in the forest to keep it from her. She found them, and sat there for four days and four nights, never taking off her clothes, sleeping in snatches on plantain leaves, afraid not of the armed men but of the eyes of wild animals shining at the edge of the firelight. In the end the people gave up and the accused lived. Another time an Egbo band from a far-off town came to seize the goods of a widow for a debt. Mary locked one of them in her yard, ordered the rest out, and made them give back what they had taken.

Once a slave couple came to her door with their child left behind. Their master had driven the wife from her cooking with a sword, fired a gun at the husband, and carried off the baby, threatening to kill it. “What does it matter?” the husband had said. “We are his; he can kill us if he likes; we have nothing to live for.” Mary sent word to the master. He came the next day, drunk, and lay down at her feet. During a palaver of several hours he shook his fist in the slave’s face and shouted, “If it wasn’t for the reign of the white woman I would cut you in two! The white woman is your salvation.” Mary calmed them both, scolded and pleaded and joked, and in the end sent them home together, the master told to control himself and the slaves told to work faithfully and not provoke him. The baby was returned.

That story should give us pause. Mary Slessor did not free the slaves who came to her. She sent them back to their master, after getting a promise that he would treat them better. Slavery was the foundation of Okoyong society, and she had no power to abolish it. She wrote in the margin of her Bible years later, “Slavery never pays; the slave is spoiled as a man, and the master not less so.” But in the forest of the 1890s, the best she could often do was to stand between the master and his sword.

Once a free man watched her prevent the killing of anyone at a funeral, and complained: “Ma, you have spoiled our fashions. Before you came, a person took his people with him: now one must go alone like this poor girl; you have confused Okoyong too much.”

And once, when a visiting missionary watched her clear a crowded yard in a moment by shouting at it in Efik, driving out men, women, children, and the old chief himself like sheep before a dog, he saw what it cost her. When it was over she came and sat down beside him, trembling from head to foot, and said, “I am done for this day.”

Children of God

The verse at the head of this chapter is one of the Beatitudes. “Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called sons of God.” It does not say that peacemakers will be successful, or thanked, or safe. It says that they will be recognised as belonging to God’s family, because making peace is what God himself does. Paul says of Christ, “he is our peace, who made both one, and brake down the middle wall of partition” (Ephesians 2:14, ASV).

Mary Slessor spent much of her life in Okoyong breaking down walls between enemies. She did it with prayer and patience and jokes and knitting, with sealing-wax and borrowed authority, and sometimes by throwing her own clothes over the gin. She did not always succeed, and she did not always get justice. But Paul’s instruction, “If it be possible, as much as in you lieth, be at peace with all men” (Romans 12:18, ASV), describes her very well. She did as much as lay in her, and a good deal more than anyone expected of a woman on her own.

One of the women of the village had told them about the white Ma at Ekenge, who had cured her grandchild. Send for her, she said, and the chief will not die. So they sent a message, with a bottle and four brass rods, worth about a shilling, as her fee. Edem and Ma Eme told her she could not go. It was too far, the streams were too deep, the rains were too heavy. “I am going to get ready,” she said. She spent a sleepless night wondering whether she was right, and in the morning set out with an escort of women. The rain came down in torrents. First she abandoned her boots, then her stockings, then her broken umbrella, and then, one by one, most of her clothes, which the women carried on their heads in calabashes. She walked on in the lightest of garments through the dripping forest. After three hours they came to a market-place where hundreds of people were gathering. Mary, soaked and half-dressed, felt humiliated, and hurried through the crowd, wondering whether she had lost their respect. She learned later that nothing she ever did won the hearts of the Okoyong more than that walk in the rain. She reached the village, dressed herself in whatever odds and ends of clothing the women could find, and went straight to the sick man. Her medicine was not enough, and she persuaded a trader living in his canoe nearby to go across the river to the Scottish missionaries at Ikorofiong for more. He came back with what she needed, and with a letter and some tea from the missionary’s wife. She brewed the tea in a basin and thought it a feast. The chief recovered. No one was killed. The people began to talk about making peace with Calabar and learning to read. From then on, Livingstone says, Okoyong was open to her. The Woman’s God That chief did not forget her. At the end of 1890, as she was packing to leave for her furlough, messengers arrived from a distant township. A young freeman had accidentally shot himself in the hand while hunting, and they wanted medicine. She sent it. Then secret word came that the young man had died, that his brother had wounded a chief of a neighbouring town in revenge, and that the chief’s warriors were preparing to attack at dawn. Everyone told her not to go. She was ill. She would miss the steamer. The men were savage, they said, the forest would be full of armed men firing at anything that moved, and in the dark no one would recognise her. She went anyway, with two armed attendants carrying lanterns, and stopped at the house of a chief eight miles away to ask for a free man to beat the Egbo drum before her, so that the warriors would know a protected person was coming. The chief sent back a diplomatic answer. He had heard of no war, he said, and would inquire in the morning. And if there was a war, a woman who went into it only proved her ignorance of a people who had always loved fighting and were not likely to be helped by a woman. Mary sent him a reply that has been remembered ever since: In measuring the woman’s power, you have evidently forgotten to take into account the woman’s God. She went on without him. At the first village she was surrounded in the dark by armed men, who questioned her and then let her rest until cock-crow, when they would take her with them. At the second cock-crow they were gone before she was on her feet, running down the hillside like wild goats. The women stood at every door crying, “Run, Ma!” She ran as fast as her weakness allowed, lost sight of them, and fell back on prayer. She found the war-party in the bush a hundred yards from the enemy village, and told them to behave like men and not like fools, as if they were schoolboys. Then she walked on to the village, where a wall of armed men stood silent. As she was about to push through them, an old man stepped out of the line and knelt at her feet. He asked her to help them make peace. It was the chief she had walked through the rain to heal. What followed took all day. Two chiefs laid down their arms and knelt before the other side, begging them to accept a fine. Mary knelt too, and asked that arbitration might take the place of war. Bands of armed men kept arriving and demanding the old, manly way of settling things. In the end a fine was agreed, heavier than she thought fair, and part of it was paid on the spot in trade gin. As the boxes of gin were brought forward, she saw another fight about to start over the drink, so she took off as many of her outer garments as she decently could and threw them over the bottles, which put them under her protection by Egbo law. She then poured one glass for each of the senior men and kept the rest under her clothes. One band of young men begged to be allowed “a small scrap” on the way home, so as not to go back “like women” without having fought. She walked with them until they were past the danger. That night, too tired to hold a service, she spoke quietly to the people about Christ and walked home alone through the forest. Knitting After she came back from her furlough, the palavers grew larger. Ma Eme would send the signal bottle when trouble was brewing, and Mary would go. Sometimes, if she could not get there in time, she used a trick. She would scribble some words, any words, on a large sheet of paper, add a few blobs of red sealing-wax to make it look official, and send it by a fast runner to the chiefs. By the time they had finished puzzling over the mysterious document, which none of them could read, she had arrived. At the palavers themselves she knitted. She said it kept her from being nervous and from showing fear, and that the sight of the needles going quietly on in the middle of the uproar calmed everyone down. An official told Livingstone that she once sat knitting and listening through a whole day and night, until both sides got hungry and went home without fighting. Livingstone describes one of these meetings. Two sections of the Okoyong people had been quarrelling for some time, and she called them together in a forest clearing. Three years earlier, she said, such a meeting would have been impossible. She was frightened, and after a sleepless night she set out alone with her knitting and walked through the armed guards. Every chief was there under a great silk umbrella of blue, red, and yellow, with twenty to fifty armed men around him. A chair had been set for her in the middle, beside the oldest chief. She went round both groups first, joking, to ease the tension, then sat down, took out her knitting, and let them talk. She spoke only now and then, to draw out a fact or clear up a point. Night fell, torches were lit, voices rose, and when she sensed that things were getting out of hand she brought the matter to a head. An old chief summed up, she gave her verdict, and it was accepted with cheers. Under Protest Then came the oath to seal the agreement. A razor, corn, salt, pepper, and rum were brought. A free man from each side knelt at her feet and clasped the other’s fingers. Cuts were made on the backs of their hands, and when the blood flowed, salt, pepper, and corn were laid on the wounds. The two men then sucked up the blood-soaked mixture and swallowed it, and the covenant was made. Out of courtesy, the chiefs asked her to pray. She refused. Livingstone says that she always witnessed such oaths “under protest, recognising that they knew no better way.” She did not object when one of the chiefs prayed instead. It is a telling moment. She was willing to sit through the oath, because it was the only way the people knew of making an agreement binding, and because the agreement meant peace. But she would not lend her prayers to a rite she believed belonged to another religion. She drew a line, and she drew it gently. Then, after a ten-hour sitting, she walked four miles home in the dark, tired and hungry and happy. Run, Ma, Run Her letters from these years are full of interruptions. A letter will begin with household news, break off, and start again with “It is many days since I had to leave off here,” followed by the account of some sudden journey. The cry that sent her out of the house was always the same: “Run, Ma! Run!” She called this her “commonplace” work. “So, you see,” she wrote, “life here, as at home, is just a record of small duties which occupy the time, and task the strength without much to show for it.” Livingstone collected some of the episodes. A chief had died, and the people had moved the poison ordeal to a hidden place deep in the forest to keep it from her. She found them, and sat there for four days and four nights, never taking off her clothes, sleeping in snatches on plantain leaves, afraid not of the armed men but of the eyes of wild animals shining at the edge of the firelight. In the end the people gave up and the accused lived. Another time an Egbo band from a far-off town came to seize the goods of a widow for a debt. Mary locked one of them in her yard, ordered the rest out, and made them give back what they had taken. Once a slave couple came to her door with their child left behind. Their master had driven the wife from her cooking with a sword, fired a gun at the husband, and carried off the baby, threatening to kill it. “What does it matter?” the husband had said. “We are his; he can kill us if he likes; we have nothing to live for.” Mary sent word to the master. He came the next day, drunk, and lay down at her feet. During a palaver of several hours he shook his fist in the slave’s face and shouted, “If it wasn’t for the reign of the white woman I would cut you in two! The white woman is your salvation.” Mary calmed them both, scolded and pleaded and joked, and in the end sent them home together, the master told to control himself and the slaves told to work faithfully and not provoke him. The baby was returned. That story should give us pause. Mary Slessor did not free the slaves who came to her. She sent them back to their master, after getting a promise that he would treat them better. Slavery was the foundation of Okoyong society, and she had no power to abolish it. She wrote in the margin of her Bible years later, “Slavery never pays; the slave is spoiled as a man, and the master not less so.” But in the forest of the 1890s, the best she could often do was to stand between the master and his sword. Once a free man watched her prevent the killing of anyone at a funeral, and complained: “Ma, you have spoiled our fashions. Before you came, a person took his people with him: now one must go alone like this poor girl; you have confused Okoyong too much.” And once, when a visiting missionary watched her clear a crowded yard in a moment by shouting at it in Efik, driving out men, women, children, and the old chief himself like sheep before a dog, he saw what it cost her. When it was over she came and sat down beside him, trembling from head to foot, and said, “I am done for this day.” Children of God The verse at the head of this chapter is one of the Beatitudes. “Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called sons of God.” It does not say that peacemakers will be successful, or thanked, or safe. It says that they will be recognised as belonging to God’s family, because making peace is what God himself does. Paul says of Christ, “he is our peace, who made both one, and brake down the middle wall of partition” (Ephesians 2:14, ASV). Mary Slessor spent much of her life in Okoyong breaking down walls between enemies. She did it with prayer and patience and jokes and knitting, with sealing-wax and borrowed authority, and sometimes by throwing her own clothes over the gin. She did not always succeed, and she did not always get justice. But Paul’s instruction, “If it be possible, as much as in you lieth, be at peace with all men” (Romans 12:18, ASV), describes her very well. She did as much as lay in her, and a good deal more than anyone expected of a woman on her own.

fields.title: Consul and Gunboat
fields.body_html:
“He hath showed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth Jehovah require of thee, but to do justly, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with thy God?”

— Micah 6:8, ASV

The Coming of the Protectorate

When Mary Slessor arrived in Calabar in 1876, British power on the coast was little more than a consul with no soldiers and no administration. By the time she returned from her furlough in 1892, that had begun to change. In 1884 and 1885, as the European powers carved up Africa among themselves at the Berlin Conference, Britain had declared a protectorate over the coastal districts around the Niger delta and Calabar. In 1891 Sir Claude Macdonald was appointed Commissioner and Consul-General, with instructions to turn a paper claim into a working government. Two years later the territory became the Niger Coast Protectorate.

Livingstone describes this as the extension of civilised rule to a backward country, carried out, he says, “not without an occasional display of force.” That phrase deserves attention. The British did not ask the peoples of the interior whether they wished to be governed. They sent officials to make treaties, and where the treaties were refused or broken, they sent gunboats and soldiers. Villages were burned. People in Okoyong came to associate the Consul, in Livingstone’s own words, “with big guns and burnt towns.” That was the power that now stood behind Mary Slessor.

Ma’s Court

Macdonald was a man Mary liked and respected. He was sympathetic to the missions, and he took her advice seriously. When he proposed to send a British vice-consul to Okoyong, she argued that the people were not ready for strangers imposing new laws, and that there would be trouble. Macdonald accepted her view. Instead of sending an official, he authorised her to do what was necessary herself, and to organise and supervise a native court.

Later writers have usually said that she was made vice-consul for Okoyong in 1892, and that is how most biographies describe it. Livingstone is more careful. He says her position was “akin to that of a consular agent.” In practice she conducted the public business of the district. She presided over the court. Cases were referred to her from Duke Town, and she travelled round Okoyong to hear them, with a government messenger who carried her decisions back to headquarters for official signature. Chiefs and ordinary people came to ask her how their old customs could be fitted to the new laws. She took no salary for any of it. Livingstone says it was work she did not like, and that she accepted it only because she believed it was part of her loyalty to Christ.

The Caning

A British official, T. D. Maxwell, visited her court in these years and left one of the most vivid descriptions of her we have. He expected, he said, he hardly knew what, and found “a little frail old lady” with a lace shawl over her head, rocking in a chair and crooning to a black baby. Years of fever had aged her early. He was struck, he said, by her very strong Scottish accent. She made him rest after his march before any business was done. The court was held below her house, and her yard was full of litigants and onlookers, all treating her with deep respect.

Suddenly she jumped up with an angry growl. Her shawl fell off, the baby was handed to someone else, and she made for the door, where a large, overdressed man was standing. She seized him by the scruff of the neck, boxed his ears, and hustled him out into the yard, telling him plainly what would happen if he came back. Then, as suddenly as the storm had risen, it died away, and she was back in her rocking-chair with the shawl and the baby. The man was a local chief who had been rude to her and had been forbidden to come back until he apologised. He had tried to slip in on the excuse of greeting the visitor.

Maxwell had seen many Nigerian courts, and he said he had never seen one that better deserved to be called a court of justice. The litigants got justice, “sometimes, perhaps, like Shylock, more than they desired.” He gave an example. A man sued another for a small debt. The defendant admitted he owed the money, and Mary ordered him to pay. But she added that the plaintiff was a rascal. He treated his mother shamefully, neglected his children, had lately beaten one of his wives with unnecessary vigour, kept a disgraceful farm, seldom washed, and had looked suspiciously sleek around the time a neighbour’s goat went missing, though he had been acquitted. So before the debt was paid, the plaintiff would receive a good sound caning in front of everyone.

Maxwell told the story with admiration, and it is easy to see why. It is funny, and it shows a judge who knew everyone in the district and cared more about what was right than about technicalities. But a modern reader should see the other side as well. A man who came to court to recover a debt and won his case was beaten on the order of the judge for offences he had not been charged with, including one of which he had been acquitted. There was no appeal. Her justice was the justice of a mother of a large and unruly family, and it depended entirely on her being right. Often she was. Not always.

The Appeal to the Consul

In 1894 she did something she had never done before. A man had been accused of causing his master’s death by witchcraft, and his accusers, knowing that Mary would stop the ordeal, spirited him away in chains to a village beyond her reach. She decided that the time had come to ask the government for help, not only to save this man but to end killing for witchcraft throughout Okoyong. So that no African would be blamed for it, she carried the letter to the river herself.

The news spread quickly that Ma’s patience was exhausted and she had sent for the Consul. The people who had carried off the prisoner came running to beg her forgiveness, but she had already gone. The prisoner escaped that night and came to her house. His master chained all his other people in fury, then thought better of it, freed them, and sent to ask Mary to go to Duke Town and make the Consul come “in peace and not in war.”

The Vice-Consul, Ralph Moor, came up with a small guard of soldiers, who paraded through the village and made a great impression. He found Mary on the roof of her house mending the mats, and she climbed down and received him without the slightest embarrassment. At the conference that followed, the chiefs promised to stop killing at funerals, and to let Ma save twins and care for them in a special hut. A year later, when twin-killing had not stopped, she brought up Sir Claude Macdonald himself to renew the agreement. He told the chiefs that he had not come to take their country, but to help them govern it justly. After consulting together, the old spokesman explained that when they heard something only once they did not think it worth attending to, but now that they had heard it twice, they would obey. As for twins, he said, “We are not sure that no evil will happen to us if we obey you; we have our fear, but we will try.” When Mary spoke of a time when she would no longer be with them, the chiefs were alarmed. “God cannot take you away from your children,” they said, “until they are able to walk by themselves.”

“You White People”

Some time later Mary wrote an account of her first seven years in Okoyong. It was never published, and Livingstone printed much of it. It is one of the most important documents of her life, and it will appear again in the next chapter. In it she described the death of the most powerful chief in the district. Every drop of European liquor for miles around was bought for his funeral, and she was afraid of what would follow. But no one was killed, except one man, who, blamed by the witch-doctors, hanged himself because the chiefs refused to let him take the poison ordeal to prove his innocence. Afterwards some chiefs, talking about the change, said to her, “Ma, you white people are God Almighty. No other power could have done this.”

Mary recorded that remark without comment, and it is not hard to see why it troubled later readers. The chiefs were not wrong about where power lay. Behind the white woman in the rocking-chair stood the consul, and behind the consul stood the guns. The same report says that the people had “begged me to be their consul, as they neither wished black man nor white man to be their king.” It also says that they still needed “superintendence and watching, for their ideas are not so nicely balanced as ours in regard to the shades and degrees of right and wrong.” That sentence is the voice of her time and her race, and it is not attractive.

Yet there is another side to it. The chiefs had also said, back in 1889, that they were weary of the old customs and could not break them alone. Mary’s authority, backed by the government, gave them a way out. Many lives were saved. Women who would have been strangled at funerals lived. Men who would have died by the poison bean went home to their families. It was a good thing done by means that were not wholly good, in a world where there were few wholly good means available.

What the Lord Requires

A visitor to Okoyong in these years wrote that Mary was really “Queen of the whole of Okoyong district,” and that the High Commissioner left its administration in her hands. The same visitor noticed that she never let an African sit down in her presence, and never shook hands with them, though she would nurse them through the most loathsome diseases. When the visitor asked why, she said simply, “I live alone.” She seems to have meant that a woman living alone among men who had always settled their disputes with guns could not afford to let her authority be questioned. It was a hard, practical decision, and it put a distance between her and the people she loved.

The verse at the head of this chapter was spoken by the prophet Micah to a nation that thought God could be satisfied with sacrifices. What God wanted, Micah said, was simpler and harder: “to do justly, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with thy God.” Mary Slessor tried to do all three, and the three do not always sit easily together. Justice in Okoyong sometimes needed a firm hand, and she had one. Kindness was her deepest instinct, and she gave it without limit. Humility before God she practised all her life. Humility before the people she governed was harder, and it grew slowly.

Paul told the Christians in Rome that “rulers are not a terror to the good work, but to the evil” (Romans 13:3, ASV). The psalmist warned, “Put not your trust in princes, Nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psalm 146:3, ASV). Mary Slessor lived between those two verses. She was grateful for rulers who stopped the killing, and she worked with them. But she knew, too, where her own help came from, and she would soon see what the government’s power could do when it was turned on a whole people.

But she knew, too, where her own help came from, and she would soon see what the government’s power could do when it was turned on a whole people.

fields.title: Smallpox and Silence
fields.body_html:
“For though the fig-tree shall not flourish, Neither shall fruit be in the vines; The labor of the olive shall fail, And the fields shall yield no food; The flock shall be cut off from the fold, And there shall be no herd in the stalls: Yet I will rejoice in Jehovah, I will joy in the God of my salvation.”

— Habakkuk 3:17-18, ASV

No Baptisms

About seven years after she went to Okoyong, Mary was persuaded to write down an account of her work there. It was never published, and Livingstone found it among her papers. It begins with a protest.

In these days of high pressure men demand large profits and quick returns in every department of our commercial and national life, and these must be served up with the definiteness and precision of statistics. This abnormal and feverish haste has entered to some extent into our religious work.

She said that the methods and standards of business were “utterly foreign to the laws of Christ’s kingdom,” and that she shrank from reducing the working of God’s Spirit in people’s hearts to “any given number of figures on a table.” Then she gave the figures anyway, and they were stark. There had been no baptisms in Okoyong, and no communion services. No ordained minister had ever lived there. There were no formal candidates for church membership. Women, boys, girls, and a few men said that they had put themselves in God’s hands. One free-born woman of good position had suffered persecution for Christ. That was all.

She was honest about why. She was one woman, running a dispensary, a school, a court, a house full of rescued children, and a refuge for runaway slaves and threatened wives. She built and repaired her own buildings. There was no baker, no butcher, no laundry, no water supply, and no help except what the people lent her. The evangelistic work of the station, she wrote, was “manned year by year by the magnificent total of one individual. Is it fair to expect results under such circumstances?”

That was a rebuke to her Church, and she meant it as one. But she did not blame the Church alone. The report also says that the results had not been what they would have been “had we been more faithful and kept more in line with the will and spirit of God.” She always wrote “we” in her reports, never “I.” She believed she was a fellow-worker with God, and that both the failures and the successes were shared.

When friends asked about progress, she used to say, “There is not much progress to report, and yet very much to thank God for.” And she would add, “After all, it comes back to this, Christ sent me to preach the Gospel, and He will look after results.” She remembered a single line from a sermon she had heard long ago in her mother’s church in Aberdeen: “Between the sower and the reaper stands the Husbandman.” Paul had said the same thing: “I planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase. So then neither is he that planteth anything, neither he that watereth; but God that giveth the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6-7, ASV).

Akpap

In 1896 the people of Okoyong began to move away from Ekenge. Like farming peoples everywhere who worked the soil hard, they moved on to fresh land, and a new market had grown up at a place called Akpap, further inland and nearer the Cross River. Even Ma Eme moved to a distant farm. Mary saw that she must follow, and the mission agreed to build a new house there. Long before it was built, she moved into a two-roomed shed with no windows and no floor, and from there, Livingstone says, she ruled Okoyong as if from a palace.

Then disaster came. A new baby brought an infectious disease into her household, and four of her children died of it. Soon afterwards smallpox swept through the region and killed hundreds. She spent hours every day vaccinating people, and when her supply of vaccine ran out, the mission engineer, Mr. Alexander, helped her take lymph from the arms of people already vaccinated with a penknife and pass it on to others.

At Ekenge, where the epidemic was worst, she turned her old house into a hospital. The sick poured in, and everyone else fled, and she could find no one to nurse the patients or bury the dead. Ekpenyong, the elder chief whose poison beans she had once carried off, caught the disease and died, and she buried him. Then Edem, her own chief, who had taken her into his compound eight years before, fell ill. She fought for his life day and night. He died in the middle of the night. She was alone. With her own hands she made a coffin, laid him in it, dug a grave, and buried him. Then she walked through the dark, wet forest to Akpap and threw herself on her bed as dawn was breaking.

The carpenter Charles Ovens, who had come back to build the new mission house, arrived that morning with Mr. Alexander. They found the hut silent at eleven o’clock, and inside, Mary, grey and exhausted. “I had only just now fallen asleep,” she said. It was some time before they found out why. Two days later Alexander went to Ekenge to fetch materials from the old house, and found it full of corpses, with no one living anywhere near. The house was never lived in again, and the forest swallowed it.

“My Four Bairns”

News came from further up-country of people fleeing the smallpox, leaving the dead and dying in their houses, and dying in the bush themselves. Mary wrote:

They have no helper up there, and know of no Saviour. I am just thinking that perhaps the reason God has taken my four bairns is that I may be free to go up and help them.

It is a hard sentence to read. A mother whose four children have just died wonders whether God took them so that she would be free to help others. Many Christians today would not say it, and would not want anyone to say it to them. But it was her own way of refusing to believe that the deaths were meaningless. She was not explaining suffering from the outside. She was trying to find a way through it from the inside.

She did not find it easily. Livingstone says that for a time she had “no heart for anything.” He calls it an unusual note, and a sign that her strength was failing. We would call it grief, and perhaps depression. It would not be the last time.

In the evenings, Ovens watched her lead family worship in the shed. She sat on the mud floor with her back against the wall, the boys and girls in a half-circle in front of her, and behind them baskets full of twin babies. She prayed very simply. Then they sang a hymn she had written in Efik to the Scottish tune “Rothesay Bay,” and she kept time with a tambourine, which she used to tap on the heads of girls whose attention wandered.

A friend wrote to her about the great crowds at the Church’s synod in Edinburgh, and she answered:

It is easy to be good with all the holy and helpful influences about you. Away up here among heathenism, working away with the twos and the threes and the tens, one almost forgets that there are crowds who would die for Christ. … But Christ is here and the Holy Spirit, and if I am seldom in a triumphant or ecstatic mood I am always satisfied and happy in His love.

The Shy Speaker

In 1898 the mission council insisted that she take a furlough. Her clothes had been eaten by ants and she had nothing fit to wear, but a box arrived from a church in Glasgow with everything she needed, including a warm shawl for the voyage, which she took as an answer to prayer. She took four girls with her: Janie, now grown up; Mary, the child of wonder, aged five; Alice, about three; and baby Maggie.

She was more famous than ever, and shyer. At a drawing-room meeting in Glasgow, finding men in the audience, she stood up and could not speak, and finally turned to them and asked, “Will the gentlemen kindly go away?” When told they would be disappointed, she asked whether they would kindly go and sit where she could not see them. At Stirling she asked a gentleman who had slipped in to hide behind the lady in front of him. When people praised her she left the room until they had finished. In Edinburgh, overwhelmed by the welcome, she broke down, and then insisted that her work was no more remarkable than that of any other missionary in Calabar. “They all work as hard or harder than I do.”

She pleaded for workers, using the language of her age: “When Sir Herbert Kitchener, going out to conquer the Soudan required help, thousands of the brightest of our young men were ready. Where are the soldiers of the Cross? … Why should the Queen have good soldiers and not the King of Kings?” She also said, in words that would echo in her later life, that her work in Okoyong was done. She wanted an ordained minister sent to take it over, and she wanted to go further inland.

Three Years Alone

She returned at the end of 1898, and the plans to send her help broke down. For the next three years she was alone at Akpap, apart from occasional visits from women missionaries in Calabar. She had long spells of low fever and sleeplessness, and once spent three months in bed. Many of her letters from these years are dated “Midnight,” “3 A.M.,” or “Just before dawn.” She confessed that “our poor wee services here take as much out of me as the great meetings at home did.”

Sometimes the darkness came through. “All is dark,” she wrote, “except above. Calvary stands safe and sure.” And: “Life apart from Christ is a dreadful gift.” She wondered whether she would ever go home again. “How could I leave the bairns in this dreadful land? Who would mother them in this sink of iniquity?” She dreamed of a bit of land and a small house of her own, where she could “stay out my days there with my bairns and lie down among them.”

There were signs of change too. Six boys of free birth whom she had taught were now Christians, and were holding services in the villages. Two were sons of the most powerful chiefs. Once, as she and Mr. Alexander sat at breakfast, a woman came in without a word and put a large calabash on the table. Mary thought it was food and said they had already eaten. The woman said nothing. Mary lifted the lid. Inside were twin boys. A woman had brought her twins to be saved rather than thrown away. Some parents began keeping their twins at home, and Mary told the chiefs that if anyone blamed a misfortune on them, she would “make palaver.” “I feel the smallness of the returns,” she wrote, “but is the labour lost? A thousand times No!”

On 21 December 1899, according to the small marriage register Mary kept in Efik, Janie married a young man named Akibo Eyo, whom Mary called her best scholar. There was no church wedding. The two took an oath before a chief and before Ma Eme that each would marry the other alone, a pledge of faithfulness in the only form that would bind in Okoyong. (Some modern accounts give the date as 12 December.) The marriage did not last. “Difficulty and disappointment came,” Livingstone says, and Janie, now usually called Jean, came back to Mary’s household, where she stayed to the end. A baby whose mother had died in childbirth was brought to the house, and Jean took him as her own. He was named Daniel MacArthur Slessor, and Dan would become, after Jean, the best known of Mary’s children.

The Fig-Tree

The prophet Habakkuk wrote the words at the head of this chapter when he knew that invasion and ruin were coming to his country. He imagines a farm in total failure: no figs, no grapes, no olives, no grain, no sheep, no cattle. And then he says, “Yet I will rejoice in Jehovah, I will joy in the God of my salvation.”

That is not the joy of success. It is the joy of a person who has lost almost everything and discovered that God is still there. Mary Slessor’s years at Akpap were a time of empty fields. Four of her children died in a single epidemic. Her chief and protector died while she nursed him, and she buried him herself. She worked alone for three years, often ill, often sleepless, with no baptisms to report. And through it all she wrote that she was “always satisfied and happy in His love.” Not always triumphant. Not always cheerful. But satisfied. The psalmist says, “Weeping may tarry for the night, But joy cometh in the morning” (Psalm 30:5, ASV). The morning, when it came, would come in a place she did not yet expect.

fields.title: Not by Might
fields.body_html:
“Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of Jehovah unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, saith Jehovah of hosts.”

— Zechariah 4:6, ASV

The Aro

For years, from her house in Okoyong, Mary Slessor had looked across the Cross River towards the west. Beyond the river lay the country of the Ibibio and, further north, of the Igbo, millions of people whom no missionary had reached. Over much of that country one people held extraordinary power. They were the Aro, whose home was a cluster of towns called Arochukwu, which Mary knew as Arochuku.

The Aro were traders, and for two centuries they had been the great organisers of the slave trade in south-eastern Nigeria. Their power rested on an oracle, a shrine in a wooded gorge near Arochukwu called Ibini Ukpabi, which Europeans called the Long Juju. People from all over the region brought their disputes to it for judgement. Some of those who consulted it, or who were found guilty by it, never came back: they were said to have been devoured by the oracle, and in fact many were sold into slavery through the Aro trading network. Aro agents lived in towns throughout the region, bound to local people by oaths of blood-brotherhood, and trade routes, marriages, and justice all ran through them. Livingstone says that “all roads in the country led to Aro.”

Livingstone also repeats stories that the Aro and their neighbours sacrificed and ate slaves at their feasts. Such stories were widely told by Europeans at the time, and some of the region’s peoples told them about each other. They were never properly documented, and modern historians treat them with great caution. What is certain is that the Aro system was built on the buying and selling of human beings, that people died by it, and that it resisted the British advance with all its strength.

Mary knew Aro slave-traders personally. Some of them passed through Okoyong with their captives, and she made friends with them and learned how the trade worked. She told them frankly that she meant to come to their country one day. They invited her, and hinted that it might not be safe. She would have gone years before, but she could not leave Okoyong without someone to take her place, and no one was sent. “The test of a real good missionary,” she wrote while she waited, “is this waiting, silent, seemingly useless time.”

The Expedition

In 1900 the Niger Coast Protectorate became the Protectorate of Southern Nigeria, with Sir Ralph Moor, the same man who had once found Mary mending her roof, as High Commissioner. The Aro refused to accept British rule. They went on trading in slaves, raided towns that had submitted to the government, and blocked the routes inland. At the end of 1901 the British sent a military force of around sixteen hundred African soldiers under British officers, commanded by Lieutenant-Colonel A. F. Montanaro, advancing in several columns. One of them went up from Itu, on the Cross River. Arochukwu was taken at the end of December 1901. The oracle was found and destroyed. The campaign, known as the Aro Expedition, lasted about three months. At its end the Aro chiefs were made to accept disarmament, the suppression of the oracle, and the prohibition of slave-trading. More than two thousand five hundred guns were surrendered.

Livingstone, writing fifteen years later, describes the expedition as the forces of civilisation meeting the warriors of barbarism. He says the government had been “very patient and conciliatory” and that force became “absolutely necessary at last.” He gives no account of the fighting or of those killed. He calls it, in passing, a “punitive expedition.” That is exactly what it was. A foreign army invaded a country that had not attacked Britain, defeated its people, destroyed their central shrine, disarmed them, and imposed a new government on them. The fact that the Aro slave system was cruel does not change what the expedition was.

Exile in Creek Town

Mary took no part in the fighting. When the troops were being gathered, the government, anxious for her safety, asked her to come down to Calabar until the trouble was over. She went, very much against her will. The government sent a special escort for her and offered to build her a house at Creek Town for herself and her family. She refused. She did not wish, Livingstone says, “to become too closely identified with the Government.” She squeezed into part of the mission hospital instead, where she had no privacy, and longed to get away from the crowds and “the bright, the terribly bright sky.”

Okoyong stayed quiet. People came down to see her, brought their disputes for her to settle, and loaded her with food. Her boys kept up the services at Akpap. Twin babies whom she had placed with their own mothers in four different villages were safe. Then one of her oldest friends, the wife of a great chief, gave birth to twins, and Mary wrote at once to the chief telling him to put his wife in a canoe and send her down to Creek Town. She explained herself in words that are among the most revealing she ever wrote:

I am sorry for her, but we cannot make different laws for the rich and for the poor, and yet one may press too far with a chief, and incite rebellion. After all we are foreigners, and they own the country, so I always try to make the law fit in, while we adjust things between us.

“We are foreigners, and they own the country.” At the very moment when a British army was marching through the country to the west, Mary Slessor said plainly that the land belonged to its people and that she and her kind were guests in it. She did not say that the expedition was wrong. As far as we know, she never said that. She believed that God used governments to restrain evil, and she hated the slave trade with her whole heart. But her instinct as a missionary was not the instinct of a conqueror. She tried to make the law fit the people, not the people fit the law.

When the campaign was over, she asked the Commissioner for permission to go home. He asked her to wait until a certain movement of troops was finished. She smiled and said she would go at the first opportunity, and she did.

Advice to the Young

Her months in Creek Town had one good result. She met a new generation of missionaries, and some of them became her close friends. The Rev. A. W. Wilkie and his wife, and later the Rev. J. K. Macgregor, head of the Hope Waddell Institute, and his wife, gave her homes to go to when she was ill and exhausted for the rest of her life. The young missionaries found her fascinating. Her talk, one of them said, was “better than medicine.”

One young woman told her how hard it was, in a busy station like Duke Town, to know exactly what to do. Mary answered, “Do? lassie, do? You’ve not got to do, you’ve just got to be, and the doing will follow.” She told another, “Make a bold stand for purity of speech and charity of judgment.” These are the sayings of a woman who had learned, through years of exhaustion, that the work flowed from the life, and not the other way round.

Under Escort

In June 1903 Mary set out from Akpap to visit the new stations she was planting on the Cross River. She missed the government launch at Ikunetu and tramped home, saying that God had not meant her to travel that day. The next week she caught it, and found on board Colonel Montanaro himself, the commander of the expedition, on his way up to Arochukwu. He invited her to come with him, under his escort. She had no change of clothes and no food, and she thought and prayed about it all the way up the river. Livingstone records what she was thinking:

Here is the challenge to enter that region of unbroken gloom and despair. If it is not entered now, the Roman Catholics will come in, and the key position to the whole territory will be taken out of our hands.

She went. At Arochukwu, eighteen months after the expedition, she walked roads that had been trodden for centuries by captives on their way to the coast, and saw the gorge where the oracle had stood. The chiefs and traders, many of whom she already knew, welcomed her and promised to help her. A little later she came back with two boys and opened a school in the palaver shed of one of the towns. A hundred children crowded in, along with men and women and some of the old slave-dealers themselves. When she left, the people followed her to the landing-beach and called after her, “Don’t be long in coming back, Ma! If you don’t care for us, who will care for us?”

It must be said plainly. Mary Slessor entered Aro country in the company of the soldier who had conquered it, and she went partly to get there before the Catholics. And yet there is another side, and her friend Mr. Wilkie saw it. He wrote that if she had been settled in the Aro country before the expedition, “it is doubtful whether an armed expedition would have been necessary, and it is at least possible that the suppression of the slave-trade would have been achieved by the peaceable means of the Gospel.” Livingstone agreed: primitive peoples, he said in the language of his time, “often bend more quickly before Christ than break before might of arms.” Wilkie could not prove it, of course. The psalmist says the same thing: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses; But we will make mention of the name of Jehovah our God” (Psalm 20:7, ASV).

Beyond the river lay the country of the Ibibio and, further north, of the Igbo, millions of people whom no missionary had reached. Over much of that country one people held extraordinary power. They were the Aro, whose home was a cluster of towns called Arochukwu, which Mary knew as Arochuku. The Aro were traders, and for two centuries they had been the great organisers of the slave trade in south-eastern Nigeria. Their power rested on an oracle, a shrine in a wooded gorge near Arochukwu called Ibini Ukpabi, which Europeans called the Long Juju. People from all over the region brought their disputes to it for judgement. Some of those who consulted it, or who were found guilty by it, never came back: they were said to have been devoured by the oracle, and in fact many were sold into slavery through the Aro trading network. Aro agents lived in towns throughout the region, bound to local people by oaths of blood-brotherhood, and trade routes, marriages, and justice all ran through them. Livingstone says that “all roads in the country led to Aro.” Livingstone also repeats stories that the Aro and their neighbours sacrificed and ate slaves at their feasts. Such stories were widely told by Europeans at the time, and some of the region’s peoples told them about each other. They were never properly documented, and modern historians treat them with great caution. What is certain is that the Aro system was built on the buying and selling of human beings, that people died by it, and that it resisted the British advance with all its strength. Mary knew Aro slave-traders personally. Some of them passed through Okoyong with their captives, and she made friends with them and learned how the trade worked. She told them frankly that she meant to come to their country one day. They invited her, and hinted that it might not be safe. She would have gone years before, but she could not leave Okoyong without someone to take her place, and no one was sent. “The test of a real good missionary,” she wrote while she waited, “is this waiting, silent, seemingly useless time.” The Expedition In 1900 the Niger Coast Protectorate became the Protectorate of Southern Nigeria, with Sir Ralph Moor, the same man who had once found Mary mending her roof, as High Commissioner. The Aro refused to accept British rule. They went on trading in slaves, raided towns that had submitted to the government, and blocked the routes inland. At the end of 1901 the British sent a military force of around sixteen hundred African soldiers under British officers, commanded by Lieutenant-Colonel A. F. Montanaro, advancing in several columns. One of them went up from Itu, on the Cross River. Arochukwu was taken at the end of December 1901. The oracle was found and destroyed. The campaign, known as the Aro Expedition, lasted about three months. At its end the Aro chiefs were made to accept disarmament, the suppression of the oracle, and the prohibition of slave-trading. More than two thousand five hundred guns were surrendered. Livingstone, writing fifteen years later, describes the expedition as the forces of civilisation meeting the warriors of barbarism. He says the government had been “very patient and conciliatory” and that force became “absolutely necessary at last.” He gives no account of the fighting or of those killed. He calls it, in passing, a “punitive expedition.” That is exactly what it was. A foreign army invaded a country that had not attacked Britain, defeated its people, destroyed their central shrine, disarmed them, and imposed a new government on them. The fact that the Aro slave system was cruel does not change what the expedition was. Exile in Creek Town Mary took no part in the fighting. When the troops were being gathered, the government, anxious for her safety, asked her to come down to Calabar until the trouble was over. She went, very much against her will. The government sent a special escort for her and offered to build her a house at Creek Town for herself and her family. She refused. She did not wish, Livingstone says, “to become too closely identified with the Government.” She squeezed into part of the mission hospital instead, where she had no privacy, and longed to get away from the crowds and “the bright, the terribly bright sky.” Okoyong stayed quiet. She did not say that the expedition was wrong. As far as we know, she never said that. She believed that God used governments to restrain evil, and she hated the slave trade with her whole heart. But her instinct as a missionary was not the instinct of a conqueror. She tried to make the law fit the people, not the people fit the law. When the campaign was over, she asked the Commissioner for permission to go home. He asked her to wait until a certain movement of troops was finished. She met a new generation of missionaries, and some of them became her close friends. The Rev. A. W. Wilkie and his wife, and later the Rev. J. K. Macgregor, head of the Hope Waddell Institute, and his wife, gave her homes to go to when she was ill and exhausted for the rest of her life. The young missionaries found her fascinating. Her talk, one of them said, was “better than medicine.” One young woman told her how hard it was, in a busy station like Duke Town, to know exactly what to do. Mary answered, “Do? lassie, do? You’ve not got to do, you’ve just got to be, and the doing will follow.” She told another, “Make a bold stand for purity of speech and charity of judgment.” These are the sayings of a woman who had learned, through years of exhaustion, that the work flowed from the life, and not the other way round.
