fields.title: First Fruits
fields.body_html:
“For herein is the saying true, One soweth, and another reapeth.”

— John 4:37, ASV

Akom

Among the first people in Okoyong to become a Christian was a woman who had once been among its fiercest defenders of the old ways. Her name was Akom. She had been betrothed as a baby of one year to a powerful chief and had grown up in his harem. When he died she escaped the poison ordeal herself, and helped to send his wives and slaves into the grave with him. Later she married the elder chief Ekpenyong and ruled his household for twenty years.

After the death of Edem’s son Etim, when Ekpenyong himself fell under suspicion and moved away, a witch-doctor accused Akom and her son of bewitching a sick young chief. He claimed to have seen them in a vision dancing all night and stabbing the sick man with spears. Akom fled with her son to the neighbouring people of Umon, who gave her the protection of their shrine. When Mary came back from Scotland, Ekpenyong begged her to bring his wife home, and she arranged it on condition that Akom swore the most dreaded of the native oaths, which included drinking blood drawn from the wrist.

Akom came to see Mary but would not come through her gate. A twin-mother had once lived in the yard, and anyone who had sworn that oath believed they would die if they touched anything a twin-mother had touched. Mary pretended to be offended: if her house was polluted, Akom had better go home, since she did not receive visitors on the road. After a while Akom came in. Mary gave her an order for mats, which she made beautifully, and Akom began to come regularly and listen.

When twins were brought into the house, Akom mastered her fear and stayed. Then she hurt her foot, and a painful sore developed, and then a skin disease. Everyone, including Akom, believed it was the oath taking its revenge. Her husband ignored her and waited for her to die. Akom wept and despaired, and Mary spoke to her strongly. At last Akom stood up and prayed: “I am a fool; my God, my Father, listen not to my foolishness. Kill me if Thou wilt, but do not leave me.”

The disease was checked by a local remedy. Akom refused to make any sacrifice to the spirits for her recovery. “My Father owns the bush and gives us the knowledge of the medicine,” she said, “and as the Master knows what He has made He knows also how to bless it.” When the man who had accused her of witchcraft came to be friends with her, she said to Mary, “See what God has wrought. The man who demanded my life comes to tell me his affairs! I sometimes wanted to take revenge, but I have got it from God, and His revenge is of a sweeter kind than that of the Consul.”

Akom’s words are worth reading twice. She was an African woman, brought up in the deepest fears of her people, who came to trust a heavenly Father more than the oath she had sworn. She made her own theology of healing: God made the plants and gave the knowledge of medicine, so there was no need to pay the spirits. And she made her own theology of forgiveness, which was better than the Consul’s justice. She was not repeating a missionary’s words. She had found something for herself.

The First Communion

On the fifteenth anniversary of her arrival in Okoyong, in August 1903, the first communion service in the district was held at Akpap. No congregation had ever been formally organised, but the mission sent up the Rev. W. T. Weir from Creek Town to see whether there were people ready to join the Church.

On the Saturday evening, in the hall under the mission house, seven young Christians were baptised in front of the people. Others wanted to come forward, but their families held them back. “Wait and see,” they said, “until we know what the thing is.” Some parents anxiously asked Mary whether baptism was a kind of mbiam, a binding oath that would kill them if they broke it.

On the Sunday a great crowd filled the hall and overflowed into the grounds, sitting on stools and chairs and even on empty gin-boxes. Before the communion Mary presented eleven children for baptism, six of them children she had rescued. Then the first Lord’s Supper in Okoyong was celebrated. Afterwards the people sang the hundred and third psalm, in an Efik version, to the old Scottish tune “Stroudwater.” When they came to the third and fourth verses, Mary seemed lost in thought, with a far-away look and tears in her eyes. In English they run, in the version she knew from childhood:

All thine iniquities who doth most graciously forgive:

Who thy diseases all and pains doth heal, and thee relieve.

Who doth redeem thy life, that thou to death may’st not go down;

Who thee with loving-kindness doth and tender mercies crown.

In the American Standard Version the same words read: “Who forgiveth all thine iniquities; Who healeth all thy diseases; Who redeemeth thy life from destruction; Who crowneth thee with lovingkindness and tender mercies” (Psalm 103:3-4, ASV). She had watched lives taken for fifteen years in Okoyong. Now she was hearing Okoyong people sing about a God who redeems life from destruction.

At the end she spoke to those who had been baptised. “Okoyong now looks to you more than to me for proof of the power of the Gospel.” That evening she talked for a long time about what the district had been like fifteen years before, and she was glad, Livingstone says, that after all the work had not been a failure.

Livingstone calls the day the crown of her service, and adds that “alone, she had done in Okoyong what it had taken a whole Mission to do in Calabar.” That is an admirer’s exaggeration. She had not been alone. She had had Ma Eme, and Edem, and the African boys who kept the services going when she was ill, and the carpenter Ovens, and many others. And the numbers were small: seven young people and eleven children after fifteen years. But they were a beginning, and she knew it.

Planting at Itu

Earlier that year she had begun something new. With no help from the mission, and against the doubts of some of her colleagues, she had decided to plant a base at Itu, a market town on the Cross River at the mouth of the Enyong Creek. Itu had been a slave market for centuries. Now, since the Aro Expedition, it was a government station, and the Creek behind it led into the heart of Aro country. She saw that whoever held Itu could reach the Ibibio, the Igbo, and the Efik.

In January 1903 she canoed to Itu with three of her young people: two boys named Esien and Effiom, and Mana, the girl who had been kidnapped as a child and sold as a slave to Ma Eme. She left them there. Esien was to hold services, Effiom to lead the singing, and Mana to teach the girls. When she went back a few weeks later, the results had exceeded all her dreams. The old chief told her he was too old to change his ways, but the young could learn them, and that God had made him and was therefore bound to look after him whatever he did. But the children were eager, and the services were so crowded that there was no room. She built a school on the hill with her own hands, and the people began building a church, with two rooms at the end for her. A fellow missionary, Dr. Rattray, wrote when he heard, “Bravo! Uganda was evangelised by this means, and the teachers there could only read the gospels.”

By August the congregation at Itu numbered more than three hundred, meeting in a church they had built themselves. And that month, Livingstone says, Jean, Mana, Iye the mother of Susie, Akom, and Esien the teacher at Itu were baptised and sat down at the communion table. Jean’s adopted son Dan was baptised too, and Mary watched with deep joy as her oldest daughter presented him to God. Esien’s mother, who had resisted her son’s faith, sat at the service beside two twin-mothers. (Livingstone tells of these baptisms in a different chapter from the Okoyong communion, and does not say whether they took place on the same occasion.)

A Slave Girl’s Triumph

In October Mary was at Itu, watching the building of a house for herself and the teachers, and was delighted to see the men and women working together, joking and laughing. In Okoyong the sexes were kept strictly apart, she wrote, but here “they were daffin’ and lauchin’ as in Scotland.” When she worried aloud that six rooms was too much to ask of them, they said, “It’s not too much, Ma; nothing can be too much.”

One woman insisted on washing Mary’s feet in hot water, and told her, “Ma, I’ve been so frightened you would take our teacher away because we are so unworthy. I think I could not live again in darkness. I pray all the time. I lay my basket down and just pray on the road.” This woman prayed in the meetings, electrifying everyone, and had begun family prayers in her home, though her husband laughed at her. There were many others like her.

Livingstone tells us who was behind it all. It was Mana, “a black slave-girl,” who had taught and nursed and trained the women of Itu, quietly and modestly, “as a mother might.” The church at Itu owed its first life not to a Scottish missionary but to an African girl who had once been bought and sold. Paul wrote, “There can be neither Jew nor Greek, there can be neither bond nor free, there can be no male and female; for ye all are one man in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28, ASV). At Itu that verse was not an idea. It was a slave girl teaching free women to pray.

Onoyom

On one of her journeys up the Creek, a small canoe shot out from the bushes and bumped into hers. The man in it held out a letter. His master at Akani Obio had sent him to wait for her and bring her to his house. She turned aside, up a quiet creek full of water-lilies, and was received by a well-dressed young couple in a house with a concrete floor and a European bed with mosquito curtains. The man was Onoyom Iya Nya, a chief so trusted by the government that he was the only man in the district who had not been disarmed.

He told her his story. In 1875, as a boy, he had guided a Scottish missionary, Dr. Robb, through his town, and had been punished for it. He grew up in the old religion, went to the feasts at Arochukwu, and when his father died, saw ten little girls killed and buried with him. Later his house burned down and his child died, and he went looking for the sorcerer he believed was responsible, meaning to kill him. On the way he met a former mission teacher, a man who had fallen into drink and was homeless. The man asked him how he knew it was not the white man’s God who was angry with him. “Where can I find this God?” Onoyom asked. “I am not worthy to say,” the old teacher replied, “but go to the white Ma at Itu, and she will tell you.” Onoyom had the fallen teacher read him the Bible while he waited for Mary to pass. Now he asked her, “And now, will you show me what to do?”

It is one of the loveliest stories in her life, and Mary was only its last link. A missionary sowed in 1875 and never knew what came of it. A drunken, homeless man who had lost his way still pointed a chief to God. And a slave girl and two boys had made the name of the white Ma at Itu known up and down the Creek. “For herein is the saying true,” Jesus said, “One soweth, and another reapeth.” Mary Slessor had spent fifteen years sowing in Okoyong with little to show for it. Now, in a place where she had barely begun, she found herself reaping what others had sown.

She went home that night through a storm, singing and praying all the way. But she was tired, and often afraid of what lay ahead, and there were nights when she woke in the dark and cried, “Calm me, O God, and keep me calm.” Then she would go and look at the sleeping children, and say to herself, “Surely I have more reason to trust God than childhood has, after all the way He has led me.”

In Okoyong the sexes were kept strictly apart, she wrote, but here “they were daffin’ and lauchin’ as in Scotland.” When she worried aloud that six rooms was too much to ask of them, they said, “It’s not too much, Ma; nothing can be too much.” One woman insisted on washing Mary’s feet in hot water, and told her, “Ma, I’ve been so frightened you would take our teacher away because we are so unworthy. I think I could not live again in darkness. I pray all the time. I lay my basket down and just pray on the road.” This woman prayed in the meetings, electrifying everyone, and had begun family prayers in her home, though her husband laughed at her. There were many others like her. Livingstone tells us who was behind it all. It was Mana, “a black slave-girl,” who had taught and nursed and trained the women of Itu, quietly and modestly, “as a mother might.” The church at Itu owed its first life not to a Scottish missionary but to an African girl who had once been bought and sold. Paul wrote, “There can be neither Jew nor Greek, there can be neither bond nor free, there can be no male and female; for ye all are one man in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28, ASV). At Itu that verse was not an idea. It was a slave girl teaching free women to pray. Onoyom On one of her journeys up the Creek, a small canoe shot out from the bushes and bumped into hers. The man in it held out a letter. His master at Akani Obio had sent him to wait for her and bring her to his house. She turned aside, up a quiet creek full of water-lilies, and was received by a well-dressed young couple in a house with a concrete floor and a European bed with mosquito curtains. The man was Onoyom Iya Nya, a chief so trusted by the government that he was the only man in the district who had not been disarmed. He told her his story. In 1875, as a boy, he had guided a Scottish missionary, Dr. Robb, through his town, and had been punished for it. He grew up in the old religion, went to the feasts at Arochukwu, and when his father died, saw ten little girls killed and buried with him. Later his house burned down and his child died, and he went looking for the sorcerer he believed was responsible, meaning to kill him. On the way he met a former mission teacher, a man who had fallen into drink and was homeless. The man asked him how he knew it was not the white man’s God who was angry with him. “Where can I find this God?” Onoyom asked. “I am not worthy to say,” the old teacher replied, “but go to the white Ma at Itu, and she will tell you.” Onoyom had the fallen teacher read him the Bible while he waited for Mary to pass. Now he asked her, “And now, will you show me what to do?” It is one of the loveliest stories in her life, and Mary was only its last link. A missionary sowed in 1875 and never knew what came of it. A drunken, homeless man who had lost his way still pointed a chief to God. And a slave girl and two boys had made the name of the white Ma at Itu known up and down the Creek. “For herein is the saying true,” Jesus said, “One soweth, and another reapeth.” Mary Slessor had spent fifteen years sowing in Okoyong with little to show for it. Now, in a place where she had barely begun, she found herself reaping what others had sown. She went home that night through a storm, singing and praying all the way. But she was tired, and often afraid of what lay ahead, and there were nights when she woke in the dark and cried, “Calm me, O God, and keep me calm.” Then she would go and look at the sleeping children, and say to herself, “Surely I have more reason to trust God than childhood has, after all the way He has led me.”

fields.title: “I Dare Not Go Back”
fields.body_html:
“But Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plow, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.”

— Luke 9:62, ASV

A Memorandum

In November 1903 Mary Slessor did something she disliked. She wrote a formal paper for the mission council in Calabar, setting out what she thought the mission ought to do.

She began by saying what many missionaries felt and few said aloud: that the mission’s methods were “very far from adequate” for the size of the field. Churches and schools on the rivers were good, but they reached only the people who lived near them. The villages of the interior were broken up by old enmities and oaths and fears, so that even houses in the same village might keep apart. What was needed, she wrote, was “something more mobile and flexible than ordinary congregational work.” She suggested sending church members out in small bands to travel through the villages for a week at a time, having African teachers spend part of each month in outlying districts, and asking Christian traders to hold services at the trading posts up the river, where Efik traders, she knew, kept Bibles locked in their boxes.

She asked for a minister, with his wife and an African teacher, to take over Okoyong, since she could not build up a church there in the way an ordained man could. She asked for Itu to be made a proper European station. It was, she said, the natural gateway to the whole region. “It was not without reason that it was the slave mart, and that it became the Government base.” She was due for home leave at the start of 1904, after five years in Africa, and she asked instead for six months to travel up and down the Creek with her own canoe and crew. Then she added a sentence that shows her better than any description: “But I am willing to change … any plan of ours in order to let any larger undertaking make way if it should be proposed.”

The council would not take the responsibility. It passed her paper to the women’s committee in Scotland and asked her to wait. It did agree unanimously that Itu should become a medical station.

A Mere Wreck

Then her body gave way. She collapsed, and was, Livingstone says, “again far down in the dark valley.” When she recovered, she wrote, “I rose a mere wreck of what I was, and that was not much at the best. My hair is silvered enough to please any one now, and I am nervous and easily knocked up, and so rheumatic that I cannot get up or down without pain.” The council thought she should go home. Instead it gave her permission to make her tour of the Creek, on one condition: she must not commit the mission to any new work.

She accepted the condition and set off. “It seems strange,” she said, “to be starting with a family on a gipsy life in a canoe, but God will take care of us. Whether I shall find His place for me up-river or whether I shall come back to my own people again, I do not know. He knows, and that is enough.” It is the faith of Abraham, of whom the letter to the Hebrews says that “he went out, not knowing whither he went” (Hebrews 11:8, ASV).

She went at her own expense. Her salary was now a hundred pounds a year, and she spent almost nothing of it on herself. “I have no object on earth,” she wrote, “but to get my food and raiment, which are of the plainest, and to bring up my bairns.” The building was done by herself, her household, and the free labour of the people. The girls and boys who worked with her were paid nothing but their keep. Livingstone says that all the opening of the Enyong Creek to the gospel cost the mission was her salary.

Before she left she went to Duke Town to hand over the business of the Okoyong court. The Commissioner sent her an invitation to dinner, the kind of invitation that was really a command. She declined it, saying that she was not visiting. Livingstone suspects she had nothing fit to wear. The Commissioner came to see her instead.

Itu

She reached Itu in July 1904 with her family, still weak. A government doctor who visited her there found her in an unfinished native hut with almost no furniture, sitting in a chair rocking a tiny baby, while five other babies slept around the room wrapped in pieces of brown paper and old newspapers. The congregation her young teachers had gathered now numbered three hundred and fifty. “To-day,” she wrote, “as the custom is after the lesson, the bairns each took a part in prayer, and before we rose a boy started ‘Come, Holy Spirit, come.’ We sang it through on our knees.”

Calls came every day. A deputation from the Ibibio country begged, “Give us even a boy!” A chief on the Creek sent word, “It is not book that I want; it is God!” Onoyom came from Akani Obio to say that his people had three pounds saved to pay a teacher. And late one night fifteen young men from Okoyong arrived by torchlight to tell her that the women missionaries sent to Akpap had already left, and they had no Ma. She sent them to shelter for the night and spent the rest of it in prayer. “Oh Britain,” she wrote, “surfeited with privilege! tired of Sabbath and Church, would that you could send over to us what you are throwing away!”

Cement

In November 1904 she went to the mission council for the first time in six years, and reported what had been done. At Itu there was a church, a teacher’s house, a day school, and a class of forty people preparing for baptism. At Arochukwu there was a school on land given by the chiefs. There were small congregations beginning in four more places along the Creek. The council gave her permission to continue for another six months, on the same condition as before: no expense to the mission.

She laid the cement floors of her houses herself. Once, when colleagues met her at a landing-place and remarked on how many trunks she was travelling with, she explained that they were full of cement; she had nothing else to carry it in. A lady in Scotland later asked her whether she had ever had lessons in using cement. “No,” she said. “I just stir it like porridge, turn it out, smooth it with a stick, and all the time keep praying, ‘Lord, here’s the cement, if to Thy glory, set it,’ and it has never once gone wrong.”

It is a funny story, and it tells us something about how she prayed. Her prayers were not separate from her work. They were said over the cement bucket.

God Is Stronger Than Juju

Meanwhile Chief Onoyom was building a church at Akani Obio with eight hundred pounds of his own savings. At first he planned a building of mud and thatch, but then he reflected that if he were building a house for himself it would have iron walls, and he could not do less for God. So he built it with iron walls, a cement floor, and a bell-tower. For the seats and pulpit he chose a huge tree that the town regarded as its chief shrine. The story was told that the people said the spirit would never let it be cut down. “God is stronger than juju,” said Onoyom, and went out with his men to fell it. They failed the first day, and the town rejoiced. The next morning they knelt and prayed that God would show himself stronger than the spirit, and then went back to work and brought the tree down. At the dedication, Onoyom provided food for everyone but allowed nothing stronger than palm wine. Then he came shyly up to Mary and pressed a handful of money into her hand, asking her to buy food for herself, because he did not know what kind she liked.

Later Onoyom sent away his other wives, providing for them, and took back as his only wife a woman he had once rejected because she had borne twins. Some time afterwards, the chief, his wife and their baby, a score of his people, and sixteen young men and women were baptised at Akani Obio. Mary was ill and had to be carried to the service, and she hid her face on the communion table. “Over forty sat down in the afternoon to remember our Lord’s death ‘till He come,’” she wrote. “It cannot go back this work of His. Akani Obio is now linked on to Calvary.” And then, thinking of her mother, who had first told her about Calabar: “I am sure our Lord will never keep it from my mother.”

“I Dare Not Go Back”

The mission’s rules said that she was to go back to Akpap in April 1906. When she was reminded of it, Livingstone says, she was “inclined to be mutinous.”

“There is an impelling power behind me, and I dare not look backward,” she said. “Even if it cost me my connection with the Church of my heart’s love, I feel I must go forward.” And again: “I am not enthusiastic over Church methods. I would not mind cutting the rope and going adrift with my bairns, and I can earn our bite and something more.” She thought seriously of taking a government post, or of opening a shop with her girls, so that she could support herself and stay where she was.

She wrote to the secretary of the women’s committee in Scotland. The government was building roads into the country around her faster than anyone had imagined, she said, and God had led her step by step to exactly the right place. “And the minutes says ‘I am to return to Akpap in April!’” Okoyong was very dear to her, she wrote, “but to leave these hordes of untamed, unwashed, unlovely savages and withdraw the little sunlight that has begun to flicker out over its darkness! I dare not think of it. Whether the Church permits it or not, I feel I must stay here and even go on farther as the roads are made.” She could no longer walk far, she admitted, but if the roads were good she could have four wheels made and a box put on them, and the children could pull her about. “With such facts pressing on me at every point you will understand my saying I dare not go back.” At the end she added, “This is not for publication; it is for digestion.”

The phrase about “untamed, unwashed, unlovely savages” is painful to read, and it is her own. It was the language of her time, and she used it even about the people she was risking everything to serve. But it is worth noticing why she used it. She was not arguing that the people were unworthy. She was arguing that they were in greater need than the people of Okoyong, and that she could not abandon them.

Set Free

Livingstone, who worked for the Church, is at pains to defend the committees. They were stewards of limited money, he says, and had to be sure of every step, while she, “all afire with energy and enthusiasm, would have gone on in faith.” Both sides had a point. A mission cannot be run on one woman’s impulses, and the committees were right to worry about who would pay for the new work when she was gone. But the Church had also left her alone in Okoyong for years, and she was right that the chance in the Creek would not wait for committees.

In the end the Church gave way. It decided to free her from the ordinary rules and let her work as a pioneer missionary, going where she thought right. Livingstone calls it a remarkable position, and so it was. The committee in Scotland passed a resolution recognising that it was the Church’s duty to occupy the region, regretting that its funds were too stretched to send new staff at once, and thanking Miss Slessor for her generosity and her brave pioneer work. A minister, the Rev. John Rankin, was sent to survey the country, and came back full of enthusiasm. Within three miles of Arochukwu, he reported, there were nineteen large towns. Some of the chiefs were persecuting the young Christians, and when the teachers asked the converts what they had said to the chiefs’ threats, they answered, “You can put us out of our country, but you cannot put us away from God.” The women said they would die for Jesus Christ. The head chief of the Aro, who had once controlled the oracle itself, offered to build a house for any missionary who would come. Rankin was appointed to Arochukwu, and it became a regular station of the mission. The work Mary had begun alone had been taken up by the Church.

No Looking Back

The verse at the head of this chapter is one of the hardest sayings of Jesus. A man offered to follow him, but first wanted to go home and say goodbye to his family. Jesus answered that no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God. A ploughman who looks over his shoulder cuts a crooked furrow.

Mary Slessor was often tempted to look back. She loved Okoyong more than anywhere on earth. She loved her Church and was afraid of losing it. She was ill and tired and nearly sixty. But she had heard, as she believed, a voice behind her saying, as Isaiah put it, “This is the way, walk ye in it” (Isaiah 30:21, ASV), and she would not turn round. It made her difficult to manage. It made her, at times, “mutinous.” It also opened the Enyong Creek to the gospel.

fields.title: On the Bench
fields.body_html:
“learn to do well; seek justice, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.”

— Isaiah 1:17, ASV

“A Voluntary”

By 1905 the British government of Southern Nigeria was setting up a system of native courts across the country. Each court was made up of local chiefs who sat in turn, with the District Commissioner as its president and a permanent vice-president to keep it running. Before Mary left Itu she was asked, informally, whether she would take charge of the court business of her district, as she had done in Okoyong, but this time on an official footing. If she agreed, the court would be moved to Ikot Obong, near where she was living, to spare her strength.

She was pleased, and she agreed. She was already, in practice, the person everyone went to with their disputes. An official position, she thought, would give her more power to protect the poor and the oppressed, and above all women. “It will be a good chance,” she said, “to preach the Gospel, and to create confidence and inspire hope in these poor wretches, who fear white and black man alike; while it will neither hamper my work nor restrict my liberty.”

When she was told that a salary went with the post, she refused it. “I’m born and bred,” she said, “and am in every fibre of my being, a voluntary.” She meant something quite specific. The United Presbyterian Church had been founded on the principle known as Voluntaryism: that the Church should be supported by the free gifts of its members, never by the state. She was not going to take the government’s money for doing what she thought of as Christian service.

The formal offer came in May 1905. The High Commissioner invited her to become a member of the Itu Native Court with the status of permanent vice-president. He proposed to pay her a nominal salary of one pound a year and to give her the rest, forty-seven pounds a year, for her mission work. She thanked him, accepted the post, and declined the money. In October she took over the court’s books, and for years she did much of the clerk’s work herself.

It is often said that she was the first woman magistrate in the British Empire. That may be true, but it has never been properly established, and it is safest to say that she was one of the first women anywhere in the Empire to exercise a magistrate’s powers.

“God Help These Poor Helpless Women!”

The cases that came before her were grim. One of the first was a murder charge in which a woman was involved, and many of the rest concerned marriage, and with it poisoning, sacrifice, debts, oaths, and cruelty. She was often sick with disgust. “God help these poor helpless women!” she wrote one evening. “What a crowd of people I have had to-day, and how debased! They are just like brutes in regard to women. I have had a murder, an eséré case, a suicide, a man for branding his slave-wife all over her face and body; a man with a gun who has shot four persons. It is all horrible!”

Some of her sentences survive in her own handwriting. A man found guilty of brawling in the market and snatching eight brass rods from a woman’s basket: one month’s hard labour. A man who chased a girl into the bush intending to harm her: one month’s hard labour. A man who seized a woman in the market, kept her chained for fourteen days by the neck and wrists, and put a curse on her to kill her if she told the white people: six months’ hard labour, which was the most the court could give.

She used her position above all for women. She fined a whole town three pounds for failing to provide water for twin-mothers. She granted a woman a divorce on the spot from a husband she had good reason to leave, and made her fellow missionary witness it. The government’s report for 1907 recorded that the District Commissioner had summoned a number of husbands who had deserted their wives for bearing twins, and that every one of them had agreed to take his wife back, and that other men in the same position had then done the same without being summoned. It called this “a sign of the civilising influence worked through the Court by that admirable lady, Miss Slessor.”

Her Kind of Justice

She was not a conventional judge. Three chiefs sat beside her on the bench and a jury sat behind, but she ruled the court. An official saw her stand up and box the ears of a chief who had gone on interrupting after being warned, to the great amusement of the other chiefs. She would try a group of men, lecture them, and fine them, and when they had no money she would take them up to her house and set them to work to earn it, feeding them well and talking to them while they worked. Livingstone says that often, instead of administering the law, “she administered justice by giving the prisoner a blow on the side of the head!” He meant it as praise.

People trusted her court because she heard their stories in their own language, without an interpreter. One District Commissioner spent three days on a single case and got nowhere, and she settled it to everyone’s satisfaction with two questions. Once, standing by while a government doctor questioned a chief through an interpreter, she suddenly broke in, and the chief crumpled in front of her. He had told a lie. “To think,” she said afterwards, “he could have expected to deceive me!”

The court also used the oath of the old religion. A witness would promise to tell the truth while a member of the court drew a foul mixture from a bottle across his tongue and face, and touched his arms and legs with it, in the presence of a skull. It was believed that anyone who lied under this oath would die. Soon after Mary joined the court, a witness who had plainly lied collapsed and died on his way out of the building, and the oath was held in great respect for some time afterwards.

This is uncomfortable material for a Christian biography, and it should not be hidden. A missionary who had refused to pray at a blood covenant presided over a court that swore witnesses on an oath believed to kill, and a man appears to have died of his fear of it. Her court combined a fierce care for the weak with procedures no modern court would allow: summary blows, fines worked off as labour at the judge’s house, and verdicts that depended on her knowing, or thinking she knew, who was lying. It was, as she knew, justice by a strong personality, and it was only as good as she was.

When two ministers from Scotland visited her court at the end of her time there, they watched her hear a case in which a man, drunk on trade gin, had attacked his wife with a machete because she had stumbled against him. Mary wanted a severe sentence. The jury did not. The headman laid down the principle that men had a perfect right to do whatever they liked with their wives, or wives would become unmanageable. Out of deference to what he called the white woman’s peculiar views, the jury agreed to send the man to prison for a short term. It was a reminder of how far she had to push against the settled convictions of the men she sat with. She told the visiting minister that she did not care for the work at all. “The moral atmosphere of a native court is so bad,” she said, “that I would never go near one were it not that I want the people to get justice.”

As her health failed, she began to sit in her room reading or writing while the girls of her household questioned the people who came to her, reported the facts, and carried her answers back. Sometimes she simply called her ruling out of the window. People sent her letters addressed, to be on the safe side, to “Madam, Mr., Miss, Slessor.” In November 1909, or possibly a year later, worn out, she resigned. The Commissioner of the Eastern Province wrote to thank her for her services to the country. Livingstone says she was glad to be free of it.

“Failed, Failed”

One episode from these years has been quoted in almost every popular life of Mary Slessor, and it needs to be handled with care.

In 1908, while she was at Duke Town, the High Commissioner invited her to dinner at Government House to meet a visiting woman writer. She did not want to go. She had nothing to wear and did not want to be put on show. The Macgregors, with whom she was staying, persuaded her. As she set off in the hammock the government sent for her, Mr. Macgregor noticed “the light of battle in her eyes,” and laughed, because he knew she loved a prank. She came back with her face full of mischief. “Ay,” she said, “I met your lady writer, and I made her greet four times and she gied me half a sovereign for my bairns!” To “greet,” in Scots, is to weep.

The writer published an account of the meeting in the London Morning Post under the title “But yet the pity of it.” She described a woman close on sixty in a skimpy tweed skirt and a broken green picture-hat with a knot of red ribbon, holding out hands scraped raw from work and saying, “Ye’ll excuse my hands.” She reported Mary telling, in broad Scots, how she had put the death-oath on a man accused of stealing plantains, and how he had died on his way to Calabar: “I put mbiam on him, an’ he knew he had stolen them and died.” And she ended with Mary looking out into the sunshine and saying of her whole life’s work, “My time’s been wasted. The puir bairns. They’d be better dead. Failed, failed.”

Livingstone says flatly that the article “excited laughter and derision in the Calabar bush,” and that Mary had been deliberately “mystifying” a writer she did not take to, spinning her a tale of gloom and getting half a sovereign out of it for the children. That is quite possible. Her own report of the evening sounds like a woman pleased with a joke. But it is also possible that Livingstone, who wanted to protect her reputation, explained away something real. She did have dark moods, as we have seen and will see again. She was exhausted and ill that year. She was quite capable of saying “Failed, failed” in a black moment and laughing about it afterwards. We cannot know. What we can say is that the most famous despairing quotation attributed to her comes from a stranger’s newspaper article that her friends thought was a leg-pull, and it should not be quoted as her settled judgement on her life.

Seeking Justice

The verse at the head of this chapter was addressed by Isaiah to the rulers of Jerusalem, who were very religious and very unjust. God told them he was sick of their sacrifices. What he wanted was that they should “seek justice, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.” The law of Moses put it more starkly still: “That which is altogether just shalt thou follow, that thou mayest live” (Deuteronomy 16:20, ASV).

Mary Slessor’s court was not altogether just, and she knew it. But she sat in it, unpaid, for four years, because she believed that without her the women who came before it would get no justice at all. Twin-mothers were taken back into their homes. Women who had been chained and branded saw the men who did it sent to prison. A woman who wanted to leave a brutal husband was set free. It was an imperfect instrument in imperfect hands, used for the people Isaiah named: the oppressed, the fatherless, and the widow.

fields.title: Children of the Desolate
fields.body_html:
“Sing, O barren, thou that didst not bear; break forth into singing, and cry aloud, thou that didst not travail with child: for more are the children of the desolate than the children of the married wife, saith Jehovah.”

— Isaiah 54:1, ASV

An Old Woman Who Lived in a Shoe

Mary Slessor never had a child of her own. She had, in the end, a household larger than most mothers ever know. She would stand in the middle of it sometimes, pretending to be at her wits’ end, and recite the nursery rhyme about the old woman who lived in a shoe and had so many children she didn’t know what to do. “I have only three girls at present,” she once wrote, “and I have nine babies, and what with the washing and the school and the palavers and the visitors, you may be sure there are no drones in this house.”

She was candid about her failings as a housekeeper. “I have not an elaborate system or method of work,” she wrote. “It is just everything as it comes. I am afraid my mind is not a trained machine. It only works as it chooses.” The mission frowned on missionaries adopting children, and her household was a constant strain on her money and her strength. She did it anyway. On Sundays there was tea at a big table in the hall, where Jean, Mana, Annie, Mary, Alice, and Maggie sat round her, with small boys and girls on the floor, and the boxes of treats from Scotland were opened.

Most of the babies who came to her died, or were returned to their families. But a core of children grew up in her house and were hers for life. The historian Jeanette Hardage counts nine. We know something about most of them, though less than we would like, and they deserve more than a list.

Jean

Jean, first called Janie, was the twin girl Mary had carried out of Old Town in 1883, whose brother had been killed. She was baptised in Dundee and grew up in Mary’s house. Her Efik name was Atim Eso. Her marriage in 1899 failed, and she came home. She adopted the motherless baby Dan and raised him as her own. As the years went on she became Mary’s right hand. She ran the household, cared for the babies and their mothers, taught in the school, and ran into the bush to rescue twins when Mary was too weak to go. In the Ikpe years she worked as a teacher and evangelist at a place called Nkanga, where she gathered some two hundred men and women to hear her preach, and Mary thought her the best Efik teacher she knew. Like Mary at her loom, she read with a book propped open wherever she worked.

For most of those years Jean worked for her board alone. Around 1907, Livingstone says, Mary “felt it was time to acknowledge her services,” and began to pay her a shilling a week. It is a small detail, but an honest biography should notice it. Mary Slessor gave everything she had to her work, and she expected her household to do the same, and Jean did, for almost nothing.

Mary loved her deeply. In 1907 a story about Jean, spread by someone in the district, reached Mary in Scotland, and she cut short her last furlough to rush back. Livingstone does not say what the story was. When she got home she found it was untrue, and she was “too grateful to be angry.” In 1909 doctors advised an operation for an internal illness Jean had suffered in silence for years. Mary was against it, and sent her to Duke Town for treatment instead. We do not know whether she was right. “Jean has as many faults as myself,” she wrote in 1913, “but she is a darling … and a treasure.” Jean nursed her through her last illness, went with her on her only holiday, and was at her deathbed. She died herself at Use in the influenza epidemic of 1918, aged about thirty-six.

Annie, Mary, Alice, Maggie

Annie came to Mary as a baby in the Okoyong years. Livingstone calls her “the drawer of water and hewer of wood, kind willing worker.” She married, and she and her husband joined the church together, and later led the services at Use while Mary was at Ikpe, and then worked at Nkanga. Their little boy died at the age of two, and was the first person to be given a Christian burial in the part of the Ibibio country where Mary was then working. A little girl followed, who used to run about the church at Use calling to “Ma.”

Mary, the “child of wonder” who had lain for five days by the market road, grew into what one visitor called “the smart, handsome favourite.” She had suitors in Okoyong and in the Ibibio country and turned them all down. “Why can’t I stay at home with you?” she asked. Then the government’s new motor car came to Use, and with it a young African driver named David, an educated Anglican from Lagos. He won her. They were married first before the District Commissioner, and Mary insisted that her daughter stay at home until they had been married in church as well. At the wedding breakfast the guest of honour was an old Muslim in white robes, a friend of David’s family, who had once taken Mary’s hand, kissed it, and told her that only God could make her such a mother to everybody. Livingstone notes that few tributes from white men had touched her more, “though she was half-afraid her feeling was scarcely orthodox.” David asked her to pray for them before they left, and she did. A baby followed.

Alice, another rescued twin, was steady and dependable, and later came to faith and said so. Maggie, whom one visitor called “fusionless,” meaning scatter-brained, was the youngest of the four girls Mary took to Scotland in 1898. When Alice and Maggie were older, Mary worried that, having no family and no betrothal, they had no one to protect them from insult, and she sent them to board at a mission girls’ school in Calabar. Their later lives are not well recorded. There are hints in the modern biographies that at least one of the younger girls had a hard life after Mary’s death, without her protection.

Dan, Whitie, Asuquo

Dan, Jean’s adopted son, whose full name was Daniel MacArthur Slessor, went with Mary to Scotland in 1907 at the age of about six, and became almost as well known there as Jean. When he fell in love with the government motor car and its driver, Mary sent him off to the Hope Waddell Institute at Duke Town, “in terror for the safety of his body and his morals.” He was the best educated of her children. He was with her in her last year, helping in the school and interpreting. He lived until about 1970, and in 1958 he wrote down his reminiscences of her, which are kept in Dundee and were used by later biographers.

Whitie, whose full name was Madge White Slessor, was the last twin Mary saved. She trained as a nurse. Asuquo, one of the last babies to join the household, went to the Hope Waddell Institute with Dan, and is said to have run away from school to go to sea. Of both their later lives little is known.

When Mary died, the girls wept in the night, and among the things they cried out was this: “We shall be counted as slaves now that our mother is dead.” It is a terrible sentence. Mary had given them love, a home, education, and a name. What she had not been able to give them was a secure place in the society around them, because by the customs of the country a child without a family had no protection. They knew it.

The Problem of the Women

That problem, the place of women without a family, was one Mary had thought about for years. In the Ibibio country, Livingstone says, a woman had no place outside the harem. A girl who was not betrothed to someone had no protection in law, and could be insulted or injured with impunity. Women who became Christians, or who were driven out as twin-mothers, had nowhere to go.

Mary concluded that the root of the problem was economic. Until women could support themselves without depending on men, they would never be free. Some of the more thoughtful women told her frankly that they saw no future for themselves except the harem. So she began to plan a settlement: a home in the countryside where her own girls, twin-mothers, abandoned children, and Christian women with nowhere else to go could live and support themselves by farming and simple industries, such as laundry, baking, basket-making, weaving, and shoemaking. It had to be based on the land, and it had to pay for itself. She did not believe in homes that were kept alive by money from outside.

As a European she could not buy land. So she arranged, with the government’s help, to acquire it in the names of Jean and the other girls, and to give the mission a permanent interest in it. In 1908 she fixed the site at Use, near Ikot Obong, where she was living. The government sent fruit trees: mangoes, guavas, pawpaws, avocados, and pineapples. She began to think about rubber and cocoa. She bought a cow, to save its owner from prison for debt, and it became famous in the mission as “Ma Slessor’s coo” for running away with the whole household, and once with two senior missionaries, hanging on to its rope. She did not want the settlement named after herself, and suggested it be named after Mrs. Anderson or Mrs. Goldie, the missionary wives of her early years.

The settlement never became the institution her friends hoped for. She did not want a large institution, and other places kept calling her away. After her death the Church raised money for a memorial home for women and girls in her name. But the idea behind it was far ahead of its time. She saw that the gospel had to give women not only a new heart but a way to live, and she saw that the way to live was work and land of their own.

The Last Visit Home

In 1906 she became so ill that a government doctor told her to go home or die. She did not go until 1907, when she could no longer walk more than a few steps. She took Dan with her. “Oh, the dear homeland,” she wrote. “How I long for a wee look at a winter landscape, to feel the cold wind, and see the frost in the cart-ruts … to take a back seat in a church.”

She was in Scotland from May to October. Her friends were shocked to see “an old wrinkled lady huddled in a corner of a carriage.” She visited her old haunts in Dundee with a friend from the factory, and met three women with whom she had begun mission work there nearly forty years before. On the night before she left, friends found her weeping in bed. She had been overcome, she said, by the feeling that she was homeless in her own country. “I’m a poor solitary with only memories.” When they told her she had troops of friends who loved her, she said, “Yes, I ken, and I am grateful, but it’s just that I’ve none of my ain folk to say good-bye to.” She never went back to Scotland again.

More Are the Children of the Desolate

The verse at the head of this chapter was written to Jerusalem in exile, a city that had lost its people and seemed to have no future. God told her to sing, because the children of the desolate would outnumber the children of the married. The psalmist says the same of God: “He maketh the barren woman to keep house, And to be a joyful mother of children” (Psalm 113:9, ASV). And again: “God setteth the solitary in families” (Psalm 68:6, ASV).

Mary Slessor was a solitary woman who had lost her own family and never married. She was also the mother of a large household, and the “Ma” of a whole region. The children of the desolate were more than she could count. They were not an easy family. Some died, some struggled, and some were left exposed when she was gone. But they were a family, and she loved them fiercely, and they loved her. James wrote that “pure religion and undefiled before our God and Father is this, to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27, ASV). She did not only visit them. She took them home.

We do not know whether she was right. “Jean has as many faults as myself,” she wrote in 1913, “but she is a darling … and a treasure.” Jean nursed her through her last illness, went with her on her only holiday, and was at her deathbed. She died herself at Use in the influenza epidemic of 1918, aged about thirty-six. Annie, Mary, Alice, Maggie Annie came to Mary as a baby in the Okoyong years. Livingstone calls her “the drawer of water and hewer of wood, kind willing worker.” She married, and she and her husband joined the church together, and later led the services at Use while Mary was at Ikpe, and then worked at Nkanga. Their little boy died at the age of two, and was the first person to be given a Christian burial in the part of the Ibibio country where Mary was then working. A little girl followed, who used to run about the church at Use calling to “Ma.” Mary, the “child of wonder” who had lain for five days by the market road, grew into what one visitor called “the smart, handsome favourite.” She had suitors in Okoyong and in the Ibibio country and turned them all down. “Why can’t I stay at home with you?” she asked. Then the government’s new motor car came to Use, and with it a young African driver named David, an educated Anglican from Lagos. He won her. They were married first before the District Commissioner, and Mary insisted that her daughter stay at home until they had been married in church as well. At the wedding breakfast the guest of honour was an old Muslim in white robes, a friend of David’s family, who had once taken Mary’s hand, kissed it, and told her that only God could make her such a mother to everybody. Livingstone notes that few tributes from white men had touched her more, “though she was half-afraid her feeling was scarcely orthodox.” David asked her to pray for them before they left, and she did. A baby followed. Alice, another rescued twin, was steady and dependable, and later came to faith and said so. Maggie, whom one visitor called “fusionless,” meaning scatter-brained, was the youngest of the four girls Mary took to Scotland in 1898. When Alice and Maggie were older, Mary worried that, having no family and no betrothal, they had no one to protect them from insult, and she sent them to board at a mission girls’ school in Calabar. Their later lives are not well recorded. There are hints in the modern biographies that at least one of the younger girls had a hard life after Mary’s death, without her protection. Dan, Whitie, Asuquo Dan, Jean’s adopted son, whose full name was Daniel MacArthur Slessor, went with Mary to Scotland in 1907 at the age of about six, and became almost as well known there as Jean. When he fell in love with the government motor car and its driver, Mary sent him off to the Hope Waddell Institute at Duke Town, “in terror for the safety of his body and his morals.” He was the best educated of her children. He was with her in her last year, helping in the school and interpreting. He lived until about 1970, and in 1958 he wrote down his reminiscences of her, which are kept in Dundee and were used by later biographers. Whitie, whose full name was Madge White Slessor, was the last twin Mary saved. She trained as a nurse. Asuquo, one of the last babies to join the household, went to the Hope Waddell Institute with Dan, and is said to have run away from school to go to sea. Of both their later lives little is known. When Mary died, the girls wept in the night, and among the things they cried out was this: “We shall be counted as slaves now that our mother is dead.” It is a terrible sentence. Mary had given them love, a home, education, and a name. What she had not been able to give them was a secure place in the society around them, because by the customs of the country a child without a family had no protection. They knew it. The Problem of the Women That problem, the place of women without a family, was one Mary had thought about for years. In the Ibibio country, Livingstone says, a woman had no place outside the harem. A girl who was not betrothed to someone had no protection in law, and could be insulted or injured with impunity. Women who became Christians, or who were driven out as twin-mothers, had nowhere to go. Mary concluded that the root of the problem was economic. Until women could support themselves without depending on men, they would never be free. Some of the more thoughtful women told her frankly that they saw no future for themselves except the harem. So she began to plan a settlement: a home in the countryside where her own girls, twin-mothers, abandoned children, and Christian women with nowhere else to go could live and support themselves by farming and simple industries, such as laundry, baking, basket-making, weaving, and shoemaking. It had to be based on the land, and it had to pay for itself. She did not believe in homes that were kept alive by money from outside. As a European she could not buy land. So she arranged, with the government’s help, to acquire it in the names of Jean and the other girls, and to give the mission a permanent interest in it. In 1908 she fixed the site at Use, near Ikot Obong, where she was living. The government sent fruit trees: mangoes, guavas, pawpaws, avocados, and pineapples. She began to think about rubber and cocoa. She bought a cow, to save its owner from prison for debt, and it became famous in the mission as “Ma Slessor’s coo” for running away with the whole household, and once with two senior missionaries, hanging on to its rope. She did not want the settlement named after herself, and suggested it be named after Mrs. Anderson or Mrs. Goldie, the missionary wives of her early years. The settlement never became the institution her friends hoped for. She did not want a large institution, and other places kept calling her away. After her death the Church raised money for a memorial home for women and girls in her name. But the idea behind it was far ahead of its time. She saw that the gospel had to give women not only a new heart but a way to live, and she saw that the way to live was work and land of their own. The Last Visit Home In 1906 she became so ill that a government doctor told her to go home or die. She did not go until 1907, when she could no longer walk more than a few steps. She took Dan with her. “Oh, the dear homeland,” she wrote. “How I long for a wee look at a winter landscape, to feel the cold wind, and see the frost in the cart-ruts … to take a back seat in a church.” She was in Scotland from May to October. Her friends were shocked to see “an old wrinkled lady huddled in a corner of a carriage.” She visited her old haunts in Dundee with a friend from the factory, and met three women with whom she had begun mission work there nearly forty years before. On the night before she left, friends found her weeping in bed. She had been overcome, she said, by the feeling that she was homeless in her own country. “I’m a poor solitary with only memories.” When they told her she had troops of friends who loved her, she said, “Yes, I ken, and I am grateful, but it’s just that I’ve none of my ain folk to say good-bye to.” She never went back to Scotland again. More Are the Children of the Desolate The verse at the head of this chapter was written to Jerusalem in exile, a city that had lost its people and seemed to have no future. God told her to sing, because the children of the desolate would outnumber the children of the married. The psalmist says the same of God: “He maketh the barren woman to keep house, And to be a joyful mother of children” (Psalm 113:9, ASV). And again: “God setteth the solitary in families” (Psalm 68:6, ASV). Mary Slessor was a solitary woman who had lost her own family and never married. She was also the mother of a large household, and the “Ma” of a whole region. The children of the desolate were more than she could count. They were not an easy family. Some died, some struggled, and some were left exposed when she was gone. But they were a family, and she loved them fiercely, and they loved her. James wrote that “pure religion and undefiled before our God and Father is this, to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27, ASV). She did not only visit them. She took them home.

fields.title: Ikpe
fields.body_html:
“And he hath said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my power is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.”

— 2 Corinthians 12:9, ASV

A Call From the North

The call to her last field came, of all ways, out of a war. During one of the smaller military expeditions that followed the Aro campaign, government troops were attacked by the people of a district at the upper end of the Enyong Creek, who fled, Livingstone says, “at the first experience of disciplined firing.” A young man who had been used by the soldiers as a guide persuaded some of them to go and ask advice of the great white Ma at Use. They came, and talked with her long and earnestly. Later more came, saying they wanted to be “God-men.”

Their home was Ikpe, two days up the Creek by canoe, an old slave-trading town that had been allied with the Aro and had long closed its market to outsiders. When Mary first visited, the older chiefs were sullen. She understood why. “Poor old heathen souls,” she wrote, “they have good reason to be, with all they have to hope from tumbling down about their ears.” But young men were already building a church, with two rooms for her at the back, though none of them could read and their only teacher knew barely more than the alphabet.

She knew she was too old and too ill to start again. She was over sixty. She could not walk far, and was carried to church. But the thought of people worshipping a God they barely knew, with no one to teach them, broke her down. “Why cannot the Church send two ladies there?” she asked. “If the wherewithal should fail at the end of two years, let them take my salary. I shall only be too glad to live on native food with my bairns.” No ladies were sent. So she went herself. “I must go,” she said. “I am in honour bound to go.”

In a short time she was back at Ikpe with fifty sheets of corrugated iron. “I am committed now,” she wrote. “No more idleness for me. I am entering in the dark as to how and where and when. How I am to manage I do not know, but my mind is at perfect peace about it, and I am not afraid. God will carry it through. The Pillar leads.” The pillar was the pillar of cloud that went before Israel in the wilderness. She had used the image for years: she would not move until God moved.

Real Life

She lived in two rooms behind the church, with a camp-bed and a few dishes, and at times had as many as two hundred and fifty people clearing bush for her. Livingstone says the people of Ikpe were hostile to white people as a whole, and wanted neither them nor their religion. But there was nothing warlike about the frail old woman in the camp-bed, and “her very helplessness protected her.”

Her courage had not left her. One Sunday, during the service, a fight broke out in the market with sticks and swords. She went out, seized one man’s wrist, and stopped it. When government agents came with a police escort to vaccinate the people against smallpox, the crowd took the vaccine for the white man’s witchcraft, guns appeared, and there was about to be bloodshed. The people were asked to trust Ma. They said they would be vaccinated if she did it herself, so she sent for vaccine and spent days doing it, joking and coaxing when she was near fainting. “This poor frail woman is the broken reed on which they lean,” she wrote of herself. “Isn’t it strange?”

She described her life at Ikpe in one of her best letters:

It is a real life I am living now, not all preaching and holding meetings, but rather a life and an atmosphere which the people can touch and live in and be made willing to believe in when the higher truths are brought before them. In many things it is a most prosaic life, dirt and dust and noise and silliness and sin in every form, but full, too, of the kindliness and homeliness and dependence of children who are not averse to be disciplined and taught, and who understand and love just as we do.

The journeys between Use and Ikpe were brutal. She was once asked how she could stand them in her state. “Oh,” she said, “I just had to take as big a dose of laudanum as I dared, and wrap myself up in a blanket, and lie in the bottom of the canoe all the time, and managed fine.” Laudanum was opium dissolved in alcohol, the ordinary painkiller of the time, and she used it, as she used sleeping draughts, to get through pain and sleeplessness. It is one of the details Livingstone kept that the legend leaves out.

Once she reached the landing-beach at half past five on Christmas morning after a night in the canoe, carrying, as Livingstone puts it, “the usual motherless baby.” A message was waiting for her: “Ekereki said I was to tell you that his mother is asleep.” It meant that the woman had died. Mary was struck that the Christian way of speaking of death as sleep had already entered the language of a people who had once thought every death the work of a witch. Annie’s little son had been the first Christian buried there. Now this woman was laid beside him, the first adult to receive a Christian burial in that part of the Ibibio country. That New Year’s Eve she was down with fever, and at midnight an army of driver ants poured into the house from every side and dropped from the roof. “My ‘first-feet’ were driver ants,” she wrote, using the Scottish word for the first visitor of the New Year.

The Autocratic Doctor

In 1911 a young doctor named Hitchcock came to the mission hospital at Itu, and began riding over every other day to examine her. He suspected she was not eating enough. Her diary shows that he was right. On 14 June she wrote: “Market Morning. Have only 3d. in cash in the house; sent it with 2 Ikpats (the first Efik schoolbook) and New Testament to buy food, and sold all 3 books for 6d.” There was money for her in Duke Town, but she seldom had cash in hand, and she would not ask.

The doctor forbade her to go to Ikpe, to cycle, or to take services. She laughed, went to church, and held two services, and nearly collapsed. He sent her to bed and sent over a chicken with instructions for cooking it. “I’m not a meat eater, doctor,” she said. When he suggested she go to Duke Town for a rest, she said, “I cannot draw a salary and not do what I can.” A friend told her she had done enough in the past to have no qualms. “I’ve been paid for all I’ve done,” she said. Late in the year she escaped, in her words, from “the dearest and cleverest and most autocratic Mission doctor that ever lived,” and went straight back to Ikpe.

A Box on Wheels

In 1912 the mission council offered to send two women to Ikpe, but first asked for a medical report on the site. It was bad: the house stood on land that flooded. Mary refused to accept the verdict and stayed. She was growing deaf, and said she felt like “a spluttering candle.” She hated being carried in a hammock. “I feel a brute in it,” she wrote, “it seems so selfish to be lying there, while four boys sweat like beasts of burden. To push a little carriage is like skilled labour and no degradation.” The women of a Glasgow church sent her a basket-chair on wheels, a kind of cart, and her boys pushed her through the bush in it. It was the “box on wheels” she had written about in 1906.

In September 1912 she completed thirty-six years as a missionary, and took stock of herself: “I’m lame and feeble and foolish; the wrinkles are wonderful, no concertina is so wonderfully folded and convulated. I’m a wee, wee wifie, verra little buikit, but I grip on well, none the less.” An old doctor told her that by ordinary rule she should have been dead long ago.

That winter a friend in the women’s committee paid for her to take the first real holiday of her life, a few weeks in the Canary Islands with Jean. She protested that it was selfish and extravagant, and then enjoyed it. “I sat and knitted and crocheted and sewed and worked through the Bible all the day long,” she wrote. “He is so near and so dear.” A woman who met her at the hotel said that of all the people she had ever met, Mary Slessor impressed her most as “the perfect embodiment of the Christian life.”

The Ikpe Twin

Back at Ikpe, the chiefs turned against the church. They did not mind schools, they said, but they wanted no interference with their customs, and if houses of God were built, everyone would die. “I shall never give you teachers without the Gospel,” she told them. “If you don’t take the one, you won’t have the other.” When they announced, with an air of great generosity, that they would allow some worship but would not themselves join in “the confusions of the church,” she replied, “God will doubtless be immensely pleased and benefited by your wondrous condescension.” Livingstone says they laughed.

Then twins were born in Ikpe. Mary slept with the babies in her own bed, while people watched outside in the dark. The father wanted to kill the surviving boy and throw the mother into a swamp. Mary made him swear an oath not to harm the child, and when he grandly agreed to let it live, she bowed ironically to the ground, which unnerved him completely. By now, Livingstone says, “she had come to realise that it was not good to take twins from their mother,” and she insisted that the child stay at home. Jean went to live with the mother, and then the mother and baby were brought to a lean-to under Mary’s verandah, with Jean sleeping beside them. “It is really far braver and kinder of her to live with that heathen woman with her fretting habits,” Mary wrote, “than it is for her to go out in the dark and fight with snakes.”

One Sunday, while they were at church, the mother broke the baby’s thigh and gave him poison. With care he recovered. For weeks they watched over him, hoping that when his parents saw how healthy and handsome he was they would keep him. At last the parents agreed to take him home. Four days later they sent for Jean, who came back carrying “a weak, pinched form that had death written on its face.” He died soon afterwards. Livingstone ends the story with a single sentence: “that was the end of ‘Ma’s’ strenuous fight and Jean’s ten weeks’ toil by night and day.”

It is one of the saddest stories in her life, and it is right that it is told. Near the end, after nearly forty years, she could still lose. Belief is not changed by argument or by a single act of love. It changes, if it changes at all, over generations.

Odoro Ikpe

In 1914 she pushed on once more, to a government rest-house on a hill five miles from Ikpe called Odoro Ikpe. It had no door and a mud floor. She borrowed a camp-bed, and the girls slept on the floor among the lizards. When an old chief offered her a place to build and told his young men to build “a house for book,” she said, “No! We don’t begin or end either with a house. We begin and end with God in our hearts.” A young man in a hat, who had not taken it off to speak to her, told her they could not accept God’s word if she brought twins and twin-mothers into their town. She looked at him, Livingstone says, “as witheringly as she could,” and said, “I speak with men and people worthy of me, and not with a puny bush-boy such as you have shown by your manners you are.” The hat came off, and the crowd cried, “Ma, forgive! forgive! he does not know any better.”

Her tongue could still wound, and she knew it. She was also, in these last years, a woman of her time in ways that are hard to admire. When the government began taking batches of men from each village, with the chiefs’ consent, to work in the coalfields and on the railway, Livingstone records that she approved. When her own workmen were lazy, she resorted to what she called “muscular Christianity,” which amused everyone, and which seems to have meant cuffing them. She was in debt to her carpenter and labourers, and once borrowed five shillings from a government doctor. She was a very old, very ill woman, in debt, supervising a building site from a chair in the sun, and still, some nights, writing by candlelight that she was “the happiest and most grateful woman in the world.”

Strength in Weakness

“I begin every day,” she said in these years, “almost every journey in pain, and in such tiredness that I am sure I can’t go on, and whenever I begin, the strength comes, and it increases.” That is almost a paraphrase of the verse at the head of this chapter. Paul had asked three times for his “thorn in the flesh” to be taken away, and was told, “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Isaiah says, “He giveth power to the faint; and to him that hath no might he increaseth strength” (Isaiah 40:29, ASV). Mary Slessor was not healed. She was not made strong. She was given, each morning, enough strength to begin.
