When her own workmen were lazy, she resorted to what she called “muscular Christianity,” which amused everyone, and which seems to have meant cuffing them. She was in debt to her carpenter and labourers, and once borrowed five shillings from a government doctor. She was a very old, very ill woman, in debt, supervising a building site from a chair in the sun, and still, some nights, writing by candlelight that she was “the happiest and most grateful woman in the world.” Strength in Weakness “I begin every day,” she said in these years, “almost every journey in pain, and in such tiredness that I am sure I can’t go on, and whenever I begin, the strength comes, and it increases.” That is almost a paraphrase of the verse at the head of this chapter. Paul had asked three times for his “thorn in the flesh” to be taken away, and was told, “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Isaiah says, “He giveth power to the faint; and to him that hath no might he increaseth strength” (Isaiah 40:29, ASV). Mary Slessor was not healed. She was not made strong. She was given, each morning, enough strength to begin.

fields.title: A Poor Exponent of Faith
fields.body_html:
“Straightway the father of the child cried out, and said, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.”

— Mark 9:24, ASV

On a Log Among the People

An old friend from her Dundee mission days, J. H. Smith, was collecting testimonies for a book called Our Faithful God: Answers to Prayer, and he asked Mary Slessor for hers. She wrote it sitting in the open air:

My life is one long daily, hourly, record of answered prayer. For physical health, for mental overstrain, for guidance given marvellously, for errors and dangers averted, for enmity to the Gospel subdued, for food provided at the exact hour needed, for everything that goes to make up life and my poor service, I can testify with a full and often wonder-stricken awe that I believe God answers prayer. … I am sitting alone here on a log among a company of natives. My children, whose very lives are a testimony that God answers prayer, are working round me. … Food is scarce just now. We live from hand to mouth. We have not more than will be our breakfast to-day, but I know we shall be fed, for God answers prayer.

It is a confident statement, and she meant it. But it would be a mistake to stop there, as popular books often do, and make her a saint who never doubted. Livingstone, who had her letters, knew better, and so do we.

Unanswered

To someone who complained that God had not answered his prayers, she wrote: “You thought God was to hear and answer you by making everything straight and pleasant. Not so are nations or churches or men and women born; not so is character made. God is answering your prayer in His way.” And to another, in the same mood, she wrote the sentence that we met in the first chapter of this book: “I know what it is to pray long years and never get the answer. I had to pray for my father. But I know my heavenly Father so well that I can leave it with Him for the lower fatherhood.”

She did not pretend that every prayer was answered in the way she wanted. The prayer of her girlhood, for her drunken father, never was. Her faith was not that God always gives what we ask. It was that God can be trusted when he does not.

A Poor Exponent

Nor did she pretend that her own faith was strong. “I am a poor exponent of faith,” she said. “I ought to have full faith in our Father that He will do everything, but I am ashamed of myself, for I want to ‘see,’ and that sends faith out of court. I never felt more in sympathy with that old afflicted father before in his prayer, ‘Lord, I believe, help Thou my unbelief.’ Every syllable suits me.”

The words at the head of this chapter were spoken by a father whose son had been tormented since childhood. The disciples could not help, and when Jesus came, the father said, “If thou canst do anything, have compassion on us, and help us.” Jesus answered, “If thou canst! All things are possible to him that believeth.” And the father cried out, “I believe; help thou mine unbelief.” Jesus healed the boy. He did not wait for the father’s faith to be perfect. He accepted the faith the man had, doubts and all.

That was the faith of Mary Slessor. It was real and it was mixed. She had seasons of darkness that today we might call depression. We have met them in this book: the first Sunday in Okoyong, when she was on the edge of tears; the time after the smallpox when she had “no heart for anything”; the years alone at Akpap, when she wrote “All is dark except above.” Before her last public meetings in Scotland in 1907 she wrote, “I am suffering tortures of fear, and yet why is it that I cannot rest in Him?” In 1909, covered in boils and unable to sleep, she said, “Only sleeping draughts keep me from going off my head.” Late in life she spoke of times “when I’m not well and the doldrums come very near.”

Her comments in the margins of the book of Job show how she read her own experience. When Job cries out against God, she did not think he was rebelling. “His plaint was a relief to his own spirit, and an appeal for sympathy,” she wrote. Beside one chapter she wrote, “The atmosphere is clearing; the clouds are scattering … the spirit swings back on its pivot and begins to see God.” And further on: “Right, Job, turn to God! Leave it to Him. The fit of depression will pass when you have sounded the depths, and profit will follow.” She was writing about Job. She was also writing about herself.

Talking to Her Father

Her prayers were not formal. At a tea-table in Scotland after a tiring journey, she was heard to say, as if speaking to someone in the room, “Thank ye, Faither. Ye ken I’m tired.” When a lady asked her how she had come to such closeness with God, she said, “Ah, woman, when I am out there in the bush I have often no other one to speak to but my Father, and I just talk to Him.” At a meeting of women missionaries in Duke Town, when everyone was laughing and chattering, it struck her that they ought to be praying, and she said so, and they all got up and went into the next room to pray. Sometimes she called her household to prayer at odd hours, and when Jean protested that the time was long past, she said, “Jean, the gate of heaven is never shut.”

She believed profoundly in the prayers of others. She was sure, she said, that the only explanation for how she had survived so many dangers, and why so many people had submitted to her, was that she had been prayed for more than most. “Prayer-waves pulsate from Britain all through Calabar,” she wrote. “Pray on, dear one. The power lies that way.” She also said, “Praying is harder work than doing, at least I find it so.” Paul, who knew the same difficulty, wrote that “we know not how to pray as we ought; but the Spirit himself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered” (Romans 8:26, ASV).

Her own prayers for her friends grew simpler as she grew older. She used to ask for many particular things for them. In the end, Livingstone says, her prayer was only this: “Lord give them Thy best and it shall suffice them and me.”

The Bible With a Pen

She read her Bible every morning from first light, about half past five, with a fine pen in her hand. She underlined the key words and wrote in the margins, and would sometimes spend three days on a single chapter. When one Bible was full she began another. Several of them survive, crowded with her notes. Some of those notes are short enough to remember:

God is never behind time.

Good is good, but it is not enough; it must be God.

The secret of all failure is disobedience.

Blessed the man and woman who is able to serve cheerfully in the second rank, a big test.

Slavery never pays; the slave is spoiled as a man, and the master not less so.

It were worth while to die, if thereby a soul could be born again.

She read the Old Testament as if it were set in Calabar. Beside one passage she wrote, “this happens in Okoyong every day.” When Laban and Jacob set up a heap of stones and said, “Jehovah watch between me and thee,” she wrote, “Beautiful sentiment, but a mbiam oath of fear.” Of Jael, who killed a sleeping enemy with a tent peg, she wrote, “Not a womanly woman, a sorry story; would God not have showed her a better way if she had asked?” Of part of Deborah’s song: “Fine poetry, poor morality.” John was her favourite book. Beside the verse about the crowds looking for Jesus, she wrote, “The secret of our failures in winning men; they don’t find Him with us.”

One more note from her Bibles has become famous, though it is not in Livingstone. Later biographers report that she wrote in one of them the words “God and one are always a majority.” It was not her own saying. It was an old proverb, already in print in the 1860s and attributed by some to the American reformer Frederick Douglass. But she wrote it down, and it fits her.

“Not Goody-Goody at All”

In her last years her friends noticed that she was growing gentler. She had always known her faults. “I don’t half live up to the ideal missionary life,” she said. “It is not easier to be a saint here than at home. We are very human, and not goody-goody at all.” Livingstone says she was often “deep in the valley of humiliation over hasty words spoken.” She began to say things she would not have said when she was younger: “My opinions may not just suit every one, and it is possible other people may be right and I far wrong.” Of a very serious young missionary she wrote that what was needed was “one to laugh, to hitch on to the yoke, and joke over all that we don’t like.”

She refused to take credit for her work. “I have lived my life very quietly and in a very natural and humble way,” she said. “It isn’t Mary Slessor doing anything, but Something outside of her altogether uses her as her small ability allows.” When a friend wrote that her reward would be a starry crown in heaven, she answered, “What would I do with starry crowns except to cast them at His feet?” It is the spirit of Jesus’ words to his disciples: “when ye shall have done all the things that are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants; we have done that which it was our duty to do” (Luke 17:10, ASV).

A Royal Honour

In 1913 that humility was put to a test. Some of her friends in Calabar, missionaries and officials, had been trying for two years to have her work publicly recognised. J. K. Macgregor wrote an account of her life for the government. When Sir Frederick Lugard became Governor-General of the newly united Nigeria, he sent a strong recommendation to the Colonial Secretary in London, and she was chosen, with the approval of King George V, as an Honorary Associate of the Order of the Hospital of St John of Jerusalem. The badge was a silver Maltese cross, to be worn on a black ribbon on the left shoulder.

When the official letter came, she said to herself, “Now, who has done this? Who am I, and what is my distinction that I should have it?” She told no one. When the badge arrived in Calabar, her friends knew she would never come down to receive it unless she were cornered. So they wrote telling her that she surely would not want to receive it secretly, and that it was her duty to come, and they enclosed a telegraph form already filled in with the single word “Coming.” They knew she would have no peace until she had sent it. She sent it.

The night before she left, she read the story of Peter’s denial to her household and told them that Peter had fallen because he followed Jesus “afar off.” “Eh, bairns,” she said, “it’s the wee lassie that sits beside her mother at meal times that gets all the nice bittocks. Keep close to Jesus the Good Shepherd all the way.”

The presentation was made in the Goldie Memorial Hall in Calabar, in front of the European community and the students of the Hope Waddell Institute. She arrived in an old cotton dress, a straw hat, and cloth shoes, and sat with her head in her hands while the Provincial Commissioner spoke about her. When she rose, she could not at first find any words. Then she turned to the African boys and girls in the hall and told them in Efik to be faithful to the government, because at bottom it was Christian, and friendly to the missions, as the badge proved.

That remark, which Livingstone records with approval, belongs with the other evidence of how closely she identified British rule with Christianity. It was a sincere belief, and she had seen much good done by men she trusted. It was also a belief that the history of the following century would not bear out, and it is not one this book can share.

Then she spoke in English. The day before she had watched soldiers in a mock battle and had been struck that the officers always went in front, leading their men. “If I have done anything in my life,” she said, “it has been easy because the Master has gone before.” Afterwards she wrote to friends in Scotland: “Don’t think that there is any difference in my designation. I am Mary Mitchell Slessor, nothing more and none other than the unworthy, unprofitable, but most willing, servant of the King of Kings.” And as the congratulations poured in, she fled to Ikpe. “I shall never look the world in the face again,” she said, “until all this blarney and publicity is over.”

Help Thou Mine Unbelief

The honour did not change her faith, and neither did her doubts. Both are part of her story. She could write that her life was “one long daily, hourly, record of answered prayer,” and in the same years call herself “a poor exponent of faith.” She could sit on a log with nothing but breakfast in the house and say she knew they would be fed, and lie awake at night unable to rest in God. The psalmist knew the same double experience: “Why art thou cast down, O my soul? And why art thou disquieted within me? Hope thou in God; for I shall yet praise him” (Psalm 42:11, ASV). A faith like that is not less than a faith without doubts. It may be more honest. It is certainly more useful to the rest of us.

fields.title: The Time of the Singing of Birds
fields.body_html:
“For, lo, the winter is past; The rain is over and gone; The flowers appear on the earth; The time of the singing of birds is come, And the voice of the turtle-dove is heard in our land”

— Song of Solomon 2:11-12, ASV

Back to the Old Haunts

In July 1913 she went back to Akpap for the first time in eight years. The station now had two women missionaries and a new church. People came from all over Okoyong to greet her, and she remembered their names and their family histories. The twins she had rescued were now healthy young men and women. Mana and Iye were there. And Ma Eme came, still a devoted follower of the old religion, and the two old women sat together all day and talked about the killing time. More than four hundred people came to a service in the unfinished church, the largest congregation Okoyong had ever seen. She thought of the words of Jesus about one who sows and another who reaps.

At Christmas 1913 a new church was opened at Use, built by the people under her direction without outside help, and more than eighty visitors were fed. “A bonnie kirk it is,” she wrote, “the biggest Christmas I’ve ever had in Calabar.” She added a remark that shows how far she had come from the young woman who ran everything herself: “Jean and Annie do not hesitate to set it aside quietly in their superior way; it often works out better than mine, truth to tell.”

The War

In August 1914, while she was building her house at Odoro Ikpe, rumours began to reach the bush of fighting in the white men’s world. Trade stopped. Canoes that went down to Calabar for rice and kerosene came back with their loads of palm oil unsold. On 13 August letters arrived with the news that Britain was at war with Germany. Nigeria bordered the German colony of Kamerun, and she feared for Calabar. Prices doubled. Her kerosene ran out, and she read the Bible at family prayers by the light of burning sticks.

When her first war mail came, she read why Britain had entered the war and said, “Thank God! our nation is not the aggressor.” Then she read about the invasion of Belgium, and tried to stand up, and could not. The girls carried her to bed, and she lay in a fever for a fortnight. She grew steadily weaker. She was not afraid of death, but she was afraid of dying alone in the bush, because she knew that her skull might be taken and worshipped as a powerful charm.

At last she lay in a stupor, and the church boys at Odoro Ikpe lifted her in her camp-bed and carried her five miles to Ikpe. The next morning they put her in a canoe under a tarpaulin and paddled her down the Creek to the landing-place for Use. She lay in the road in the moonlight, scarcely breathing, while a trader sent for the doctor from Itu. He stayed all night, not expecting her to live. All through the night her mind was on the soldiers in the trenches.

She recovered a little. She sent for her colleague Martha Peacock, and told her it might be the end. “Oh,” she said, “if only the war were over and my children safe in the Kingdom, how gladly would I go!” She called the children together and told them what to do when she died.

The war stirred her in ways that are not easy to read now. When two government officers she counted among her oldest friends were drowned on naval service, she grieved for them deeply. At times she wrote with fierce patriotism: “Oh if I were thirty years younger, and if I were a man! We must not have peace until Germany licks the dust.” Scottish women, she told a nervous friend, were not Belgians; “they would stand up to William the Execrated.” But she also wrote, in calmer moods, “Miss Slessor, why do you worry? Is God not fit to take care of His own universe and purpose?” She rested, Livingstone says, on the words “The Lord reigneth,” as on a soft pillow. She prayed that her nation might be “sent from its pleasures to its knees.” At the Christmas service she did not like having to explain to her African congregation why Christian nations were at war with each other.

She wrote to a friend that Christmas:

There will be few merry Christmasses in Europe this year. But, thank God, there will be a more profound sense of all Christ came to be and do for mankind. He will Himself draw near, and will fill empty chairs in lonely homes and hearts, and make His people … to know that here and now He is the Resurrection and the Life, that he that believeth in Him shall never die.

She was echoing Jesus’ words at the grave of Lazarus: “I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth on me, though he die, yet shall he live; and whosoever liveth and believeth on me shall never die” (John 11:25-26, ASV).

Plans

She knew now that only a voyage home might heal her, and she made plans. Mrs. Arnot, who as Miss Young had been one of the missionaries Mary recruited and had since been widowed, offered to take a small house in Scotland where they could live quietly together. Mary accepted, with tears. She would go in the spring. She would visit her mother’s grave in Devon. She wrote to ask a friend to send her a hat and boots, and other things “which civilisation demanded.” Her only regret was Ikpe. “It is ten years since I first took them on, and they have never got a teacher yet. It is bitterly hard!”

Her colleagues noticed that the old power of recovery was gone. One day she told them she had been going through her desk and tearing up letters, “in case anything should happen.”

On New Year’s Day, 1915, Martha Peacock and another missionary, Miss Couper, came to tea. Miss Peacock had made her a plum pudding, and when they arrived it was on the table with a rose from the garden stuck in the top. Mary was, Miss Peacock said, as happy as a girl, and admitted she had had to use great self-control not to taste the pudding before they came. Two men were sent running to Itu for the doctor. They had forgotten the clock and did not know the time. A cock crowed, and one of the girls said, “Day must be dawning,” but when Miss Peacock drew back the curtain it was still pitch dark.

At half past three in the morning, on 13 January 1915, Mary Slessor died. She was sixty-six. Miss Peacock wrote that there was no great struggle at the end, and that “Ma Akamba, ‘The Great Mother,’ entered into the presence of the King.” (The government Gazette announced her death “at Itu,” the district in which Use lay.)

She used to say that “the time of the singing of birds” was wherever Christ was. For her, as the Song of Solomon has it, the winter was past, the rain was over and gone, and the time of the singing of birds had come.

At dawn it was brought ashore at the government beach at Duke Town. The flags of the town were at half-mast. Officials, merchants, and missionaries followed. She was buried in the old mission cemetery on the hill above Duke Town, where she had first gone ashore thirty-nine years before.

When the procession came near and some women began to wail, the old woman stood up. “Kutua oh, kutua oh,” she said. “Do not cry, do not cry. Praise God from whom all blessings flow. Ma was a great blessing.” As the coffin was lowered, she said one word: “Safe.” A slip from the rose bush at Use was planted in the earth. Afterwards Mammy Fuller said, “I have been just near heaven all the time.”

fields.title: Everybody’s Mother
fields.body_html:
“But we were gentle in the midst of you, as when a nurse cherisheth her own children: even so, being affectionately desirous of you, we were well pleased to impart unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls, because ye were become very dear to us.”

— 1 Thessalonians 2:7-8, ASV

What She Left

When Mary Slessor died, the churches she had begun along the Enyong Creek were small, poor, and young. Livingstone, writing the next year, counted nearly fifty churches and schools in the district she had opened, with nearly fifteen hundred members and more than two thousand pupils. He printed the accounts of five of the Creek congregations for 1914. Asang had four hundred and twenty-eight members. Onoyom’s town, Obufa Obio, had a hundred and eighteen and more than seven hundred pounds in the bank. Itu, where Mana and two boys had begun the work in 1903, had a hundred and nine. All of them were paying their own way.

By the standards of the Church at home these were modest numbers, and Mary knew it. Livingstone says that at the end of her life she was troubled by how little had been done. After seventy years, the whole Calabar mission had a Christian community of about ten thousand, eight hundred people and a communion roll of three thousand, four hundred, and it had barely touched the interior. The Church at home, she felt, had never risen to the opportunity. It was interested in her, but not in Nigeria.

Livingstone was an admirer, but he was honest enough to record the criticism too. “It was not … the broad policy she originated that was criticised,” he wrote, “so much as matters of detail, and no doubt there was sometimes justification for this. She admitted that she had no gifts as an organiser.” She was a pioneer, and she knew it. She opened doors and left others to build the rooms behind them.

The Legend

Within a year of her death she had become a legend, and the legend grew for the rest of the century. Livingstone’s biography, and his version for children, were followed by dozens of popular lives. Missionary societies used her story to recruit and to raise money. Her face appeared, from 1997 until a redesign in 2009, on the Clydesdale Bank’s ten-pound note. When Queen Elizabeth II visited Nigeria in 1956, she laid a wreath on Mary Slessor’s grave. There is a park named after her in Dundee, and a charity in her name runs a clinic at Akpap, in Okoyong.

In Nigeria, too, she is remembered. In Calabar there is a Mary Slessor roundabout, with a bronze statue of her carrying twin babies. There are schools named after her, including one at Arochukwu, and the mission hospital at Itu bears her name. In 2000 the people of Calabar chose her as one of the city’s people of the millennium. The Presbyterian Church of Nigeria, which grew out of the mission she served, honours her as a mother of the church, and a centenary service was held in Calabar in January 2015. Newspapers there still call her “the woman who stopped the killing of twins.”

Some of this honour is deserved and some of it is legend. Historians have tried to separate the two.

What the Historians Say

The Scottish historian Esther Breitenbach has studied how Mary Slessor became famous. In a 2017 article she argues that the icon owed much to “deliberate acts of invention,” and to the meeting of British expansion in south-eastern Nigeria with missionary enthusiasm and the hopes of Scottish women for careers of their own. She suggests that there was little that was unique in Slessor’s practice as a missionary, and sets out to show the gap between the myth and the historical reality.

There is truth in that. Other missionaries rescued twins before her and alongside her. Other women lived alone on remote stations. The killing of twins had been banned in Calabar before she arrived, and it did not end when she died. Her authority rested in part on British power, and she welcomed that power and sometimes praised it in terms that are hard to read now. The “White Queen of Okoyong” was a title invented in Scotland. The people of Okoyong called her Ma.

But other historians see more. The historian Jeanette Hardage, whose 2008 study is the fullest academic life of Slessor, asked whether she was an agent of imperialism or a liberator of the oppressed, and answered, “Both, to some degree.” She noted that Slessor admired much of British culture and wanted to share it, but that she did not spare colonial officers when she thought them arrogant or cruel, and that she knew local law and custom better than most of them. The Nigerian church historian Ogbu Kalu wrote that her vision was “much broader and more activist” than her fellow missionaries could imagine. She rejected the idea that a missionary should live in a compound apart from the people, and, in the words of the Dictionary of African Christian Biography, she was a “catalyst that challenged the mission to change.”

Nigerian writers themselves have taken different views. Some honour her as the mother of the church and the saviour of the twins. Others point out that the Efik rulers, the consuls, and earlier missionaries had acted before her, and that the story of a lone Scotswoman rescuing Africa from itself leaves out the Africans who made change possible. Both are right to speak.

What This Book Has Found

This book has tried to tell her story with the Africans left in. It has found that the real woman was more interesting than the legend, and in some ways more admirable.

She was a factory girl with almost no schooling, afraid of crowds, of public speaking, of cows in fields, who walked alone into the most feared district of Calabar and stayed there fifteen years. She was not fearless. She was afraid and went anyway.

She did not work alone. Ma Eme warned her, again and again, of killings that were planned, at the risk of her own life, and never became a Christian. Edem took her into his compound and protected her, and she buried him with her own hands. Mana, a former slave girl, began the church at Itu with two boys, and taught its women to pray. Onoyom built a church with his own savings and cut down his town’s sacred tree. Jean ran her house, rescued twins, preached to two hundred people, and was paid a shilling a week. The story of Mary Slessor is also theirs.

She did not always win. The man whose life she saved was flogged and cut. The young man who died for his brother died after a verdict she had declined to give, and she grieved over it. The Ikpe twin was poisoned by his own mother. Many of the babies she carried home were buried in the little cemetery full of tiny graves. Her first district saw no baptisms for fifteen years.

She was not always right. She could be imperious and harsh. She boxed ears, caned a man who had won his case, and spoke with withering contempt to those who crossed her. She approved of the government’s drafts of village men for the coalfields and railway, she shared the racial assumptions of her age, and she told African children that the British government was Christian at bottom. She was bitter about Roman Catholics, though she counted Catholic officials among her friends. She knew many of her faults, and grieved over her “hasty words.”

And she was loved. When she died, the girls she had raised were terrified of what would become of them, and the whole district came to mourn. The people of Okoyong, who had once been ready to kill any stranger, had called her Mother. The people of the Creek, whom she had described in her worst moments as “untamed, unwashed, unlovely,” built churches with their own hands and paid for them with their own money. An old Muslim kissed her hand and said only God could make someone such a mother to everybody. The chief whose household she saved from slaughter stepped out of a line of warriors and knelt at her feet.

The Alabaster Box

Livingstone ended his biography with the story of the woman who broke an alabaster box of precious ointment over the head of Jesus, a few days before his death. The disciples complained about the waste. Jesus defended her: “She hath done what she could; she hath anointed my body beforehand for the burying” (Mark 14:8, ASV). Livingstone thought Mary Slessor had done the same with her life: broken it open, and poured it out for Christ, and let people call it a waste.

It is a good image. But the verse at the head of this chapter may fit her better still. Paul was writing to a young church in Thessalonica, a church he had founded and had been forced to leave. He reminded them how he had lived among them: “we were gentle in the midst of you, as when a nurse cherisheth her own children: even so, being affectionately desirous of you, we were well pleased to impart unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls, because ye were become very dear to us.”

Not the gospel only, but our own souls. That is what Mary Slessor gave the people of the Cross River. She preached the gospel to them in their own language for nearly forty years, and she also gave them herself: her salary, her health, her nights, her home, her chance of marriage, and in the end her life. They had become very dear to her. It was not a perfect gift. It came mixed with the prejudices of her age and the flaws of her temper, and it was carried into their country on the tide of an empire. But it was a real gift, and they knew it, and they called her “Everybody’s Mother.”

Paul wrote to another church that when everything else has passed away, three things remain: “faith, hope, love, these three; and the greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13:13, ASV). Mary Slessor’s faith was often weak, by her own account. Her hope was sometimes dark. But her love was the one thing that no one who knew her ever doubted.

Onoyom built a church with his own savings and cut down his town’s sacred tree. Jean ran her house, rescued twins, preached to two hundred people, and was paid a shilling a week. The story of Mary Slessor is also theirs. She did not always win. The man whose life she saved was flogged and cut. The young man who died for his brother died after a verdict she had declined to give, and she grieved over it. The Ikpe twin was poisoned by his own mother. Many of the babies she carried home were buried in the little cemetery full of tiny graves. Her first district saw no baptisms for fifteen years. She was not always right. She could be imperious and harsh. She boxed ears, caned a man who had won his case, and spoke with withering contempt to those who crossed her. She approved of the government’s drafts of village men for the coalfields and railway, she shared the racial assumptions of her age, and she told African children that the British government was Christian at bottom. She was bitter about Roman Catholics, though she counted Catholic officials among her friends. She knew many of her faults, and grieved over her “hasty words.” And she was loved. When she died, the girls she had raised were terrified of what would become of them, and the whole district came to mourn. The people of Okoyong, who had once been ready to kill any stranger, had called her Mother. The people of the Creek, whom she had described in her worst moments as “untamed, unwashed, unlovely,” built churches with their own hands and paid for them with their own money. An old Muslim kissed her hand and said only God could make someone such a mother to everybody. The chief whose household she saved from slaughter stepped out of a line of warriors and knelt at her feet. The Alabaster Box Livingstone ended his biography with the story of the woman who broke an alabaster box of precious ointment over the head of Jesus, a few days before his death. The disciples complained about the waste. Jesus defended her: “She hath done what she could; she hath anointed my body beforehand for the burying” (Mark 14:8, ASV). Livingstone thought Mary Slessor had done the same with her life: broken it open, and poured it out for Christ, and let people call it a waste. It is a good image. But the verse at the head of this chapter may fit her better still. Paul was writing to a young church in Thessalonica, a church he had founded and had been forced to leave. He reminded them how he had lived among them: “we were gentle in the midst of you, as when a nurse cherisheth her own children: even so, being affectionately desirous of you, we were well pleased to impart unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls, because ye were become very dear to us.” Not the gospel only, but our own souls. That is what Mary Slessor gave the people of the Cross River. She preached the gospel to them in their own language for nearly forty years, and she also gave them herself: her salary, her health, her nights, her home, her chance of marriage, and in the end her life. They had become very dear to her. It was not a perfect gift. It came mixed with the prejudices of her age and the flaws of her temper, and it was carried into their country on the tide of an empire. But it was a real gift, and they knew it, and they called her “Everybody’s Mother.” Paul wrote to another church that when everything else has passed away, three things remain: “faith, hope, love, these three; and the greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13:13, ASV). Mary Slessor’s faith was often weak, by her own account. Her hope was sometimes dark. But her love was the one thing that no one who knew her ever doubted.

fields.title: Appendix A: Lessons from the Life of Mary Slessor
fields.body_html:
“Remember them that had the rule over you, men that spake unto you the word of God; and considering the issue of their life, imitate their faith.”

— Hebrews 13:7, ASV

The lessons below gather the themes of this book so that readers can return to them. Mary Slessor would not have wanted her life to be a pattern. She would have wanted it to point beyond herself to the God who, she said, had gone before her. Each lesson therefore rests on Scripture, not on her example alone. The letter to the Hebrews tells us to consider how those who went before us lived and died, and to imitate their faith, not every detail of their lives.

1. God Uses Unlikely People

A factory girl with almost no schooling, frightened of crowds and of public speaking, became one of the best-known missionaries of her age. God does not wait for impressive people. “God chose the weak things of the world, that he might put to shame the things that are strong” (1 Corinthians 1:27, ASV).

2. A Broken Home Is Not the End of the Story

Mary grew up with a father who drank and a mother who prayed through the night. She never saw her prayers for her father answered, but she found a heavenly Father she could trust. “When my father and my mother forsake me, Then Jehovah will take me up” (Psalm 27:10, ASV).

3. Hard Years Can Be Training Years

Fourteen years at the loom taught her endurance, thrift, and an understanding of the poor that she carried into Africa. “It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth” (Lamentations 3:27, ASV).

4. Courage Is Not the Absence of Fear

She walked into Okoyong so frightened she could only pray one word. She went anyway. “Be strong and of good courage; be not affrighted, neither be thou dismayed: for Jehovah thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest” (Joshua 1:9, ASV).

5. Learn the Language of the People

She learned Efik so well that people said she spoke it better than they did. The gospel travels best in the heart language of those who hear it. “To the weak I became weak, that I might gain the weak: I am become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22, ASV).

6. Honour the Mercy of Those Outside the Faith

Ma Eme risked her life, again and again, to warn Mary of killings that were planned, and never became a Christian. Mary grieved her choice and never forgot her mercy. “Which of these three, thinkest thou, proved neighbor unto him that fell among the robbers? And he said, He that showed mercy on him” (Luke 10:36-37, ASV).

7. Speak for Those Who Cannot Speak

She sat at the entrance of a yard full of chained prisoners and would not move. “Open thy mouth for the dumb, In the cause of all such as are left desolate” (Proverbs 31:8, ASV).

8. Partial Victories Are Still Worth Winning

Many of her rescues were incomplete, and some failed. She kept going. “And let us not be weary in well-doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Galatians 6:9, ASV).

9. The Weakest Are Precious to God

Twin babies thrown into the bush, their mothers driven out as cursed: these were the people she spent her life for. “Suffer the little children to come unto me; forbid them not: for to such belongeth the kingdom of God” (Mark 10:14, ASV).

10. A Life Laid on the Altar Is Not Taken Back

When she had to choose between marriage and the people she had promised to serve, she chose the people. “Present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service” (Romans 12:1, ASV).

11. Make Peace

She knitted through palavers, knelt between armed men, and threw her own clothes over the gin. “Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9, ASV).

12. Be Wary of Borrowed Power

Her authority was partly the consul’s, and she sometimes spoke of British rule as if it were Christian. Christians who work alongside governments must remember where their help comes from. “Put not your trust in princes, Nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help” (Psalm 146:3, ASV).

13. Leave the Results With God

Her first district saw no baptisms for fifteen years. “Christ sent me to preach the Gospel,” she said, “and He will look after results.” “I planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6, ASV).

14. Rejoice When the Fields Are Empty

After the smallpox took four of her children and her chief, she wrote that she was “always satisfied and happy in His love.” “Yet I will rejoice in Jehovah, I will joy in the God of my salvation” (Habakkuk 3:18, ASV).

15. The Gospel Needs Ordinary Messengers

The church at Itu was begun by a former slave girl and two boys. Onoyom was sent to Mary by a homeless drunkard who still remembered the gospel. “There can be neither Jew nor Greek, there can be neither bond nor free, there can be no male and female; for ye all are one man in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28, ASV).

16. Do Not Look Back

When the rules said she must return to Akpap, she said, “I dare not go back.” “No man, having put his hand to the plow, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62, ASV).

17. Seek Justice, Especially for Women

She sat unpaid on a colonial court for four years so that women would get a hearing. “Seek justice, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow” (Isaiah 1:17, ASV).

18. Give People a Way to Live, Not Only a Message

She saw that women would not be free until they could support themselves, and planned a settlement on the land. Faith must care for the whole person. “Pure religion and undefiled before our God and Father is this, to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (James 1:27, ASV).

19. Strength Is Given Day by Day

“I begin every day … in pain,” she said, “and whenever I begin, the strength comes.” “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9, ASV).

20. Doubt Is Not the Opposite of Faith

She called herself “a poor exponent of faith” and said the prayer “help Thou my unbelief” suited her in every syllable. “I believe; help thou mine unbelief” (Mark 9:24, ASV).

21. Know Your Faults, and Grow Gentler

She was often sorry for “hasty words,” and in her last days said of something harsh she had written, “I wonder I could have been so hard.” “Be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving each other, even as God also in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:32, ASV).

22. Give Yourself, Not Only Your Message

She gave the people of the Cross River her salary, her health, her home, and her life. “We were well pleased to impart unto you, not the gospel of God only, but also our own souls, because ye were become very dear to us” (1 Thessalonians 2:8, ASV).

23. The Greatest of These Is Love

Her faith was often weak and her hope sometimes dark, but no one who knew her doubted her love. “But now abideth faith, hope, love, these three; and the greatest of these is love” (1 Corinthians 13:13, ASV).

fields.title: Appendix B: Chapter-by-Chapter Study and Reflection Guide
fields.body_html:
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deluding your own selves.”

— James 1:22, ASV

This guide is for personal reflection, small groups, or a reading course of about twenty weeks. Its purpose is not to make Mary Slessor an object of admiration, but to let her life hold up a mirror in which readers can examine their own discipleship under Scripture. Groups may find it helpful to begin each session with the chapter’s opening verse and to end with prayer. Some chapters raise hard questions about mission, power, and culture. They are meant to be discussed honestly, not settled quickly.

Introduction - The Legend and the Letters

Central idea

The real Mary Slessor, as her letters and the records show her, is more interesting and more useful than the legend.

Scriptures to revisit

Proverbs 18:17; John 8:32.

Reflection

1. Why do Christians like legends about their heroes? 2. What is lost when a life is simplified?

Chapter 1 - A Wild Lassie

Central idea

A childhood shaped by a drinking father and a praying mother taught her to trust a heavenly Father when her earthly father failed.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 103:13-14; Proverbs 20:1; Acts 16:31.

Reflection

1. Is there a prayer you have prayed for years without an answer? 2. What does it mean to “leave it with Him”?

Chapter 2 - Fourteen Years at the Loom

Central idea

Long, hard years of work formed endurance and an understanding of the poor that God later used.

Scriptures to revisit

Lamentations 3:27; Colossians 3:23; Psalm 119:105.

Reflection

1. How do you regard work you did not choose? 2. What might God be forming in you through it?

Chapter 3 - Taming the Roughs

Central idea

She learned to speak among the people rather than above them, and to stay where she was when she wanted to run.

Scriptures to revisit

Mark 12:37; 1 Corinthians 9:22; 2 Timothy 1:7.

Reflection

1. Where do you meet people “as one of themselves”? 2. What fear is deciding what you do?

Chapter 4 - “Pray for Me!”

Central idea

A mission first imagined by freed African Jamaicans called a factory girl who answered, “Here am I; send me.”

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 6:1-8; Matthew 9:37-38; Matthew 27:22.

Reflection

1. What surprised you about the origins of the Calabar mission? 2. What are you doing with Jesus?

Chapter 5 - Learning Calabar

Central idea

She learned the language, the laws, and the fears of the Efik, and learned not to be in a hurry.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 28:16; John 5:1-9.

Reflection

1. How would you answer the man selling rum? 2. Where is impatience harming your work for God?

Chapter 6 - Bereft

Central idea

The deaths of her mother and sisters freed her, painfully, to go where no one would worry about her.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 73:25-26; 2 Corinthians 1:3-4.

Reflection

1. How has grief changed the direction of your life? 2. Whom might you now comfort with the comfort you received?

Chapter 7 - “Father!”

Central idea

She walked into Okoyong afraid, able to pray only one word, and stayed.

Scriptures to revisit

Joshua 1:9; Romans 8:15.

Reflection

1. What “Okoyong” are you afraid to enter? 2. What does it mean that courage rests on presence, not feeling?

Chapter 8 - Ma Eme

Central idea

Her closest ally never became a Christian, yet made much of the saving of life possible.

Scriptures to revisit

Proverbs 17:17; Luke 10:25-37; Genesis 18:25.

Reflection

1. How do you honour kindness from people who do not share your faith? 2. What does it mean to leave such questions with “the Judge of all the earth”?

Chapter 9 - The Poison Bean

Central idea

Her greatest victory over the ordeal was partial and costly, and it showed that the people themselves longed to be free of the old customs.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 82:3-4; Proverbs 31:8-9.

Reflection

1. When have you had to accept a partial victory? 2. Are there people around you trapped in a system they cannot break alone?

Chapter 10 - Twin-Mothers

Central idea

She took up children whom their parents had been taught to fear, and learned over time to help families keep them.

Scriptures to revisit

Psalm 27:10; Isaiah 40:11; Mark 10:13-16.

Reflection

1. Who are the “cursed” people in your society? 2. What did Mary come to believe, late in life, about taking twins away from their mothers?

Chapter 11 - Laid on the Altar

Central idea

She wanted to marry, but would not take back a life already given to the people of Okoyong.

Scriptures to revisit

Romans 12:1-2; Psalm 84:11.

Reflection

1. What have you laid on the altar that you are tempted to take back? 2. Can singleness be a calling rather than a loss?

Chapter 12 - “The Woman’s God”

Central idea

Peacemaking in Okoyong took patience, humour, knitting, and a clear line she would not cross.

Scriptures to revisit

Matthew 5:9; Romans 12:18; Ephesians 2:14.

Reflection

1. Where could you be a peacemaker this week? 2. What did you make of her sending the runaway slaves back?

Chapter 13 - Consul and Gunboat

Central idea

She used British power to stop killings, and the story raises hard questions about justice and borrowed authority.

Scriptures to revisit

Micah 6:8; Romans 13:1-4; Psalm 146:3.

Reflection

1. When is it right for Christians to rely on the power of the state? 2. What is lost when justice depends on one strong personality?

Chapter 14 - Smallpox and Silence

Central idea

Years of loss, loneliness, and no visible fruit did not destroy her contentment in God.

Scriptures to revisit

Habakkuk 3:17-18; 1 Corinthians 3:6-7; Psalm 30:5.

Reflection

1. How do you measure success in your service? 2. Can you be “satisfied” without being “triumphant”?

Chapter 15 - Not by Might

Central idea

She walked through the door a punitive expedition had opened, while insisting that the land belonged to its people.

Scriptures to revisit

Zechariah 4:6; Psalm 20:7.

Reflection

1. How should Christians think about missions that followed conquest? 2. What did Wilkie mean by the “peaceable means of the Gospel”?

Chapter 16 - First Fruits

Central idea

After fifteen years she saw baptisms in Okoyong, and at Itu a former slave girl and two boys began a church.

Scriptures to revisit

John 4:35-38; Psalm 103:1-5; Galatians 3:28.

Reflection

1. Whose sowing are you reaping? 2. Who are the unnoticed Manas in your church?

Chapter 17 - “I Dare Not Go Back”

Central idea

Her refusal to retreat strained her relationship with the Church and opened the Enyong Creek.

Scriptures to revisit

Luke 9:57-62; Hebrews 11:8; Isaiah 30:21.

Reflection

1. When is holy stubbornness right, and when is it pride? 2. What would you do if your church told you to go back?

Chapter 18 - On the Bench

Central idea

She sat as a magistrate to get justice for women, in an imperfect court with imperfect methods.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 1:16-17; Deuteronomy 16:18-20.

Reflection

1. How do we pursue justice through imperfect institutions? 2. How should we treat famous quotations whose source is doubtful?

Chapter 19 - Children of the Desolate

Central idea

A single woman raised a large family and planned a way for women to live free.

Scriptures to revisit

Isaiah 54:1; Psalm 68:5-6; Psalm 113:9; James 1:27.

Reflection

1. How can the church be a family for the solitary? 2. What did you notice about Jean’s shilling a week?

Chapter 20 - Ikpe

Central idea

Old, ill, and in pain, she began again, and was given strength one day at a time.

Scriptures to revisit

2 Corinthians 12:7-10; Isaiah 40:28-31.

Reflection

1. What would it mean for you to “begin” today in weakness? 2. How do you respond to failures like the Ikpe twin?

Chapter 21 - A Poor Exponent of Faith

Central idea

Her faith was real and mixed with doubt, and her Bible was full of honest arguments with God.

Scriptures to revisit

Mark 9:14-29; Romans 8:26; Psalm 42; Luke 17:10.

Reflection

1. Which of her Bible notes spoke to you? 2. Is your faith more honest, or more comfortable?

Chapter 22 - The Time of the Singing of Birds

Central idea

She died among her own people, with her daughters around her, trusting that “not one precious thing can ever be lost.”

Scriptures to revisit

Song of Solomon 2:10-13; John 11:25-26; Psalm 116:15.

Reflection

1. What did her last letters reveal about her? 2. How would you like to be found at the end?

Chapter 23 - Everybody’s Mother

Central idea

Her legacy is both real and mythologised; what remains beyond dispute is her love.

Scriptures to revisit

1 Thessalonians 2:7-12; Mark 14:3-9; 1 Corinthians 13.

Reflection

1. What in her life would you like to imitate, and what would you avoid? 2. To whom are you giving not only the gospel but your own self?

Scriptures to revisit Psalm 82:3-4; Proverbs 31:8-9. Reflection 1. When have you had to accept a partial victory? 2. Are there people around you trapped in a system they cannot break alone? Chapter 10 - Twin-Mothers Central idea She took up children whom their parents had been taught to fear, and learned over time to help families keep them. Scriptures to revisit Psalm 27:10; Isaiah 40:11; Mark 10:13-16. Reflection 1. Who are the “cursed” people in your society? 2. What did Mary come to believe, late in life, about taking twins away from their mothers? Chapter 11 - Laid on the Altar Central idea She wanted to marry, but would not take back a life already given to the people of Okoyong. Scriptures to revisit Romans 12:1-2; Psalm 84:11. Reflection 1. What have you laid on the altar that you are tempted to take back? 2. Can singleness be a calling rather than a loss? Chapter 12 - “The Woman’s God” Central idea Peacemaking in Okoyong took patience, humour, knitting, and a clear line she would not cross. Scriptures to revisit Matthew 5:9; Romans 12:18; Ephesians 2:14. Reflection 1. Where could you be a peacemaker this week? 2. What did you make of her sending the runaway slaves back? Chapter 13 - Consul and Gunboat Central idea She used British power to stop killings, and the story raises hard questions about justice and borrowed authority. Scriptures to revisit Micah 6:8; Romans 13:1-4; Psalm 146:3. Reflection 1. When is it right for Christians to rely on the power of the state? 2. What is lost when justice depends on one strong personality? Chapter 14 - Smallpox and Silence Central idea Years of loss, loneliness, and no visible fruit did not destroy her contentment in God. Scriptures to revisit Habakkuk 3:17-18; 1 Corinthians 3:6-7; Psalm 30:5. Reflection 1. How do you measure success in your service? 2. Can you be “satisfied” without being “triumphant”? Chapter 15 - Not by Might Central idea She walked through the door a punitive expedition had opened, while insisting that the land belonged to its people. Scriptures to revisit Zechariah 4:6; Psalm 20:7. Reflection 1. How should Christians think about missions that followed conquest? 2. What did Wilkie mean by the “peaceable means of the Gospel”? Chapter 16 - First Fruits Central idea After fifteen years she saw baptisms in Okoyong, and at Itu a former slave girl and two boys began a church. Scriptures to revisit John 4:35-38; Psalm 103:1-5; Galatians 3:28. Reflection 1. Whose sowing are you reaping? 2. Who are the unnoticed Manas in your church? Chapter 17 - “I Dare Not Go Back” Central idea Her refusal to retreat strained her relationship with the Church and opened the Enyong Creek. Scriptures to revisit Luke 9:57-62; Hebrews 11:8; Isaiah 30:21. Reflection 1. When is holy stubbornness right, and when is it pride? 2. What would you do if your church told you to go back? Chapter 18 - On the Bench Central idea She sat as a magistrate to get justice for women, in an imperfect court with imperfect methods. Scriptures to revisit Isaiah 1:16-17; Deuteronomy 16:18-20. Reflection 1. How do we pursue justice through imperfect institutions? 2. How should we treat famous quotations whose source is doubtful? Chapter 19 - Children of the Desolate Central idea A single woman raised a large family and planned a way for women to live free. Scriptures to revisit Isaiah 54:1; Psalm 68:5-6; Psalm 113:9; James 1:27. Reflection 1. How can the church be a family for the solitary? 2. What did you notice about Jean’s shilling a week? Chapter 20 - Ikpe Central idea Old, ill, and in pain, she began again, and was given strength one day at a time. Scriptures to revisit 2 Corinthians 12:7-10; Isaiah 40:28-31. Reflection 1. What would it mean for you to “begin” today in weakness? 2. How do you respond to failures like the Ikpe twin? Chapter 21 - A Poor Exponent of Faith Central idea Her faith was real and mixed with doubt, and her Bible was full of honest arguments with God. Scriptures to revisit Mark 9:14-29; Romans 8:26; Psalm 42; Luke 17:10. Reflection 1. Which of her Bible notes spoke to you? 2. Is your faith more honest, or more comfortable? Chapter 22 - The Time of the Singing of Birds Central idea She died among her own people, with her daughters around her, trusting that “not one precious thing can ever be lost.” Scriptures to revisit Song of Solomon 2:10-13; John 11:25-26; Psalm 116:15. Reflection 1. What did her last letters reveal about her? 2. How would you like to be found at the end? Chapter 23 - Everybody’s Mother Central idea Her legacy is both real and mythologised; what remains beyond dispute is her love. Scriptures to revisit 1 Thessalonians 2:7-12; Mark 14:3-9; 1 Corinthians 13. Reflection 1. What in her life would you like to imitate, and what would you avoid? 2. To whom are you giving not only the gospel but your own self?

fields.title: Appendix C: Chronology of the Life and Times of Mary Slessor
fields.body_html:
“So teach us to number our days, That we may get us a heart of wisdom.”

— Psalm 90:12, ASV

The dates below are meant as orientation. Dates confirmed by civil records or official documents are given plainly. Where the sources disagree, the disagreement is noted. Where only Livingstone’s biography gives a date, it is followed unless it is plainly wrong.

1843 - The Invitation

The king and chiefs of the Efik towns of Calabar send a written invitation for missionaries, arranged through a Liverpool surgeon, Dr. Ferguson, and missionaries in Jamaica.

1846 - The Mission Founded

Hope Masterton Waddell leads a party from Jamaica, including Jamaicans of African descent, to found the Calabar mission. It passes to the United Presbyterian Church in 1847.

1848 - Birth

Mary Mitchell Slessor is born on 2 December at Gilcomston, Aberdeen, one of eleven children of Robert Slessor, shoemaker, and Mary Mitchell.

1849-1878 - Laws Against Twin-Killing

Efik rulers of Calabar, with British consuls, agree to ban human sacrifice and the killing of twins (1849-1855), and renew the agreements in 1878. Missionaries rescue twins from 1852.

1859 - Dundee

The family moves to Dundee. By 1861 they are in Dura Street. Mary becomes a half-timer at Baxter Brothers’ works at about eleven.

1860-1870 - Deaths in the Family

Her brother Robert dies of croup (December 1860); her brother William dies of tuberculosis (April 1870); her father dies on 16 September 1870. Her brother John dies in New Zealand soon after emigrating (date uncertain).

1874 - Livingstone’s Death

News of David Livingstone’s death moves her to offer for mission service.

1875 - Offer Accepted

In May she offers herself to the Foreign Mission Board of the United Presbyterian Church, and is accepted as a teacher for Calabar.

1876 - Sailing

After three months in Edinburgh, she sails from Liverpool on the SS Ethiopia on 5 August, and arrives at Calabar in September. (Livingstone’s “Saturday, September 11” cannot be right, since that date was a Monday.) Her salary is sixty pounds a year.

1879-1880 - First Furlough

Home from June 1879; returns in October 1880 to take charge of Old Town.

1882-1883 - Janie

She rescues twin babies, Atim Eso and her brother; the boy is killed by relatives. A tornado wrecks her house at the end of 1882, and she is invalided home in the spring of 1883 with the girl, later baptised Janie.

1883-1885 - At Home

Dundee, then Topsham, Devon, with her invalid sister. Her sister Susan dies in Edinburgh in April 1885. She sails for Calabar in November 1885 and is posted to Creek Town.

1885-1886 - Bereft

Her mother dies at Topsham in December 1885; her sister Janie dies there on 5 March 1886.

1886 - Okoyong Decided

In October the mission council decides to send her to Okoyong.

1888 - Into Okoyong

After a year of negotiation she moves to Ekenge, in Okoyong, on 4 August.

c. 1889 - Etim’s Death

The carpenter Charles Ovens arrives. Etim, son of Chief Edem, dies after an accident; Mary prevents the poison ordeal and the funeral takes place without human sacrifice.

1890-1892 - Engagement and Furlough

Engaged to Charles Morrison late in 1890; the Board declines to transfer him to Okoyong. Furlough from January 1891 to February 1892. Her letter to the Missionary Record contributes to the founding of the Hope Waddell Institute (1895).

1891-1893 - The Protectorate

Sir Claude Macdonald becomes Commissioner and Consul-General (1891). About 1892 he authorises her to run a native court in Okoyong, usually described as making her vice-consul. The Niger Coast Protectorate is named in 1893.

1894-1895 - The Consul Called

She appeals to the Consul in 1894; the chiefs agree to abandon killing at funerals. Macdonald renews the agreement the following year. Mary Kingsley visits Okoyong (probably 1895); Susie is born and later dies.

1896 - Akpap and Smallpox

She moves to Akpap. Four of her children die of an infectious disease. In a smallpox epidemic Ekpenyong and Edem die; she buries Edem herself.

1898 - Furlough

Home with Janie, Mary, Alice, and Maggie. Returns at the end of the year.

1899-1901 - Alone

Three years alone at Akpap. Janie marries Akibo Eyo by native oath on 21 December 1899 (Livingstone’s register; some modern accounts give 12 December). Dan is born about 1900.

1901-1902 - The Aro Expedition

British forces invade the Aro country; Arochukwu falls at the end of December 1901. Mary is brought down to Creek Town for about three months and declines a government house.

1903 - Itu and the First Communion

In January she plants Esien, Effiom, and Mana at Itu. In June she visits Arochukwu with Colonel Montanaro. In August the first communion is held in Okoyong, and Jean, Mana, Iye, Akom, and Esien are baptised.

1904 - The Creek

She settles at Itu in July and opens work along the Enyong Creek at her own expense. Onoyom builds his church at Akani Obio.

1905-1909 - The Native Court

Appointed permanent vice-president of the Itu native court (moved to Ikot Obong) in May 1905. She declines the salary. Resigns in November 1909 (possibly 1910).

1906 - Pioneer

After her refusal to return to Akpap, the Church frees her to work as a pioneer missionary. Arochukwu becomes a mission station.

1907 - Last Visit Home

In Scotland with Dan from May to October.

1908 - Use

She fixes the site of the women’s settlement at Use, near Ikot Obong, and makes it her headquarters.

1910-1912 - Ikpe

She opens work at Ikpe on the upper Enyong Creek. In 1912 she completes thirty-six years’ service, and takes a holiday in the Canary Islands with Jean.

1913 - Honour

Visits Akpap in July, and sees Ma Eme for the last time. Made an Honorary Associate of the Order of the Hospital of St John of Jerusalem, on the recommendation of Sir Frederick Lugard. A new church is opened at Use at Christmas.

1914 - Odoro Ikpe and the War

She builds a house at Odoro Ikpe. News of the war reaches her on 13 August. She falls seriously ill and is carried to Use.

1915 - Death

She dies at Use at 3.30 a.m. on 13 January, aged sixty-six, and is buried in the mission cemetery at Duke Town, Calabar. (The government Gazette gives the place as Itu, the district in which Use lay.)

1918 - Jean

Jean (Janie Annan Slessor) dies at Use in the influenza epidemic.

1956 - A Royal Wreath

Queen Elizabeth II lays a wreath on her grave during a visit to Nigeria.

1997-2009 - The Banknote

Her portrait appears on the Clydesdale Bank ten-pound note.

fields.title: Appendix D: Notes on Sources and Method
fields.body_html:
“it seemed good to me also, having traced the course of all things accurately from the first, to write unto thee in order … that thou mightest know the certainty concerning the things wherein thou wast instructed.”

— Luke 1:3-4, ASV

This appendix explains where the story told in this book comes from, how the sources were weighed, and which popular claims have been corrected. It is written for readers who want to check the story for themselves, and for anyone who will retell it.

Livingstone’s Biography

The main source for Mary Slessor’s life is W. P. Livingstone, Mary Slessor of Calabar: Pioneer Missionary (London: Hodder and Stoughton, 1916). It is now in the public domain. Livingstone had access to a large collection of her letters, and much of his book consists of quotations from them, together with the memories of missionaries, officials, and friends. Almost all the words of Mary Slessor quoted in this book come from Livingstone.

Livingstone was an admirer, writing for the Church that had sent her, and the book has the faults that implies. He sometimes hints that she was more than human. He defends the Church’s committees and the colonial government whenever they are criticised. He gives no account of the violence of the Aro Expedition. His descriptions of African peoples are shaped by the racial theories of his time. This book has not repeated that language except where it was necessary to show how she or her contemporaries thought.

But Livingstone was also candid in ways later popular books were not. He kept her doubts and depressions, her temper and her physical force, her use of laudanum and sleeping draughts, her quarrels with the Church, her dependence on the government, and her failures. Much of the hard material in this book is his. His dates are occasionally wrong. Two are corrected here:

Saturday, September 11. Her arrival is given as “Saturday, September 11” 1876, but 11 September 1876 was a Monday.

1893 for about 1895. Mary Kingsley’s visit is dated 1893. Kingsley’s own account, which speaks of Slessor having been eighteen years in Calabar, points to her second voyage, about 1895.

A caution for anyone checking these pages against the widely used Project Gutenberg e-text of Livingstone: it contains transcription errors that are not in the printed book. It gives “1848” for the chiefs’ invitation (the book has 1843), “April 1888” for her return home with Janie (1883), “June 1908” for her move to Itu (1903), and “18th January” in the government Gazette notice of her death (the book has 13th). Dates in this biography have been checked against a scan of the 1916 edition.

Other Early Sources

Mary Kingsley, Travels in West Africa (1897), contains the fullest independent eyewitness account of Slessor at Okoyong, including the arrival of Iye and her twins, and Kingsley’s assessment of her work. The Missionary Record of the United Presbyterian Church and its successors printed extracts from her letters and reports. Two later popular books were read for this biography, A. J. Bueltmann’s White Queen of the Cannibals and the chapter on Slessor in Mary Rosetta Parkman’s Heroines of Service (1917). Both depend on Livingstone and add invented dialogue, names, and scenes. They have not been used as sources of fact.

Records and Modern Scholarship

Scottish parish and civil registers and census returns, as quoted by family historians, have been used to correct the details of her family. The records of the Congregational church at Topsham, and the 1891 census, document her years in Devon.

This book has drawn, for facts and interpretation, on the modern scholarly literature, especially Jeanette Hardage, Mary Slessor, Everybody’s Mother: The Era and Impact of a Victorian Missionary (2008); Carol Christian and Gladys Plummer, God and One Redhead: Mary Slessor of Calabar (1970), which drew on the memories of her adopted son Daniel; James Buchan, The Expendable Mary Slessor (1980); Elizabeth Robertson, Mary Slessor: The Barefoot Missionary (2001); Esther Breitenbach, “The Making of a Missionary Icon: Mary Slessor as ‘Heroine of Empire’,” Journal of Scottish Historical Studies (2017); Elijah Obinna, “Bridging the Divide: The Legacies of Mary Slessor, ‘Queen’ of Calabar, Nigeria,” Studies in World Christianity (2011); and the entry on Slessor in the Dictionary of African Christian Biography, which quotes the Nigerian church historian Ogbu Kalu. These modern works remain in copyright, and this book has not reproduced them.

Several details of her adopted children’s lives are not in Livingstone and come from these later works and from Sally Ayres’s 2013 study of Janie for the Telling Our Stories project in Exeter: Janie’s Efik name, Atim Eso, and her death in 1918; Daniel Slessor’s 1958 reminiscences and his long life; and the fragments known about Whitie and Asuquo. They have been used with that caution.

Corrections to the Popular Story

Her family. Her mother bore eleven children, not seven. Her father was born in Aberdeen, not Buchan. Her brothers did not die of pneumonia: Robert died of croup, William of tuberculosis, and John in New Zealand.

The killing of twins. Mary Slessor did not end the killing of twins in Nigeria. The Efik rulers of Calabar, with British consuls, had banned it from 1849, and missionaries had rescued twins from 1852. The practice survived in the interior long after her death. Her contribution was to protect twins and their mothers in districts the old agreements did not reach, over decades.

“White Queen.” “The White Queen of Okoyong” was the title of a Scottish book for children, not a name used by the people. They called her Ma, and later Eka kpukpru owo, “Everybody’s Mother.”

Vice-consul. Most modern accounts say she was made vice-consul for Okoyong in 1892. Livingstone describes her position more cautiously as “akin to that of a consular agent.” She was unpaid.

First woman magistrate. The claim that she was the first woman magistrate in the British Empire has not been established.

Paid for her court work. One popular book says the government paid her. She refused all payment.

Never married. The idea that she never married because she was “married to Africa” is interpretation. She was engaged to Charles Morrison, and the engagement ended because the Church would not transfer him to Okoyong, she would not leave it, and his health failed.

Isolation by choice. Her colleagues believed she lived alone on local food by preference. Livingstone shows that she did so at first because she was sending most of her salary home, and was too proud to say so.

The lead-weight gang. The story of the young man who swung a lead weight at her head in Dundee comes from Livingstone alone, without a named witness. Later books added names and details. This book tells it as a remembered story.

Legends. A panther carrying a baby from her tent, and other dramatic scenes and names found in popular books, have no source.

Quotations

“Why should I fear? I am on a Royal Mission.” This saying, often quoted as hers, is not in Livingstone or any source from her lifetime, and the earliest printings found are devotional books of the 2000s. It should not be quoted as hers.

“God and one are always a majority.” Modern biographers report that she wrote these words in one of her Bibles. The saying was not her own; it was an older proverb, in print by the 1860s.

“Christ sent me to preach, not to baptize.” This wording is Paul’s (1 Corinthians 1:17). Livingstone does record her as saying, “Christ sent me to preach the Gospel, and He will look after results.”

“Failed, failed.” This comes from a 1908 newspaper article by a visiting writer. Livingstone says Mary was deliberately “mystifying” the writer, and her own account of the evening suggests a joke. It should not be quoted as her considered verdict on her life.

Dates Still Uncertain

Several dates remain uncertain or disputed: the date of her brother John’s emigration and death; the date of Janie’s marriage (21 or 12 December 1899); the date of her appointment in Okoyong; the year of Mary Kingsley’s visit; and whether she resigned from the Ikot Obong court in November 1909 or a year later. The later lives of several of her adopted children, and of Charles Morrison, are not well documented.

Scripture

All Scripture quotations are from the American Standard Version of 1901, in the public domain, checked against its published text. Where Mary Slessor herself quoted the King James Version, her words are given as she wrote them.

Her contribution was to protect twins and their mothers in districts the old agreements did not reach, over decades. “White Queen.” “The White Queen of Okoyong” was the title of a Scottish book for children, not a name used by the people. They called her Ma, and later Eka kpukpru owo, “Everybody’s Mother.” Vice-consul. Most modern accounts say she was made vice-consul for Okoyong in 1892. Livingstone describes her position more cautiously as “akin to that of a consular agent.” She was unpaid. First woman magistrate. The claim that she was the first woman magistrate in the British Empire has not been established. Paid for her court work. One popular book says the government paid her. She refused all payment. Never married. The idea that she never married because she was “married to Africa” is interpretation. She was engaged to Charles Morrison, and the engagement ended because the Church would not transfer him to Okoyong, she would not leave it, and his health failed. Isolation by choice. Her colleagues believed she lived alone on local food by preference. Livingstone shows that she did so at first because she was sending most of her salary home, and was too proud to say so. The lead-weight gang. The story of the young man who swung a lead weight at her head in Dundee comes from Livingstone alone, without a named witness. Later books added names and details. This book tells it as a remembered story. Legends. A panther carrying a baby from her tent, and other dramatic scenes and names found in popular books, have no source. Quotations “Why should I fear? I am on a Royal Mission.” This saying, often quoted as hers, is not in Livingstone or any source from her lifetime, and the earliest printings found are devotional books of the 2000s. It should not be quoted as hers. “God and one are always a majority.” Modern biographers report that she wrote these words in one of her Bibles. The saying was not her own; it was an older proverb, in print by the 1860s. “Christ sent me to preach, not to baptize.” This wording is Paul’s (1 Corinthians 1:17). Livingstone does record her as saying, “Christ sent me to preach the Gospel, and He will look after results.” “Failed, failed.” This comes from a 1908 newspaper article by a visiting writer. Livingstone says Mary was deliberately “mystifying” the writer, and her own account of the evening suggests a joke. It should not be quoted as her considered verdict on her life. Dates Still Uncertain Several dates remain uncertain or disputed: the date of her brother John’s emigration and death; the date of Janie’s marriage (21 or 12 December 1899); the date of her appointment in Okoyong; the year of Mary Kingsley’s visit; and whether she resigned from the Ikot Obong court in November 1909 or a year later. The later lives of several of her adopted children, and of Charles Morrison, are not well documented. Scripture All Scripture quotations are from the American Standard Version of 1901, in the public domain, checked against its published text. Where Mary Slessor herself quoted the King James Version, her words are given as she wrote them.
